Singh; Vishnupriya Raghavan; R. Raman; Nripendra P. Rana; Spyridon Samothrakis; Jak Spencer; K. Tamilmani; Annie Tubadji; Paul Walton; Michael D. Williams
abstract: As far back as the industrial revolution, significant development in technical innovation has succeeded in transforming numerous manual tasks and processes that had been in existence for decades where humans had reached the limits of physical capacity. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers this same transformative potential for the augmentation and potential replacement of human tasks and activities within a wide range of industrial, intellectual and social applications. The pace of change for this new AI technological age is staggering, with new breakthroughs in algorithmic machine learning and autonomous decision-making, engendering new opportunities for continued innovation. The impact of AI could be significant, with industries ranging from: finance, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, supply chain, logistics and utilities, all potentially disrupted by the onset of AI technologies. The study brings together the collective insight from a number of leading expert contributors to highlight the significant opportunities, realistic assessment of impact, challenges and potential research agenda posed by the rapid emergence of AI within a number of domains: business and management, government, public sector, and science and technology. This research offers significant and timely insight to AI technology and its impact on the future of industry and society in general, whilst recognising the societal and industrial influence on pace and direction of AI development.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Automation in Finance and Accounting Processes
authors: Kumru Alagur; Asegul Hulus
abstract: <jats:p>AI and automation are reshaping finance and accounting by changing how financial information is captured, processed, analysed, controlled and communicated. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation and generative AI increasingly support activities ranging from invoice processing and reconciliation to auditing, fraud detection, forecasting and management decision support. These technologies can improve speed, consistency and analytical capacity, but their value depends on data quality, system integration, professional oversight and responsible governance. Their adoption also creates material risks concerning confidentiality, cybersecurity, explainability, bias, accountability and workforce readiness. This chapter provides a critical synthesis of AI and automation across the finance and accounting lifecycle. It explains the principal technologies, examines operational and strategic applications, evaluates organisational benefits and limitations, and develops a governance-oriented view of future intelligent finance.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Automation in Finance and Accounting Processes
authors: Mehmet Akif Altunay
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines artificial intelligence and automation in finance and accounting through a process-design lens. It argues that automation suitability depends primarily on process structure, data quality, exception intensity, control requirements, and the extent of human judgment rather than on software choice alone. Business Process Management (BPM) is used to organize process discovery, as-is mapping, suitability assessment, redesign, implementation, and monitoring. Within this framework, robotic process automation (RPA), natural language processing (NLP), and machine learning (ML) are matched to structured transactions, unstructured financial text, and anomaly detection. Implementation evidence from financial close, consolidation, and audit analytics is classified by source type to distinguish technology capability from organizational use. The chapter concludes with two author-developed diagnostic tools: a five-stage Intelligent Accounting Maturity Model and a Governance Checklist for CFOs, controllers, and internal auditors.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning for Microscopy
authors: Joshua Stuckner
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article examines how deep learning (DL) and artificial intelligence (AI) models extract meaningful structural information from microscopy images. It explains image representation and feature extraction in microscopy. The article provides a detailed discussion on representation learning in image analysis. It presents encoder architectures for vision. The article describes full models and applications in materials science microscopy. It also examines emerging opportunities in microscopy image analysis, focusing on self-driving microscopes, foundation models, multi-image and multimodal learning, federated learning, and model interpretability.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence and digital capabilities on firm performance in the digital economy: A mediation model of business model innovation
authors: Xuan Hung Nguyen; Duc Nhat Anh Nguyen; Linh Chi Nguyen; Thi Hong Nhung Tran
abstract: <jats:p>PURPOSE: This study examines the relationships among AI capabilities, digital capabilities, and firm performance in the digital economy, with a particular focus on the mediating role of business model innovation. Despite substantial investments in AI and digital technologies, many firms struggle to translate these advancements into improved performance, often because they lack effective organizational mechanisms to convert technological potential into value. By addressing this issue, the study seeks to contribute to the literature by empirically examining business model innovation as a mediating mechanism linking technological capabilities and firm performance. METHODOLOGY: The study employs a quantitative approach using survey data collected from 286 firms in Vietnam. The data are analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine the direct and indirect relationships between AI capabilities, digital capabilities, and firm performance, with business model innovation as a mediating variable. FINDINGS: Both AI and digital capabilities are positively associated with firm performance, directly and indirectly through business model innovation. In addition, both AI capabilities and digital capabilities are positively associated with business model innovation, with the estimated coefficient for AI capabilities being numerically larger than that for digital capabilities. Business model innovation is also positively associated with firm performance, suggesting its role as a mediating mechanism linking technological capabilities to firm performance. IMPLICATIONS: This study contributes to the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory by highlighting the role of business model innovation as a mechanism through which technological capabilities are associated with firm performance. The findings suggest that firms may benefit from aligning AI capabilities and digital capabilities with business model innovation to enhance performance outcomes. ORIGINALITY & VALUE: This study provides empirical evidence on the mediating role of business model innovation in the relationship between AI capabilities, digital capabilities, and firm performance. By integrating the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, it offers a more comprehensive understanding of how technological capabilities are associated with firm performance in the digital economy.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning in agri-food systems: A comprehensive review of technological frontiers, socio-ethical barriers, and future roadmaps
authors: Mohsen Abbod; Naser Safaie; Safaa N. Hussein
abstract: <jats:p>Economic prosperity and human health heavily depend upon a stable food supply chain in agriculture. This essential network is fortified by modern farming techniques through boosted productivity and durability. Novel approaches are necessitated by the escalating worldwide need for nutrition. Consequently, agricultural practices and food security are positioned to be profoundly transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). In this review, cutting-edge applications of AI in agriculture were investigated. A specific focus on precision crop management, optimized resource use, climate-resilient farming systems, and advanced livestock monitoring was undertaken. The article highlights how operational efficiency and decision-making are enhanced across all phases of any agricultural production system, such as planting, irrigation, pest control, harvesting, aquaculture, food safety, and post-harvest handling. This efficiency is attributed to the massive, heterogeneous datasets usually evaluated by AI frameworks to produce practical conclusions. Despite this promise, critical hurdles must be resolved to unlock the complete capabilities of AI in agriculture. Such barriers involve restricted access to high-quality data alongside computational limitations in developing regions. Serious ethical concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and labor market disruptions also demand immediate attention. The deliberate mitigation of these complications is required to unlock the full potentials of AI for building a sustainable, fair, and food-secure tomorrow.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in MBSE Processes
authors: Ritu; G. SudhaAnanthi; Md Gauhar Hasnain; Pammi Kumari; Biswo Ranjan Mishra; T. C. Manjunath
abstract: <jats:p>AI-Driven Model Development is a major paradigm shift in modern systems engineering, software-intensive engineering, manufacturing, digital-twin development, and Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) where AI is increasingly playing a key role in model creation and evolution by accelerating, automating, analyzing and improving the engineering model. Typical model development is often based on the practice of building models manually based on domain knowledge, requirements, design assumptions, system relationships, and operational information by experienced engineers. Manual modeling can be time-consuming, hard to maintain, and can be prone to inconsistencies as systems become increasingly complex, multidisciplinary, software-intensive, interconnected, and adaptive. AI approaches aim to complement this by leveraging AI tools such as machine learning, NLP, generative AI, knowledge graphs, computer vision, optimization algorithms, and intelligent agents to support engineers throughout the modeling lifecycle.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence and SDGs, a friend or foe: A perspective of Kantianism
authors: Elizabeth Lee; Tan Seng Teck; Mohd Rushidi; Chee How Liau; Pradeep Sonar
abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Humans have keen interests with artificial objects. We consume food and drinks containing artificial coloring while FIFA approves the use of artificial turf for football matches. However, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has gripped the world with its radical changes, triggering not only physical, but also philosophical implications. In this paper, we explore the impact of AI on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and pose the question of whether the human centrality of the SDGs could diminish with the introduction of AI. Drawing on Kant’s concept of universalism and categorical imperatives, we argue that AI cannot safeguard intergenerational justice or meet Kant’s definition of a rational being. This paper presents a brief yet significant perspective, emphasizing the need for caution when integrating AI into the implementation of the SDGs, particularly concerning policy design.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Organized Cyber-Crime
authors: Hossam Nabil Elshenraki
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how organized cybercrime has changed in the age of artificial intelligence, using Southeast Asian scam networks as a case study. It explaining that cybercrime became wider and isolated; it is well-organized business that operates on a global scale. platforms and illegal financial systems support this economy of cybercrime. Using a qualitative analysis, the research finds that these networks combine cybercrime with human trafficking and money-related crimes in organized hierarchical systems like legitimate businesses. AI plays a key role by enabling automation, scalability, and targeted Scam through phishing, data analysis, deepfakes, and automated communication, also the role of cybercrime ecosystems and Cybercrime-as-a-Service models allow for globalization and outsourcing. So, cybercrime became more industrialized, making it harder for law enforcement to keep up. which requires to enhance international cooperation and improved investigative skills.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence and the future of work: Human-AI symbiosis in organizational decision making
authors: M. H. Jarrahi
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has penetrated many organizational processes, resulting in a growing fear that smart machines will soon replace many humans in decision making. To provide a more proactive and pragmatic perspective, this article highlights the complementarity of humans and AI and examines how each can bring their own strength in organizational decision-making processes typically characterized by uncertainty, complexity, and equivocality. With a greater computational information processing capacity and an analytical approach, AI can extend humans’ cognition when addressing complexity, whereas humans can still offer a more holistic, intuitive approach in dealing with uncertainty and equivocality in organizational decision making. This premise mirrors the idea of intelligence augmentation, which states that AI systems should be designed with the intention of augmenting, not replacing, human contributions.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Persistence of Moral Hazards
authors: Adil Boutfssi; Fatima Zahra Ouariach; Soufiane Ouariach
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming credit risk assessment in SME financing. While AI enhances ex-ante evaluation by expanding the information base and improving borrower differentiation, it does not fundamentally change the nature of credit risk. Drawing on theories of information asymmetry and credit rationing, the chapter argues that a significant share of risk remains linked to ex-post borrower behavior, which is difficult to observe and predict, particularly in SMEs where managerial quality and human capital are critical. AI strengthens initial screening but cannot eliminate uncertainty. The chapter therefore introduces the concept of smart credit rationing, whereby AI refines rather than removes rationing by enabling more precise borrower selection and segmentation. Using Morocco as an illustrative case, it shows that the benefits of AI remain constrained by limited data availability, informality, and the continued importance of banking relationships, highlighting the need to combine algorithmic tools with human judgment in risk assessment.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Applications for Precision Living
authors: Öznur Suçeken; Ensar Arif Sağbaş; Osman Özkaraca
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence assisted image analysis is important for translating precision health and personalized well-being into dental practice. This chapter examines panoramic and periapical radiographs, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), intraoral and cephalometric images and digital surface models in terms of anatomical information, clinical applications and limitations. AI methods are reviewed from conventional machine learning and convolutional neural networks to object detection, segmentation, transformer-based architectures, self-supervised learning and foundation models. Applications including caries, endodontic and periodontal disease detection, orthodontic analysis, oral lesion screening, implant planning and tooth numbering are evaluated based on datasets, model architectures, validation strategies and performance metrics. The chapter emphasizes that high performance does not necessarily ensure clinical utility. External validation, calibration, prevention of data leakage, human oversight, privacy and equitable performance are essential for trustworthy AI in dentistry.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Information to Improve Agricultural and Climate Change Mitigation Among Farmers in Lagos State
authors: Eric Msughter Aondover
abstract: <jats:p>This study examined Artificial Intelligence (AI) based information to improve agricultural and climate change mitigation among farmers in Lagos State, Nigeria. The study aimed to examine the level of adoption of AI based information system among farmers in Lagos State, Nigeria, identify the challenges faced by farmers in Lagos State, Nigeria when implementing AI technology for agriculture practice and climate change mitigation, and examine the effectiveness of AI based information system in improving crop yield and productivity among farmers in Lagos State. The constructivist research design approach was adopted, which informed the choice of in-depth interviews. A purposive sampling technique was employed to generate data from the participants. A semi-structured face-to-face interview method was used for the study as an instrument of data collection. Thematic analysis was used in analyzing the data using NVivo</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Spatiotemporal Clustering for Identifying Homogeneous Climatic Zones in West Java
authors: Oktaviana Indriani; Eka Ardhianto
abstract: <jats:p>Homogeneous Climatic Zones (ZOM) support operational seasonal services in Indonesia, particularly across regions where rainfall changes sharply over short distances. This study evaluates a climatic regionalization framework that combines Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) and Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) using BMKG gridded rainfall data across West Java at approximately 5 km resolution for the 1991–2020 period. Each of the 1,214 grid cells was represented by a 36-dasarian climatological rainfall profile. A search across 360 hyperparameter combinations yielded 324 executable configurations, followed by spatial absorption of transition grids and layered evaluation using the Silhouette Score, Heterogeneity Index (HI), and operational tractability. Scenario 60 (n_neighbors = 5, min_dist = 0.01, min_cluster_size = 10, min_samples = 5) produced 54 initial zones with a Silhouette Score of 0.5633 and an HI of 7.239, compared with an HI of 8.464 for the 41-zone operational baseline. Subsequent spatial refinement produced a corrected final map containing 50 sequential ZOM. Distinguishing the evaluation metrics of the 54-zone candidate stage from the 50-zone cartographic structure of the spatial refinement stage clarifies the analytical sequence and supports a more precise interpretation of cluster quality, climatic homogeneity, and final zone boundaries.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence capability: Conceptualization, measurement calibration, and empirical study on its impact on organizational creativity and firm performance
authors: P. Mikalef; Manjul Gupta
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has been heralded by many as the next source of business value. Grounded on the resource-based theory of the firm and on recent work on AI at the organizational context, this study (1) identifies the AI-specific resources that jointly create an AI capability and provides a definition, (2) develops an instrument to capture the AI capability of the firms, and (3) examines the relationship between an AI capability and organizational creativity and performance. Findings empirically support the suggested theoretical framework and corresponding instrument and provide evidence that an AI capability results in increased organizational creativity and performance.

title: Artificial-Intelligence-Driven Corrosion Analysis Used by the U.S. Army
authors: Thomas Considine; Robert Jensen; James Snyder; John Kelley; Nicholas Josselyn; Biao Yin; Elke Rundensteiner; Ziming Zhang
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article presents an introduction to corrosion testing. It discusses the use of artificial intelligence in corrosion assessment. The article describes the traditional corrosion testing process and corrosion image data processing. It explains baseline nonexpert human corrosion assessment performance. The article provides an overview of deep learning classification models and corrosion segmentation. It also provides a vision for outdoor corrosion assessment and domain adaptation. The article also presents an integrated analytics web dashboard and iOS application.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence-driven three-dimensional modeling of biliary strictures using magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography for quantitative assessment and stent planning
authors: Ji-Hun Chun; Jin-Woo Hong; Jong-Uk Hou; Kyong Joo Lee; Da Hae Park; Hye Won Cha; Se Woo Park; Seon Jeong Min; Wooyoung Yu
abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) depicts the biliary tree three-dimensionally but is used mainly for qualitative diagnosis rather than quantitative procedural planning. Endoscopic drainage of biliary strictures, particularly hilar and intrahepatic lesions, depends on an accurate understanding of stricture location, length, ductal curvature, and branch involvement, yet MRCP information is seldom converted into reproducible measurements. Artificial intelligence (AI) may bridge this gap by transforming diagnostic imaging into quantitative, procedure-oriented geometry. We hypothesized that MRCP-derived biliary anatomy could be converted into an interpretable three-dimensional (3D) model supporting biliary stricture assessment and candidate stent-planning geometry.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To develop and evaluate a proof-of-concept AI workflow that converts MRCP-derived biliary anatomy into a quantitative 3D stricture model.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This single-center study analyzed 384 MRCP examinations (242 controls and 142 with suspected biliary stricture). Expert-corrected masks and 3D annotations were used to train or evaluate modules for region-of-interest localization, bile duct segmentation, projection-based multi-view classification, synthetic morphology restoration, and centerline-guided tubular mesh generation. Binary stricture detection and three-class severity classification were assessed with patient-level cross-validation after excluding unavailable or task-incompatible labels. Segmentation and restoration were evaluated using Dice scores.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In 380 evaluable cases, projection-based binary classification achieved an accuracy of 0.9770, balanced accuracy of 0.9721, macro F1 score of 0.9749, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of 0.9953. Three-class severity classification was less accurate (accuracy 0.8711), indicating that severity stratification is more difficult than binary detection. The best Dice score was 0.8113 in the segmentation comparison and 0.8944 in the extended normal-group experiment. In synthetic restoration, DiceFocalLoss produced the highest Dice score (0.7531), and lesion weighting improved reconstruction of interrupted duct segments. In anatomically simple cases, restored geometry was converted into a centerline-guided tubular mesh, whereas complex hilar or intrahepatic branching remained vulnerable to projection overlap.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>MRCP-based AI modeling of biliary strictures is feasible for quantitative 3D assessment and exploratory stent-planning geometry. External validation and prospective clinical evaluation are required before procedural implementation.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Green Prodrug Design and Sustainable Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
authors: Shakuntala Santosh Chopade; Shreeya Patil; Yash Dhoka; Samiha Rahul Kulkarni
abstract: <jats:p>The growing need for sustainable and energy-efficient production of drugs has led to the combination of green chemistry practices and artificial intelligence (AI) during the development of drugs. Prodrugs, which have proven effective at improving pharmacokinetics and targeted drug delivery, could particularly benefit from the current developments. The present review explains the benefits associated with using solvent-free synthesis, biodegradable reagents, energy-efficient techniques, and reduced waste during the production of prodrugs. At the same time, an assessment of how AI and machine learning can be used to optimize the process of prodrug design and predict pharmacokinetics is provided. The potential for sustainable and cost-effective pharmaceutical development through the combination of environmentally friendly methods and modeling tools will be explained.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence, ESG Reporting, and Corporate Accountability
authors: Gazala Sharif; Insha Hamid
abstract: <jats:p>The rise of digitalization and AI has transformed corporate accountability, pushing ESG reporting from a voluntary exercise to a governance imperative. Yet greenwashing, carbon misreporting, and deceptive sustainability disclosures have surged, exposing the limits of traditional forensic accounting. This chapter examines how Machine Learning, Natural Language Processing, predictive analytics, blockchain, and robotic process automation can be integrated into forensic accounting to detect ESG fraud. A conceptual AI-Enabled Sustainable Forensic Governance framework is proposed, combining technological innovation with legal compliance and ESG accountability</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation
authors: T. Babina; A. Fedyk; A. He; James Hodson
abstract: We study the use and economic impact of AI technologies among U.S. firms. We propose a new measure of firm-level AI investments, using a unique combination of worker resume and job postings datasets. Our measure reveals a stark increase in AI investments across sectors. AI-investing firms see increased growth in sales, employment, and market valuations. This growth comes primarily through increased product innovation, reflected in trademarks, product patents, and product updates. AI-powered growth concentrates among ex-ante larger firms, leading to higher industry concentration and reinforcing winner-take-most dynamics. Our results highlight that new technologies can contribute to growth through product innovation.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Enhancing Resilience
authors: N. Rane; S. Choudhary; Jayesh Rane
abstract: In an increasingly complex and unpredictable world, resilience-the ability to withstand and recover from adverse conditions is essential across various sectors. This research paper investigates the transformative potential of artificial intelligence (AI) in enhancing resilience across multiple domains. We explore how AI technology can be utilized to develop resilient infrastructure, providing advanced predictive maintenance and real-time monitoring capabilities that ensure robustness and longevity. The study examines the role of AI in improving disaster response, offering rapid data analysis and decision-making support to enhance emergency management outcomes. In climate change, AI-driven strategies are assessed for their effectiveness in fostering climate resilience, including predictive modeling of extreme weather events and optimizing resource allocation. The paper also discusses AI applications in healthcare resilience, such as enhancing diagnostics, patient care, and operational efficiency during crises. Business continuity and crisis management are examined, highlighting AI's capability to anticipate disruptions and maintain operational stability. The paper emphasizes the importance of strengthening cybersecurity resilience using AI to detect and mitigate threats proactively. AI's role in enhancing community and social resilience is analysed, particularly in supporting vulnerable populations and fostering social cohesion. Additionally, we explored AI-powered solutions for urban resilience, focusing on smart cities and sustainable development. The study also covers AI's contributions to environmental and ecological resilience, resilient supply chain management, and resilience in the hospitality and tourism industry. Finally, we investigated AI's potential in fostering psychological resilience, providing personalized mental health support and stress management tools. Through these diverse applications, the paper underscores AI's critical role in building a resilient future.

title: Artificial intelligence for imaging-based detection of gallbladder cancer: A systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis
authors: Jia-Yun Zhu; Hao Lin; Jing-Wei Zhao; Zi-Yi Yang
abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Early diagnosis of gallbladder cancer (GBC) remains challenging because malignant lesions can mimic benign inflammatory or polypoid gallbladder disease. Artificial intelligence (AI) imaging models have been reported for ultrasound-, computed tomography-, and radiomics-based diagnosis; however, the evidence often conflates clinical validation cohorts with image-level model-development experiments.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To evaluate the diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) of AI-assisted imaging for detecting GBC and to distinguish patient-level clinical validation evidence from technical benchmark studies.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 and the PRISMA-DTA extension. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed with a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 framework tailored to AI imaging. The primary synthesis used a Reitsma bivariate random-effects model. Robustness was examined using a generalized linear mixed model following the meta-analysis of DTA implementation, leave-one-out analyses, exclusion of internal validation, modality/model subgroup analyses, and Hartung-Knapp random-effects diagnostic odds ratio analysis.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Of 485 records, 32 studies met the inclusion criteria and five patient-level validation datasets suitable for 2 × 2 reconstruction, including four independent, external, or prospective validation settings and one internal non-training validation cohort, comprising 615 patients/cases, were meta-analyzed. In these five validation datasets, AI-assisted imaging was associated with pooled sensitivity of 0.888 (95% confidence interval: 0.834-0.927) and moderate-to-high specificity of 0.838 (95% confidence interval: 0.717-0.914), with a summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of 0.921. Prediction intervals were wider for specificity than sensitivity (0.529-0.959 vs  0.785-0.946), indicating less stable false-positive performance across settings. Because only five datasets were available, these estimates should be interpreted as preliminary and context-dependent.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AI-assisted imaging showed promising sensitivity and moderate-to-high specificity for GBC detection in a small set of patient-level validation datasets. However, the quantitative evidence rested on only five datasets, included heterogeneous modalities, target contrasts, models, thresholds, and validation designs, and showed greater uncertainty for specificity than sensitivity. Current evidence is most consistent with AI as a triage or second-reader adjunct requiring further external and prospective validation, not as a stand-alone diagnostic replacement.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence for Intergenerational Innovation: Knowledge Transfer, Legacy, and Sustainable Futures
authors: Julia M. Puaschunder
abstract: <jats:p>The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents one of the most transformative technological advancements of the 21st century. AI is rapidly transforming human societies and their knowledge transfer systems. While AI’s immediate impacts are currently widely monitored and studied on a broad basis, its implications for the intergenerational compound in society remain underexplored. This chapter investigates how AI innovations reshape intergenerational knowledge creation, transfer, and preservation. Drawing on theories of knowledge management, organizational learning, and intergenerational equity, the chapter conceptualizes AI as an agent of innovation and cultural continuity. Case studies on climate change mitigation, sustainable development, and digital legacy highlight the potentials and risks of AI in fostering intergenerational knowledge flows. The analysis underscores both the benefits of AI – such as enhanced cultural transmission, digital legacies, and novel forms of intergenerational literacy – as well as the costs, including sustainability concerns, cultural homogenization, and ethical dilemmas. The research outcomes cover the use of AI for intergenerational transfers. Positive potentials but also potential downfalls of AI in society in regard to the intergenerational compound will be discussed. The chapter concludes with recommendations for responsible governance frameworks that ensure AI-driven intergenerational knowledge transfer remains equitable, sustainable, and inclusive.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence for literature reviews: opportunities and challenges
authors: Francisco Bolaños; Angelo Salatino; Francesco Osborne; E. Motta
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Systematic Literature Reviews (SLRs). A SLR is a rigorous and organised methodology that assesses and integrates prior research on a given topic. Numerous tools have been developed to assist and partially automate the SLR process. The increasing role of AI in this field shows great potential in providing more effective support for researchers, moving towards the semi-automatic creation of literature reviews. Our study focuses on how AI techniques are applied in the semi-automation of SLRs, specifically in the screening and extraction phases. We examine 21 leading SLR tools using a framework that combines 23 traditional features with 11 AI features. We also analyse 11 recent tools that leverage large language models for searching the literature and assisting academic writing. Finally, the paper discusses current trends in the field, outlines key research challenges, and suggests directions for future research. We highlight three primary research challenges: integrating advanced AI solutions, such as large language models and knowledge graphs, improving usability, and developing a standardised evaluation framework. We also propose best practices to ensure more robust evaluations in terms of performance, usability, and transparency. Overall, this review offers a detailed overview of AI-enhanced SLR tools for researchers and practitioners, providing a foundation for the development of next-generation AI solutions in this field.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Materials Science and Engineering
abstract:
<jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly changing how materials are discovered, designed, characterized, processed, and qualified. Applied appropriately, these tools can compress development timelines, extract insight from large and complex datasets, and enable real-time control of manufacturing processes; applied without adequate data, validation, or domain expertise, they can produce unreliable results. That is why understanding both the capabilities and the limitations of AI and ML is so critical for materials scientists and engineers. Volume 26 provides foundational coverage of AI and ML concepts and emerging trends, along with industrial perspectives on materials data analytics. It then surveys the core tools and methods, including unsupervised and supervised learning, generative AI for materials discovery and design, uncertainty quantification, ML for mechanics, data-driven and parametrically upscaled constitutive modeling, and the data infrastructure required to support materials and manufacturing AI.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Industry use of AI and ML is addressed through discussion of the opportunities and challenges of deployment in metallurgical industries, applications in steel design and processing, AI for manufacturing quality, and human-AI collaboration for building trustworthy expertise in materials engineering systems. The Volume also covers AI and deep learning for microscopy and microstructure analysis, including industrial and defense perspectives, experimental data generation, and ground truth assignment. Coverage of materials design and computational simulation includes informatics workflows, surrogate models for molecular simulation data, co-optimization of materials and parts, and the linking of materials properties with larger-scale product models. AI-enabled simulation, optimization, and digital manufacturing are examined, with emphasis on surrogate models for simulation-driven optimization, advanced electronic materials, and digital twins and yield prediction for semiconductor packaging. Lastly, the Volume addresses autonomous, real-time materials synthesis and fabrication, including best practices for autonomous laboratories, accelerated scale-up of manufacturing processes, and ML applied to battery design and manufacturing.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence for Multi-Disease Eye Diagnosis
authors: Harsh Kumar; Aijaz Ahmad Chopan; Zubair Fayaz; Makinder Kour
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning are revolutionizing ophthalmology by automating the diagnosis of conditions like diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, macular degeneration, and cataracts from medical imagery. This article provides a comprehensive review of AI-driven, multi-disease eye diagnosis, exploring key imaging modalities, public datasets, advanced network architectures, and the vital role of explainable AI (XAI). It features a practical case study using the Ocular Disease Intelligent Recognition (ODIR) dataset to compare the classification performance of ResNet50, EfficientNetB3, ConvNeXt, and Vision Transformers (ViT). Finally, the review addresses critical hurdles to clinical adoption—such as dataset limitations, class imbalance, and model generalization—while mapping out future frontiers like multimodal learning, federated learning, and vision-language foundation models.</jats:p>

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR THE REAL WORLD
authors: T. Davenport; Rajeev Ronanki

title: Artificial intelligence for waste management in smart cities: a review
authors: Bingbing Fang; Jiacheng Yu; Zhong-Hao Chen; A. Osman; M. Farghali; I. Ihara; E. Hamza; D. Rooney; P. Yap
abstract: The rising amount of waste generated worldwide is inducing issues of pollution, waste management, and recycling, calling for new strategies to improve the waste ecosystem, such as the use of artificial intelligence. Here, we review the application of artificial intelligence in waste-to-energy, smart bins, waste-sorting robots, waste generation models, waste monitoring and tracking, plastic pyrolysis, distinguishing fossil and modern materials, logistics, disposal, illegal dumping, resource recovery, smart cities, process efficiency, cost savings, and improving public health. Using artificial intelligence in waste logistics can reduce transportation distance by up to 36.8%, cost savings by up to 13.35%, and time savings by up to 28.22%. Artificial intelligence allows for identifying and sorting waste with an accuracy ranging from 72.8 to 99.95%. Artificial intelligence combined with chemical analysis improves waste pyrolysis, carbon emission estimation, and energy conversion. We also explain how efficiency can be increased and costs can be reduced by artificial intelligence in waste management systems for smart cities.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Christian Religious Education: Reconstructing Teachers' Roles in Developing Students' Digital Literacy and Critical Thinking
authors: Yunardi Kristian Zega; Andrea Elfata Ratulangi; Ryanto Adilang; Stefanus Meo Nekin; Sharon Long Saging
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of artificial intelligence, particularly generative artificial intelligence, is transforming how students access information and learn, including in Christian Religious Education. While artificial intelligence offers opportunities for personalized learning and richer engagement with biblical and theological content, it also raises concerns about inaccurate or biased religious content, over-reliance, weakened critical thinking, ethical risks, and the erosion of the relational and spiritual dimensions of faith formation. This study aims to reconstruct the roles of Christian religious education teachers in artificial intelligence-based learning so that it strengthens students' digital literacy and critical thinking within Christ-centered formation. A qualitative design using library research and conceptual analysis was employed. A corpus of 52 sources, comprising peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2026 together with seminal works and policy documents regardless of publication year, was selected through explicit criteria and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and conceptual synthesis. The synthesis indicates that artificial intelligence shifts Christian Religious Education from content transmission toward guided inquiry; that its opportunities are realized only when its risks are mediated pedagogically and ethically; that teachers' roles must be reconstructed as learning facilitators, spiritual mentors, and digital ethics guides; and that digital literacy and critical thinking can be integrated through the evaluation and theological discernment of machine-generated content. The study proposes the Christ-Centered EEDE Framework (exploring, evaluating, discerning, and embodying), which integrates these elements into a teacher-guided learning cycle and offers a testable foundation for ensuring that artificial intelligence serves, rather than replaces, faith formation.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence in education: Addressing ethical challenges in K-12 settings
authors: Selin Akgun; Christine Greenhow
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of study that combines the applications of machine learning, algorithm productions, and natural language processing. Applications of AI transform the tools of education. AI has a variety of educational applications, such as personalized learning platforms to promote students’ learning, automated assessment systems to aid teachers, and facial recognition systems to generate insights about learners’ behaviors. Despite the potential benefits of AI to support students’ learning experiences and teachers’ practices, the ethical and societal drawbacks of these systems are rarely fully considered in K-12 educational contexts. The ethical challenges of AI in education must be identified and introduced to teachers and students. To address these issues, this paper (1) briefly defines AI through the concepts of machine learning and algorithms; (2) introduces applications of AI in educational settings and benefits of AI systems to support students’ learning processes; (3) describes ethical challenges and dilemmas of using AI in education; and (4) addresses the teaching and understanding of AI by providing recommended instructional resources from two providers—i.e., the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s (MIT) Media Lab and Code.org. The article aims to help practitioners reap the benefits and navigate ethical challenges of integrating AI in K-12 classrooms, while also introducing instructional resources that teachers can use to advance K-12 students’ understanding of AI and ethics.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Review
authors: Lijia Chen; Ping-Ping Chen; Zhijian Lin
abstract: The purpose of this study was to assess the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on education. Premised on a narrative and framework for assessing AI identified from a preliminary analysis, the scope of the study was limited to the application and effects of AI in administration, instruction, and learning. A qualitative research approach, leveraging the use of literature review as a research design and approach was used and effectively facilitated the realization of the study purpose. Artificial intelligence is a field of study and the resulting innovations and developments that have culminated in computers, machines, and other artifacts having human-like intelligence characterized by cognitive abilities, learning, adaptability, and decision-making capabilities. The study ascertained that AI has extensively been adopted and used in education, particularly by education institutions, in different forms. AI initially took the form of computer and computer related technologies, transitioning to web-based and online intelligent education systems, and ultimately with the use of embedded computer systems, together with other technologies, the use of humanoid robots and web-based chatbots to perform instructors’ duties and functions independently or with instructors. Using these platforms, instructors have been able to perform different administrative functions, such as reviewing and grading students’ assignments more effectively and efficiently, and achieve higher quality in their teaching activities. On the other hand, because the systems leverage machine learning and adaptability, curriculum and content has been customized and personalized in line with students’ needs, which has fostered uptake and retention, thereby improving learners experience and overall quality of learning.

title: Artificial intelligence in education: A systematic literature review
authors: Shan Wang; Fang Wang; Zhenzhou Zhu; Jing-Xuan Wang; T. Trần; Zhao Du

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN EDUCATION: CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
authors: S. A. Vakhabova; V. Kosulin; Ana Zizaeva
abstract: The article analyzes the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in the transformation of the educational sphere in the context of achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The purpose of the study is a comprehensive assessment of the potential benefits and risks of introducing AI into education in terms of their impact on sustainable development. Tasks include: identification of key AI application opportunities to improve the quality, accessibility, and inclusivity of education (SDG 4); analysis of issues related to ethics, algorithm bias, digital inequality, and the need for retraining; assessment of the impact of AI on the formation of competencies necessary for a sustainable future. The results show the significant potential of AI in personalizing learning, automating routine tasks, and providing access to knowledge, but also reveal serious risks of exacerbating social inequality (SDG 10) and ethical dilemmas. The scientific novelty lies in the systematic consideration of the relationship between the introduction of AI in education and the achievement of the SDGs, offering a balanced view of the challenges and opportunities. The practical significance lies in the formulation of recommendations for policy makers, educators, and developers on responsible and sustainability-oriented implementation of AI in educational systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence In Education: Promises and Implications for Teaching and Learning
authors: W. Holmes; Maya Bialik; Charles K. Fadel

title: Artificial intelligence in environmental monitoring: in-depth analysis
authors: Emran Alotaibi; Nadia Nassif
abstract: This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric and in-depth analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications in environmental monitoring, based on 4762 publications from 1991 to 2024. The research highlights a notable increase in publications and citations since 2010, with China, the United States, and India emerging as leading contributors. Key areas of research include air and water quality monitoring, climate change modeling, biodiversity assessment, and disaster management. The integration of AI with emerging technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and remote sensing, has significantly expanded real-time environmental monitoring capabilities and data-driven decision-making. In-depth analysis reveals advancements in AI/ML methodologies, including novel algorithms for soil mapping, land-cover classification, flood susceptibility modeling, and remote sensing image analysis. Notable applications include enhanced air quality predictions, water quality assessments, climate impact forecasting, and automated wildlife monitoring using AI-driven image recognition. Challenges such as the “black-box” nature of AI models, the need for high-quality data in resource-constrained regions, and the complexity of real-time disaster management are also addressed. The study highlights ongoing efforts to develop explainable AI (XAI) models, which aim to improve model transparency and trust in critical environmental applications. Future research directions emphasize improving data quality and availability, fostering interdisciplinary collaborations across environmental and computer sciences, and addressing ethical considerations in AI-driven environmental management. These findings underscore the transformative potential of AI and ML technologies for sustainable environmental management, offering valuable insights for researchers and policymakers in addressing global environmental challenges.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Greenwashing Detection
authors: Ashlin Merin Roy; S. Anjana; Rinu Jayaprakash; Roshna Varghese; Terezin Mathew
abstract: <jats:p>Corporate sustainability reporting has increased over the last ten years. Companies have become more proficient in crafting environmental reports that satisfy regulators, customers and investors, while lacking true dedication to improvement. Greenwashing has expanded to exploitative marketing, becoming a critical issue for corporate governance, for which traditional audit and forensic accounting techniques were not addressed. This chapter integrates artificial intelligence, especially natural language processing and machine learning, with forensic accounting skills and offers the most credible solution. The three disciplines of machine learning, computational linguistics, and forensic accounting have proven more effective when incorporated together rather than utilised independently. The discussion looks into greenwashing definitions, typological difficulties, and the regulatory environment in the EU, UK, US, and growing international frameworks, combined with a three-tier detection architecture that is both practically applicable and theoretically validated.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: past, present and future
authors: F. Jiang; Yong Jiang; H. Zhi; Yi Dong; Hao Li; Sufeng Ma; Yi-Long Wang; Q. Dong; Haipeng Shen; Y. Wang
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) aims to mimic human cognitive functions. It is bringing a paradigm shift to healthcare, powered by increasing availability of healthcare data and rapid progress of analytics techniques. We survey the current status of AI applications in healthcare and discuss its future. AI can be applied to various types of healthcare data (structured and unstructured). Popular AI techniques include machine learning methods for structured data, such as the classical support vector machine and neural network, and the modern deep learning, as well as natural language processing for unstructured data. Major disease areas that use AI tools include cancer, neurology and cardiology. We then review in more details the AI applications in stroke, in the three major areas of early detection and diagnosis, treatment, as well as outcome prediction and prognosis evaluation. We conclude with discussion about pioneer AI systems, such as IBM Watson, and hurdles for real-life deployment of AI.

title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming the practice of medicine
authors: J. Bajwa; Usman Munir; Aditya V. Nori; Bryan Williams
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is a powerful and disruptive area of computer science, with the potential to fundamentally transform the practice of medicine and the delivery of healthcare. In this review article, we outline recent breakthroughs in the application of AI in healthcare, describe a roadmap to building effective, reliable and safe AI systems, and discuss the possible future direction of AI augmented healthcare systems.

title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
authors: Helen Crompton; D. Burke
abstract: This systematic review provides unique findings with an up-to-date examination of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education (HE) from 2016 to 2022. Using PRISMA principles and protocol, 138 articles were identified for a full examination. Using a priori, and grounded coding, the data from the 138 articles were extracted, analyzed, and coded. The findings of this study show that in 2021 and 2022, publications rose nearly two to three times the number of previous years. With this rapid rise in the number of AIEd HE publications, new trends have emerged. The findings show that research was conducted in six of the seven continents of the world. The trend has shifted from the US to China leading in the number of publications. Another new trend is in the researcher affiliation as prior studies showed a lack of researchers from departments of education. This has now changed to be the most dominant department. Undergraduate students were the most studied students at 72%. Similar to the findings of other studies, language learning was the most common subject domain. This included writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. In examination of who the AIEd was intended for 72% of the studies focused on students, 17% instructors, and 11% managers. In answering the overarching question of how AIEd was used in HE, grounded coding was used. Five usage codes emerged from the data: (1) Assessment/Evaluation, (2) Predicting, (3) AI Assistant, (4) Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), and (5) Managing Student Learning. This systematic review revealed gaps in the literature to be used as a springboard for future researchers, including new tools, such as Chat GPT. A systematic review examining AIEd in higher education (HE) up to the end of 2022. Unique findings in the switch from US to China in the most studies published. A two to threefold increase in studies published in 2021 and 2022 to prior years. AIEd was used for: Assessment/Evaluation, Predicting, AI Assistant, Intelligent Tutoring System, and Managing Student Learning.

title: Artificial intelligence in plant breeding.
authors: M. Farooq; Shang Gao; Muhammad Adeel Hassan; Zhang-Ping Huang; Awais Rasheed; S. Hearne; B. Prasanna; Xin-Hai Li; Hui-Hui Li
abstract: Harnessing cutting-edge technologies to enhance crop productivity is a pivotal goal in modern plant breeding. Artificial intelligence (AI) is renowned for its prowess in big data analysis and pattern recognition, and is revolutionizing numerous scientific domains including plant breeding. We explore the wider potential of AI tools in various facets of breeding, including data collection, unlocking genetic diversity within genebanks, and bridging the genotype-phenotype gap to facilitate crop breeding. This will enable the development of crop cultivars tailored to the projected future environments. Moreover, AI tools also hold promise for refining crop traits by improving the precision of gene-editing systems and predicting the potential effects of gene variants on plant phenotypes. Leveraging AI-enabled precision breeding can augment the efficiency of breeding programs and holds promise for optimizing cropping systems at the grassroots level. This entails identifying optimal inter-cropping and crop-rotation models to enhance agricultural sustainability and productivity in the field.

title: Artificial intelligence in radiology
authors: A. Hosny; C. Parmar; John Quackenbush; L. Schwartz; H. Aerts
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, particularly deep learning, have demonstrated remarkable progress in image-recognition tasks. Methods ranging from convolutional neural networks to variational autoencoders have found myriad applications in the medical image analysis field, propelling it forward at a rapid pace. Historically, in radiology practice, trained physicians visually assessed medical images for the detection, characterization and monitoring of diseases. AI methods excel at automatically recognizing complex patterns in imaging data and providing quantitative, rather than qualitative, assessments of radiographic characteristics. In this Opinion article, we establish a general understanding of AI methods, particularly those pertaining to image-based tasks. We explore how these methods could impact multiple facets of radiology, with a general focus on applications in oncology, and demonstrate ways in which these methods are advancing the field. Finally, we discuss the challenges facing clinical implementation and provide our perspective on how the domain could be advanced. In this Opinion article, Hosny et al. discuss the application of artificial intelligence to image-based tasks in the field of radiology and consider the advantages and challenges of its clinical implementation.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Service
authors: Ming-Hui Huang; R. Rust
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping service by performing various tasks, constituting a major source of innovation, yet threatening human jobs. We develop a theory of AI job replacement to address this double-edged impact. The theory specifies four intelligences required for service tasks—mechanical, analytical, intuitive, and empathetic—and lays out the way firms should decide between humans and machines for accomplishing those tasks. AI is developing in a predictable order, with mechanical mostly preceding analytical, analytical mostly preceding intuitive, and intuitive mostly preceding empathetic intelligence. The theory asserts that AI job replacement occurs fundamentally at the task level, rather than the job level, and for “lower” (easier for AI) intelligence tasks first. AI first replaces some of a service job’s tasks, a transition stage seen as augmentation, and then progresses to replace human labor entirely when it has the ability to take over all of a job’s tasks. The progression of AI task replacement from lower to higher intelligences results in predictable shifts over time in the relative importance of the intelligences for service employees. An important implication from our theory is that analytical skills will become less important, as AI takes over more analytical tasks, giving the “softer” intuitive and empathetic skills even more importance for service employees. Eventually, AI will be capable of performing even the intuitive and empathetic tasks, which enables innovative ways of human–machine integration for providing service but also results in a fundamental threat for human employment.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Shaping Psychological Behavior Towards Over-the-Top Platforms
authors: Vaishali; Nilesh Arora
abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Over-The-Top (OTT) platforms has fundamentally altered the digital entertainment environment by enabling personalized content delivery and influencing consumer psychological behavior. This study looks at how AI-driven consumer behavior on OTT platforms has changed over time, what the current trends are, and how research is done on this topic by looking at important keywords, changing research themes, and global collaboration networks. This study employs a quantitative method using bibliometric data from the Scopus database to find 382 different publications that were published between 2015 and 2026. In addition, data was also analyzed using several other advanced analytical programs like Biblioshiny (RStudio), VOSviewer, which were then used for performance measuring analysis, maps for co-occurrences, thematic mapping and trending analysis of topics, enabling the completion of systematic evaluations of the entire area of research.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Smart Cities—Applications, Barriers, and Future Directions: A Review
authors: R. Wolniak; K. Stecuła
abstract: As urbanization continues to pose new challenges for cities around the world, the concept of smart cities is a promising solution, with artificial intelligence (AI) playing a central role in this transformation. This paper presents a literature review of AI solutions applied in smart cities, focusing on its six main areas: smart mobility, smart environment, smart governance, smart living, smart economy, and smart people. The analysis covers publications from 2021 to 2024 available on Scopus. This paper examines the application of AI in each area and identifies barriers, advances, and future directions. The authors set the following goals of the analysis: (1) to identify solutions and applications using artificial intelligence in smart cities; (2) to identify the barriers to implementation of artificial intelligence in smart cities; and (3) to explore directions of the usage of artificial intelligence in smart cities.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Knowledge Diversity, and Sociopreneurship on Hospital Performance: Moderating Role of Service Quality in Central Java
authors: Tri Darsono; Tulus Haryono; Ahmad Ikhwan Setiawan; Mugi Harsono; Heri Wijayanto; Rohwiyati Rohwiyati
abstract: <jats:p>Objective: Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) Theory, this study examines how technological interventions and medical staff capabilities interact to influence healthcare service performance in hospitals. Specifically, the study seeks to understand the relationships among these key resources within the context of healthcare service delivery. Method: A quantitative survey was conducted using descriptive statistics from Likert-scale questionnaires (1-5) distributed online to 102 respondents, including medical staff, managers, and administrators at type B hospitals in Central Java. Given the research objectives of prediction, exploration, or structural theory development, data were processed using SmartPLS 4.0. The independent variables in this study were Implementing Artificial Intelligence (AI), Knowledge Diversity, and Sociopreneur, while the dependent variable was Organizational Performance, with Service Quality as a moderating variable. Results: The findings indicate that each variable has a good level of validity (LF ≥ 0.70) and significance; the evaluation of discriminant validity using the Fornell-Larcker criterion, cross-loadings, and HTMT met the requirements; the f-test result of 0.037 (high) indicates the significant moderating effect of service quality on the relationship between AI implementation and organizational performance. Based on the model fit assessment, the influence of AI implementation has an R² of 0.787% (strong); the SRMR is 0.093, which is < 0.10, indicating that the model fits the empirical data well. Novelty: The implementation of AI can improve operational efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and data management, thereby enhancing quality and service in hospitals. The follow-up to this research is the need to consider the infrastructure and medical staff expertise when implementing AI in type B hospitals in Central Java to improve healthcare services.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy for Technology Education
authors: Karin Stolpe; Jonas Hallström
abstract: The interest in artificial intelligence (AI) in education has erupted during the last few years, primarily due to technological advances in AI. It is therefore argued that students should learn about AI, although it is debated exactly how it should be applied in education. AI literacy has been suggested as a way of defining competencies for students to acquire to meet a future everyday-and working life with AI. This study argues that researchers and educators need a framework for integrating AI literacy into technological literacy, where the latter is viewed as a multiliteracy. This study thus aims to critically analyse and discuss different components of AI literacy found in the literature in relation to technological literacy. The data consists of five AI literacy frameworks related to three traditions of technological knowledge: technical skills, technological scientific knowledge, and socio-ethical technical understanding. The results show that AI literacy for technology education emphasises technological scientific knowledge (e.g., knowledge about what AI is, how to recognise AI, and systems thinking) and socio-ethical technical understanding (e.g., AI ethics and the role of humans in AI). Technical skills such as programming competencies also appear but are less emphasised. Implications for technology education are also discussed, and a framework for AI literacy for technology education is suggested.
