abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
authors: Malak Gamal El-Din; Yasser Shoukry; Salma Elmalaki
abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
authors: Sion Israel Sion
abstract: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice

title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
authors: Alina Avanesyan; Alexey Boldyrev; Liqun Deng; Denis Derkach; Mary Godunova; Mikhail Hushchyn; Dmitry Ilvovsky; Irina Knyazeva; Irina Piontkovskaya; Dmitry Polubotko; Fedor Ratnikov; Ekaterina Trofimova; Zhenhe Zhang
abstract: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

title: Benchmarking Reasoning Reliability,Prior_Evidence Contrast,and Spectral Discrimination in Remote-Sensing Geological Image Interpretation
authors: Jun Wang; Fengpeng Li; Wei Han; Yuxuan Li; Tianjin Huang; Jining Yan; Sheng Wang; Kan Sun; Lizhe Wang
abstract: Reliable lithology interpretation requires accurate geological recognition and reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Although Multimodal Large Language Models show promise in remote sensing, their reliability in geological interpretation remains unclear. We introduce HyGeoBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 10,000 questions based on hyperspectral imagery across three dimensions: reasoning reliability, prior_evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination. It covers ten task types, with both multiple-choice and open-ended response formats. Integrating hyperspectral satellite imagery with geological annotations and verified evidence, HyGeoBench examines reasoning errors, conflicts between geological priors and visual evidence, and cross-band inconsistencies. Evaluations reveal limitations in fine-grained recognition and evidence-grounded interpretation. To address these challenges, we propose HyGeoAgent, a tool-augmented framework integrating region observation, text knowledge retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis through adaptive tool use. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, improving geological image interpretation across diagnostic dimensions.

title: Better Retrieval, Not Better Binding: Pretraining Exposure in Egocentric Video Retrieval
authors: Yuqi Guo; Michael Wray
abstract: Video-language models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on video-text retrieval and are increasingly used for egocentric video understanding. Yet, despite gains in zero-shot retrieval, they have shown limitations in compositional understanding, and it remains unclear whether they understand compositional relationships between verbs and nouns. In this work, we introduce Ego-ExBind, a compositional diagnostic protocol for analyzing pretraining exposure and verb-noun binding in egocentric video-text retrieval. Ego-ExBind consists of an Exposure Ledger built from the EgoClip pretraining corpus used by EgoVLPv2, which defines Seen Composition, Unseen Composition, and Unseen Atom splits for EPIC-KITCHENS-100 multi-instance retrieval (MIR). We further probe noun and verb binding channels through controlled noun-swap and verb-swap negatives. We find that zero-shot retrieval is positively associated with pair exposure within seen compositions, even after controlling for the marginal frequencies of verbs and nouns. However, higher pair exposure is associated with larger noun-swap margins and slightly smaller verb-swap margins. This asymmetry motivates us to test whether exposure reweighting can improve retrieval with little change in the measured swap margins. To isolate the effect of exposure input, we keep the trained checkpoint fixed and replace only the exposure input at inference. We demonstrate that this exposure reweighting can improve video-text retrieval without stronger verb-noun compositional understanding, and that the gain depends on the correct sample-level exposure correspondence. By separating exposure-driven retrieval gains from verb-noun binding, Ego-ExBind provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating whether future improvements in egocentric MIR reflect compositional understanding rather than pretraining familiarity.

title: Beyond Additive Composition: Interventional Modeling of State-Dependent Cross-Degradation Responses for Composite Image Restoration
authors: Zongda Tang; Jie Feng; Wenda Zhao; Mingtao Feng; Yuping Liang; Ronghua Shang; Weisheng Dong
abstract: Composite image restoration aims to recover images corrupted by multiple coexisting degradations. Existing methods predominantly decompose composite corruptions into individual factors, relying on these isolated priors to guide restoration. However, coexisting degradations are inherently interdependent: the manifestation of one degradation dynamically shifts with the states of others, inducing non-additive interactions that factor-wise paradigms fail to capture. To bridge this gap, we formulate state-dependent cross-degradation responses and propose PROBE, an interventional framework that explicitly models how coexisting degradations influence one another. Specifically, we first construct unified degradation axes by aligning visual and textual degraded-clean offsets. Along these axes, a calibrated coordinate head estimates current degradation states, while bidirectional feature perturbations are injected to probe cross-coordinate responses under the current states. Contrasting these responses with corresponding intensity-matched single-degradation references quantifies intrinsic non-additive deviations, allowing the resulting response descriptors and state coordinates to jointly guide restoration. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce SCD-15, a new benchmark covering all 15 nonempty combinations of four degradation factors at three severity levels. Experiments demonstrate that PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CDD-11, AWMM-100K, and SCD-15 composite restoration datasets using a compact model with modest GPU memory requirements.

title: Beyond Alignment: Whitening Geometry, Profile Synthesis, and Heterogeneous Ensembles for Cross-Environment WiFi Action Recognition
authors: Lei Wang
abstract: Cross-environment deployment is the central obstacle to practical WiFi sensing: a pipeline reaching 0.89+ top-1 in its training environments collapses to 0.408 under Leave-One-Domain-Out (LODO) evaluation with only K-shot labels. A ceiling analysis shows the collapse is not an alignment problem: the action signal is strong across seen environments (about 0.89 K10), environment identity is decodable from the encoder (0.965), and the failure concentrates in the encoder's extrapolation to the novel environment. A pre-registered falsification chain confirms that "align the domains" methods--training-time alignment, readout-level prototype alignment, adversarial confusion, and covariance/subspace alignment (CORAL -3.8pp, subspace -8.3pp)--degrade performance, and that source-domain statistics anti-correlate with cross-environment contribution. The effective levers lie elsewhere; we combine them into Dec-H: (i) closed-form source within-class whitening, provably re-geometrizing the readout's L2 regularization (+8.6pp, zero cost); (ii) profile-mixing augmentation (+1.0pp); (iii) few-shot adaptation with alternating whitening refit (+1.5pp; fixed preconditioners are 20/20 negative); (iv) heterogeneous decision ensembles (+1.7pp); homogeneous scaling and source-weighted stacking are saturated or harmful. Dec-H reaches 0.560 K10 (0.812 K40), +15.2pp over the baseline, consistent across all four environments and seeds; all thirteen configurations were pre-registered with frozen criteria.

title: Beyond Appearance: Evidence-Guided Programmatic 3D Scene Reconstruction with Agentic Lighting Reasoning
authors: Zeting Luo; Yifan Li; Shuai Yang
abstract: Image-to-code methods for 3D scene reconstruction produce executable code that generates editable digital content and supports visual simulation. However, existing methods primarily rely on appearance similarity, which provides limited guidance for distinguishing errors in geometry, materials, and illumination. Light shapes scene appearance through its interactions with geometry and materials, influencing shading, cast shadows, and reflections. We therefore present LightHarness, a VLM-based agentic framework that incorporates explicit lighting reasoning into iterative scene reconstruction. To be specific, we leverage complementary geometric, intrinsic, and illumination cues to jointly refine scene structure and appearance, and propose Lighting Reasoning Memory to maintain light-source hypotheses, which supports evidence, and revision history throughout iterations. Together, they support reasoning about partially visible and unseen sources, with evidence-guided verification directing subsequent revisions. Our framework reconstructs explicit scenes through coherent reasoning about geometry, materials, and illumination without additional training or differentiable rendering. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior image-to-code reconstruction accuracy under challenging shadows and complex illumination, further supporting downstream scene editing, object insertion, and versatile relighting.

title: Beyond Backtests
authors: N. Sathyanarayana; V. Lava Kumar; Varanasi Rahul; G. Laxmana Rao; Madireddi S. S. V. Sri Kumar
abstract: <jats:p>Machine learning is now central to investment research, yet many strategies that perform well in historical backtests fail after deployment in live markets. This disconnect arises primarily from evaluation practices that prioritise predictive accuracy while overlooking transaction costs, liquidity constraints, execution uncertainty, strategy capacity, and governance requirements. This chapter argues that evaluation should be treated as an end-to-end discipline aligned with real market and regulatory conditions rather than as a purely statistical exercise. It presents a structured framework for assessing machine learning–based investment strategies using robust backtesting methodologies, leakage-aware validation, cost and capacity modelling, and sim-to-live transition mechanisms such as paper trading and post-trade attribution. By shifting focus from model accuracy to tradable, scalable, and auditable performance, the chapter offers practical guidance for responsible deployment in regulated financial environments.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Classical Limits
authors: Jaya Saxena; Sonali Patil
abstract: <jats:p>Classical computation is becoming increasingly inadequate for financial analytics: Monte Carlo risk engines, high-dimensional portfolios and data-hungry learning models have their limits when speed and fidelity are required in the face of regulation and competition. The literature is scattered between physics and finance and enthusiasm often exceeds evidence, but quantum computing holds the promise of principled speedups on these workloads. This chapter connects peer-reviewed research (2018–2025) on quantum algorithms for pricing, risk measurement, portfolio optimization and machine learning, with the post-quantum security transition, while addressing the lack of a synthesis and a critical analysis from the finance point of view.The insights dampen the urgency of their immediate expectations and help to find a path towards potential long-term value, providing an evidence-based agenda for researchers, risk managers and policy makers who are on the journey to the quantum transition.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Eduardo Reck Miranda; Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost
abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

title: Beyond Covers and Titles: Evidence-First Ranking for Robust Cold-Start Recommendation
authors: Fuyi Wang; Yuxin Cao; Yifan Liao; Renyang Liu; Lin Li; Wei Song
abstract: Short-video platforms rank new uploads before anyone has watched them, using content towers that read a video's cover, title and frames. Existing attacks on content-aware recommenders perturb pixels or features and ignore platform re-encoding, and existing defenses train against norm-bounded perturbations that neither match real edits nor preserve recommendation quality. We show with REAP, a realizable attack through {a simulated platform channel (H.264 transcoding, rescaling, cropping and JPEG)}, that packaging edits raise a cold video by 32.0 rank-percentile points in unrelated audiences. We then observe that cold-start ranking does not need the packaging at all: a tower that sees only the video body ranks cold items best. Building on this, we propose Evidence-First Ranking (EFR), which scores cold videos from their body, admits packaging only through a support-gated residual bounded by $γ$, and merges cold and warm rankings by rank percentile, yielding an exact certificate against any packaging edit. On MicroLens-100K, EFR cuts the attack gain by 81% and raises cold-start Recall@100 from 0.1133 to 0.170, while keeping the merged NDCG@10 within 4% of the undefended system.

title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
authors: Rafsan Jany; Md Rafid Islam; Mohammad Fahim Islam; Hafiz Abdur Rahman
abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

title: Beyond Easy Clients: Difficulty- and Improvement-Aware Aggregation for Federated Reinforcement Learning in Robot Navigation
authors: Ye Lin Tun; Chu Myaet Thwal; Eui-Nam Huh; Choong Seon Hong
abstract: Federated reinforcement learning enables a fleet of robots to jointly learn a shared navigation policy without exchanging raw experience. In practice, however, the robots rarely operate in the same conditions: an open aisle is far easier to navigate than a cluttered room, and takes less learning to master. Standard federated aggregation rules ignore this. Uniform averaging weights every client equally, whether or not it is still learning, and weighting by episode return is worse, since easy environments permit high returns by construction. Both failures stem from what we call the \emph{plateau problem}: once a client masters its environment, its updates carry little new information even though its reported return remains high. We propose \emph{FedDIA}, which scores each client by how much its local training improves the global model it received, amplified by the difficulty of its environment. Difficulty is inferred from the model's own performance, without requiring any description of the environment. Both signals are measured against the global model, so they are comparable across clients. On a mapless navigation task with eight heterogeneous clients, FedDIA reaches a mean success rate of $75.5\%$ across training and held-out environments, against $68.7\%$ for the strongest federated baseline. Its advantage holds when the models are transferred to hand-authored warehouse and living-space layouts, or when one of the clients is defective.

title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering
authors: Jiatong Ma; Yuchen Liu; Longteng Guo; Yichen Yuan; Yuze Wu; Dongze Hao; Ru Zhen; Yanhao Zhang; Haonan Lu; Jing Liu
abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Anastasiia Lukianenko; Yash J. Patel; Nurbolat Kenbayev; Vedran Dunjko
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Shuaidi Wang; Zhuocheng Gong; Xuejie Liu; Jianguo Li; Yu Zhang
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

title: Beyond Resemblance: Image Fusion Reimagined
authors: Hao Zhang; Yumin Huang; Linfeng Tang; Junjun Jiang; Jiayi Ma
abstract: Image fusion often lacks ground-truth fused images, forcing existing deep methods to indirectly define fusion objectives by requiring the fused image to simultaneously resemble multiple source images. However, the distinct imaging characteristics of different modalities can impose competing constraints on the fused result, potentially limiting the effective integration of their complementary information. To address this long-standing challenge facing the image fusion community, we propose ApexFuse, a novel generative image fusion paradigm that moves beyond source-resemblance constraints toward learning a general distribution of high-quality scene representations. Specifically, we develop a human-LMM-in-the-loop pipeline that leverages large multimodal generative models and iterative human feedback to translate abstract fusion objectives into reliable visual references, thereby defining the target distribution of ideal fusion outcomes. Through target-distribution-guided adaptation, we transfer the rich generative priors of pretrained FLUX to image fusion, enabling high-quality scene reconstruction conditioned on multimodal observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ApexFuse harmoniously integrates salient thermal targets, natural colors, and fine textures, achieving superior visual quality as well as semantic segmentation and object detection performance over previous source-resemblance methods. Moreover, ApexFuse exhibits remarkable cross-task generalization, extending from infrared-visible fusion to multi-exposure fusion, multi-focus fusion, and visible-depth fusion without additional fine-tuning.

title: Beyond Restoration: Content-Degradation Factor Unfolding for Real-World Concealed Object Segmentation
authors: Rihan Zhang; Fengyang Xiao; Yuhan Chen; Sina Farsiu
abstract: Reliable visual perception under degradation requires distinguishing task-relevant content from degradation-induced variations, especially in concealed object segmentation (COS), where foreground cues are inherently weak. The central challenge is not merely improving visibility, but identifying reliable content evidence amid degradation-induced variations. RGB-space segmentation often entangles content and degradation cues, while restoration-based methods primarily focus on image recovery and task interaction. This motivates explicit factorization to distinguish content evidence from degradation effects and assess its reliability. Retinex provides a spatially aligned basis for this separation but remains illumination-centric. We therefore extend it to content-degradation formation with task-asymmetric factor roles. The Factor Unfolding Network (FUN) uses the content factor R as the sole source of direct semantic evidence for segmentation, while the degradation factor L captures degradation-related variations and generates a spatial reliability map to calibrate this evidence. A unified energy couples observation formation with reliability-weighted foreground-background separation, and its alternating updates yield a coarse-to-fine network without clean-image supervision. In this way, FUN factorizes degradation for perception rather than removing it. Extensive experiments across clean and degraded conditions and diverse segmentation tasks demonstrate robust performance and generalization. Code will be released.

title: Beyond the Alphabet: Communicating in Ancient Greece, c. 1200–500 BCE
authors: Heidelberg University

title: Beyond the Sink Token: Sink-Guided Key Editing in Vision-Language Models
authors: Hui Zhu; Saleh Zare Zade; Rafi Ibn Sultan; Xiangyu Zhou; Dongxiao Zhu
abstract: In vision-language models (VLMs), a few sink tokens attract a disproportionate share of attention. While previous studies have examined why these tokens attract attention, we investigate how the sink-key direction affects attention to image and question tokens. Across four probed VLMs, boosting the magnitude of positive sink-aligned components increases attention on average, whereas boosting negative components decreases it; these responses persist through later layers. This identifies the native sink key as a reference for controlling attention beyond its own position. Motivated by this finding, we propose SHRINK, a training-free method that partially reduces sink-aligned components across visible keys during generation. On nine benchmarks under sampled reasoning, it improves mean accuracy by 5.1 and 2.7 percentage points on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B, with smaller gains on the other two main models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Gemma-3-4B. Beyond SHRINK, rescaling sink-aligned key components can replace the attention operations of two existing attention-steering methods, GIFT and ACG, with comparable accuracy on hallucination benchmarks.

title: Beyond the Storefront
authors: Soumi Ghosh; Ritik Raj
abstract: <jats:p>Storefronts are no longer just flat; they are becoming more three-dimensional and avatar-driven. This chapter presents an AI-Avatar-based Personalization for Metaverse Environments (AAPME) framework that combines conversational, visual, and behavioral cues to enable personalized and immersive shopping experiences with an AI avatar. Drawing on a critical synthesis of the metaverse-marketing, avatar-theory, and AI-personalization literatures, the chapter directly compares AAPME with three existing metaverse-retail frameworks and identifies two implementation-level algorithms, evaluates the computational scalability and deployment implications (including edge-computing and latency-hiding demands), and follows illustrative single-session walkthroughs of AAPME in two complementary retail verticals, before proposing a concrete pilot-validation and offline-benchmarking plan and a three-part evaluation protocol.</jats:p>

title: Beyond the Virtual Concierge
authors: Muhammad Usman Tariq
abstract: <jats:p>Integrating metaverse technologies has significantly changed business, bringing together immersive virtual spaces and smart chatbots. Modern AI chatbots are not simply tools for interacting with customers; they have become assistants and even virtual friends that help users navigate complex customer experiences. Such chatbots may provide advice, help immediately when needed, explore products with customers, and engage them both offline and online. As a result, new opportunities emerge to improve customer experience. At the same time, problems arise around the trustworthiness, privacy, transparency, identity, and ethical use of personal data. To use the metaverse's potential responsibly, one should consider not only the latest technology but also proper design that protects customers' freedom and enables relationship-building. This chapter addresses integrating AI chatbots into the customer experience in the metaverse and proposes an approach to designing chat systems properly.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
authors: BoHao Chen
abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

title: Bias-Only Training Dynamics in ReLU Networks
authors: Shreyas Chaudhari; Jose M. F. Moura
abstract: Neural networks with randomly initialized, fixed weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, yet the dynamics of bias-only training remain largely unexplored. We study these dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks through activation codes, the binary patterns of active neurons that partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions. We show that the gradients with respect to the biases depend on each input only through its activation code, and hence the training dynamics can be characterized with these codes. In particular, as long as the activation codes remain fixed, training reduces to a linear least-squares problem with the codes as features. Training can then be understood as a sequence of least-squares problems, with transitions occurring when neurons change their activation states. We show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as the network widens, and the training dynamics approach those of linear least squares on the initial activation codes in the infinite-width limit. Our experiments support these theoretical findings, showing that while activation switches can noticeably affect training in narrower networks, their relative frequency and the associated changes in the dynamics diminish as the width increases.

title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models
authors: Zhengbo Zhou; Dooman Arefan; Shandong Wu
abstract: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.

title: Bionavigator Personalized Learning Package In General Biology 2
authors: Joriane Lorenz Deocampo
abstract: Personalized learning has the potential to address differences in learners' readiness and pace, yet evidence on its use in senior high school biology remains limited in local public-school contexts. This study evaluated BioNavigator, a personalized learning package in General Biology 2, and examined learners' and the teacher-implementer's experiences during its use. A quasi-experimental nonequivalent control-group design with a qualitative component was employed among 66 Grade 12 Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics learners at Zarraga National High School. Thirty-three learners received BioNavigator-based instruction, while 33 received the lecture method. A validated 60-item General Biology 2 Understanding Assessment with a Kuder-Richardson 20 reliability coefficient of 0.825 was administered as pre-test and post-test. Descriptive statistics, Mann-Whitney U tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and thematic analysis were used. The groups had comparable pre-test performance (U = 461.150, p = .878). Both groups improved significantly, but the BioNavigator group obtained a higher post-test mean (M = 49.45, SD = 2.36) than the lecture group (M = 47.12, SD = 3.67), with a significant between-group difference (U = 308.000, p = .033). Qualitative findings indicated that the package stimulated curiosity, deepened conceptual understanding, strengthened scientific reasoning, supported mastery and confidence, and helped learners connect science with societal issues. The teacher-implementer likewise observed stronger participation and independent learning, while recommending differentiated supports and more collaboration. BioNavigator therefore offers a promising supplementary approach for improving understanding in General Biology 2 when implemented with structured teacher guidance, differentiated materials, and collaborative learning opportunities.

title: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation
authors: Deepali Singh; Deepesh Parpani; Aviral Gupta
abstract: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM \cite{b1}, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.

title: Bits, Not Boxes: Label-Free Layer Selection for Visual Localization in VLMs
authors: Haisheng Fu; Gexin Huang; Haikai Zhao; Jie Liang; Zhenman Fang; Jingning Han; Xiaoxiao Li
abstract: Attention maps cheaply show where a vision-language model (VLM) looks, but attention sinks make them unreliable for localization. Contrasting the question with a generic prompt suppresses sinks, yet only some layers localize the queried object. Existing methods find these layers with box annotations or fixed rules. We show that attention itself can identify them. A question changes how much a head attends to the image and where this attention goes. The two effects separate exactly, and the second, measured in bits on unlabeled questions, indicates which layers localize. WhereBits turns these where-to-look bits into a layer prior and combines it with per-head contrastive scores. Its three design constants were fixed once on labeled COCO data, and a new model or resolution needs only unlabeled questions. Across eight VLMs, WhereBits matches the pointing accuracy of box-tuned layers on COCO and RefCOCO and ranks target tokens better. This advantage holds on a held-out model family and at higher resolutions. Its COCO pointing accuracy is 0.72, against 0.22 for mean attention. In training-free zoom-in, its crops raise V* accuracy by 6.0 points under forced-choice evaluation.

title: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
authors: Liang Yue; Eric A. Vance
abstract: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels. A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

title: Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technology in Accounting and Auditing Transparency, Automation, and Continuous Assurance
authors: Partap Singh; Farmida; Aditi Madaan; Deepak Ranjan; Bhawna Garg
abstract: <jats:p>Abstract- Block-chain are revolutionizing the accounting and auditing process by enhancing transparency, reliability, automation, and continuous assurance. This chapter explores the potential impact of block-chain as a solution to improve the quality of accounting information, automate the process by using smart contracts and improve the quality of corporate reporting through intelligence. The study employs a descriptive research design based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) Theory, and the Resource-Based View (RBV) and involves 380 accounting, auditing, finance and academic professionals who participated in a survey. Although implementation and adoption of block-chain faces some hurdles, including implementation costs, lack of technical expertise, uncertainty regarding regulations, and scalability issues, the findings show that the potential benefits of block-chain are considered to be significant in enhancing the traceability of transactions, financial reporting quality, audit efficiency and corporate governance.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain-Based Secure Data Integrity Models
authors: Sachin Jain; Vishal Jain; Abu Bakar Abdul Hamid; Golnoosh Manteghi
abstract: <jats:p>In traditional centralized systems, only a select few administrators or trusted third parties have the authority to change records, despite the fact that data integrity is essential for reliable decision-making in healthcare, banking, supply chains, and public administration. This chapter uses a narrative review approach while also developing a conceptual framework to explain the benefits and drawbacks of blockchain technology in relation to data integrity. Integrity is defined differently from authenticity, privacy, authenticity, provenance, confidentiality, availability, and data accuracy. A formal threat model is also provided, which differentiates between risks that distributed ledgers can address and those that cannot. Following Chapters expands on this study by proposing LB-DIAF, a six-layer model that includes a taxonomy of blockchain-based integrity and trust models, data origin, off-chain storage, on-chain anchoring, consensus, smart-contract logic, and governance.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain-Enabled Data Security and Trust Frameworks for Digital Microbiology Workflows
authors: Ayesha Riaz; Iqra Farooq; Afsheen Mansoor; Emaan Mansoor; Ezza Mansoor; Efrah Mansoor; Adnan Afzal; Hafiz Aamir Ali Kharl; Muhammad Nouman Arif; Amina Arif; Imrana Amir; Saima Nousheen
abstract: <jats:p>The workflows of digital microbiology are becoming more and more based on the production of large-scale data, automation, and collaboration between institutions, which brings up critical issues regarding the security, integrity, and trust of data. The blockchain technology provides a decentralized and non-tamper able system, which can be used to overcome these issues because of the ability to share data securely, transparent provenance history, and automated control through smart contracts. This chapter discusses how blockchain-based systems of data security and trust in digital microbiology can be used and applied, and the various areas of implementation in clinical, environmental, and industrial settings. Ethical, legal, and regulatory issues are also mentioned, as well as future outlooks of integrating blockchain into a robust and reliable digital microbiology ecosystem.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain-Enabled Evidence Preservation
authors: Varanasi Rahul; B. N. Manoj; H. V. Sathyananda Swamy; V. K. Pavithra; Noor Zaiba; Manjari Pandey
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the role of blockchain technology in enhancing evidence preservation by ensuring integrity, transparency, chain of custody, and legal trust. With the growing use of digital evidence in criminal investigations, corporate compliance, intellectual property protection, and cross-border litigation, traditional centralized evidence management systems face challenges such as tampering, cyberattacks, unauthorized access, and loss of authenticity. Blockchain provides a decentralized, immutable, and cryptographically secure framework for recording evidence-related transactions. Through hashing, timestamping, distributed ledgers, and smart contracts, blockchain enables tamper-evident storage, automated verification, and reliable audit trails. The chapter proposes a conceptual framework consisting of evidence capture, hashing and timestamping, blockchain ledger, smart contract, and legal compliance layers. It also discusses regulatory, privacy, admissibility, scalability, and emerging technological challenges.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain-Integrated AI Framework for Cyber Attack Risk Prioritization and Governance
authors: Vasudha Dwivedi
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of digital technologies, cloud computing, and network systems has increased the frequency and complexity of cyberattacks, including ransomware, APTs, phishing, and zero-day vulnerabilities. Conventional cybersecurity methods reliant on manual oversight and fixed regulations are inadequate to tackle these advancing threats. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is essential in boosting cybersecurity by enhancing detection precision, speeding up response times, and facilitating more flexible defense strategies. This chapter highlights the significance of AI in handling cyber threats and analyzes current worldwide attack patterns. To maintain trust and transparency in decision-making, blockchain technology is used to secure log threat information, risk assessments, and response measures, generating an unalterable audit trail. The suggested framework integrates AI with blockchain to facilitate efficient risk prioritization, flexible governance, instant auditing, and safe sharing of threat intelligence across organizations.</jats:p>

title: BlockSmartGov
authors: Pradip Subedi; Devendra Chapagain; Suresh Raj Sharma; Soba Raj Paudel
abstract: <jats:p>The increasing complexity of digital ecosystems characterized by distributed cloud infrastructures, cross-organizational data flows, and evolving cyber threats has exposed critical limitations of traditional, manual cybersecurity governance. Existing compliance models rely on human interpretation, periodic audits, and fragmented controls, resulting in delays, inconsistencies, and governance blind spots. This chapter proposes BlockSmartGov, a framework leveraging blockchain-based smart contracts to automate cybersecurity governance by embedding policies directly into digital systems. Translating rules into self-executing code ensures consistent, transparent, and auditable enforcement while reducing reliance on human intervention. The chapter explores how smart contracts operationalize governance rules in real time, enforce access controls, validate compliance continuously, and integrate with existing risk management systems. The framework is illustrated through governance scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving compliance, transparency, and real-time enforcement.</jats:p>

title: Body Form and Architectural Elements for Conservation-Led Daylight Optimization in Cultural Museum: A Case Study of Ikom, Cross River State, Nigeria
authors: Charles Bassey Ephraim; Eugene Ehimatie Atamewan
abstract: Daylight is a valued architectural resource in museum design, yet uncontrolled daylight exposes cultural artifacts to fading, embrittlement, colour change, ultraviolet degradation, glare, and thermal stress.This exploratory article examines how the body form and architectural elements of a cultural museum in Ikom, Cross River State, Nigeria, can optimize daylight while protecting light-sensitive artifacts. Using an exploratory, mixed-methods, design-based approach, and the study integrates literature review, climate and site analysis, cultural heritage assessment, case-study review, and daylight-performance simulation. The article proposes a “Sheltered Grove of Memory” concept: a compact, clustered museum form in which bright public and circulation spaces are separated from low-light, conservation-controlled galleries. The proposed strategy uses deep-plan gallery cores, shaded courtyards, high-level clerestories, roof monitors, light wells, external shading fins, light shelves, diffusing ceilings, ultraviolet-filtered glazing, and automated shading. Conservation thresholds guide the design: a maximum of approximately 50 lux for highly sensitive artifacts, 150–200 lux for moderately sensitive artifacts, and up to 300 lux for durable materials such as stone, ceramic, and metal. The study argues that successful tropical museum daylighting depends not on maximizing transparency but on controlling luminous contrast, solar exposure, and cumulative light dosage

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
authors: Hui Zhu; Saleh Zare Zade; Rafi Ibn Sultan; Deng Pan; Arun Ross; Dongxiao Zhu
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

title: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form
authors: Sie Hendrata Dharmawan; Peter Chin
abstract: A graphon is determined by all of its homomorphism densities, but motif-based methods use finitely many. We compute exactly what that truncation costs in a natural family: latent structure block models whose positions lie on $K$ rays, equivalently degree-corrected block models of rank two. For a given radial law, the configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than $2K-1$ vertices form a one-dimensional fiber, which we give in closed form with explicit endpoints; the friendship graph $F_{K-1}$ is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order serves every $K$. The separating signal is suppressed by a factor of at most $m_1^{2(K-1)}$, where $m_1$ is the mean squared slope, about $10^{-4}$ at $K=4$: detecting it from motif counts would take about $10^{15}$ nodes in a single graph, at any edge density. The information is nonetheless in the graph; the fiber belongs to the statistic, not the model. Common spectral pipelines, which count no motifs, still slide along the fiber by more than a third of its length at ordinary densities, with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, while model-based fits of the same embedding do not. We give practitioners four checks: whether a fit is at risk, what to run instead, why a confidence interval will not warn, and how wide the remaining ambiguity is.

title: BPMN or EPC Process Models Too Large? Problem Solved
authors: Andreas V. Hense
abstract: Why do swimlanes consume so much space in process diagrams, and how can color-based visualization improve diagram readability?This video examines common layout challenges in business process modeling, particularly the difficulty of fitting complex diagrams onto a single page or screen. The video compares Event-driven Process Chains (EPC) and BPMN with respect to diagram length and layout characteristics and explains why swimlanes often lead to inefficient use of space. As an alternative, a color-based visualization approach for representing resources is introduced. The video presents a new feature in YAWL that automatically assigns colors based on role definitions, enabling more compact and readable process diagrams. A related scientific article discussing the underlying ideas is available (not open access):https://rdcu.be/cyluy A version of YAWL including the new visualization features can be downloaded from:https://yawlfoundation.github.io/page6.html This is video #19 of the BPASeries.

title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
authors: Xinze Shi; Litian Zhang; Zhenjie Su; Zelong Yu; Yuting Zhang; Qihua Feng; Zifeng Kang; Chaozhuo Li; Zhengxuan Hu
abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

title: Branch Caching After Step Distillation in Four- and Eight-Step Image Generators
authors: Mingyu Liang; Dingkun Xu
abstract: Can a distilled image generator save time by reusing features between its few remaining denoising steps? We study a fixed branch cache that replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule. One full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise supply a scalar correction for each branch type and reuse position. At $1024^2$, one internal reuse reduces four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising time from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds. Three reuses yield $1.51\times$ speedup on eight-step Lightning and $1.53\times$ on eight-step Hyper-FLUX. We evaluate image quality on all 200 DrawBench prompts. With the reuse positions held fixed, correction improves mean same-seed image fidelity over raw reuse by 0.66 and 0.87 dB on the two Lightning students. On Hyper-FLUX the PSNR difference is 0.01 dB, while LPIPS improves from 0.1625 to 0.1546. These results measure the effect of branch caching and correction while retaining each student's original sampling grid.

title: Breaking Noise Shortcuts in Self-Supervised Learning Via Noise-Aligned View Generation
authors: Oankar R. Patil; May D. Wang
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is increasingly applied to scientific imaging domains, such as microscopy, where labels are scarce but noisy data is abundant. These domains exhibit significant signal-dependent noise, which can create a representational shortcut: since both augmented views derive from the same noisy image, the encoder can boost view agreement by also encoding noise patterns rather than semantic content. To enable noise-robust representation learning without knowledge of underlying noise models, we introduce Self-Aligned Noise Augmentation (SEANA), a drop-in module that generates noise-aware SSL views. SEANA learns an invertible variance-stabilizing transform (VST) from noisy data, then estimates the clean signal and resamples independent noise in learned VST space, requiring no clean targets, no dataset-specific denoiser training or use at inference, and no changes to the SSL objective or encoder. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-100 under synthetic Gaussian, Poisson-Gaussian, and multiplicative noise, SEANA improves clean-test linear-probe accuracy across contrastive/non-contrastive SSL methods, indicating higher-quality representations. On real fluorescence imaging, SEANA improves Jurkat cell-cycle stage classification by up to 28.6pp over standard SSL and 27.5pp over denoiser-preprocessed baselines. In all settings, SEANA outperforms the denoiser-preprocessed SSL pipelines, demonstrating that learned VST-space noise-aligned resampling yields more robust representations than denoising alone. Code is available at: https://github.com/opatil31/SEANA

title: Bridging Financial Metrics and Sustainability Indicators for Intelligent Decision-Making
authors: Mirjana Hladika; Ivana Bernat
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how alternative ESG data, captured and processed through digital technologies, can be integrated into management control systems to bridge financial metrics and sustainability indicators. Drawing on stakeholder theory, contingency theory and the natural-resource-based view, it classifies alternative ESG data into four domains (satellite imagery, IoT sensors, textual analytics and transactional footprints) and traces how raw observations become accounting information. The chapter defines normalised, risk-adjusted and verification-paired hybrid key performance indicators, positions them against established sustainability accounting approaches and states four theoretical propositions. It illustrates them with a matrix, a numerical example with sensitivity analysis and an implementation scenario and proposes continuous cross-verification as a control mechanism. The chapter argues that the value of alternative data lies in introducing evidence the organisation does not produce itself and outlines a phased implementation path.</jats:p>

title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
authors: Takahiro Miki; Robin Schmid; Manthan Patel; Turcan Tuna; Julia Richter; Julian Nubert; Joonho Lee; Matthias Müller; Marco Hutter
abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

title: Budget Internalization: Fixed-Budget RLVR Trades Test-Time Scaling for In-Budget Accuracy
authors: Ilia Zavidnyi; Alexander Kovrigin; Arina Puchkova; Kirill Gelvan; Sergey Titov
abstract: Reasoning models often become more accurate when they can generate longer answers at test time. This behavior is known as test-time scaling. However, RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) usually trains them with a fixed rollout cap. We find that this cap changes model behavior, not only training cost. After training, models use few additional tokens beyond the training budget. They outperform the base models near that budget, but their accuracy stops improving and falls below the base model at larger budgets. The rollout cap thus becomes a learned constraint, that limits model's test-time scaling. We call this effect budget internalization. We observe it across Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma4-E2B, and Nemotron-3-Nano-4B and two reasoning training tasks: mathematical reasoning and diverse, procedurally generated problems. This effect also transfers from math training to science and coding tasks. Training-objective level ablations on Qwen3.5-4B show that most changes recover little test-time scaling. Stronger KL regularization and lower training-data truncation preserve more scaling, but stronger KL reduces in-budget accuracy. Forcing an answer on truncated training rollouts largely removes budget internalization, but also removes most of the in-budget gain. SFT on artificially truncated traces reproduces budget internalization, whereas SFT on naturally short traces does not, which shows that the effect is not specific to RL. This result links budget internalization to length-censored post-training rather than to an RL-specific objective term. Thus, a rollout cap does not only control training cost. It can trade low-budget gains for lower performance when additional inference compute is available.

title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
authors: Minh Luu; Michael Quinn; Aakash Tyagi; David Houngninou; Jiang Hu
abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
authors: John Wu; Rushi Qiang; Yuchen Zhuang; Guowang Li; Girish Narayanswamy; Max Xu; Sam Schmidgall; Mark Malhotra; Shwetak Patel; Jimeng Sun; Daniel McDuff; Bo Dai; Xin Liu
abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

title: Building Intelligent Accounting Through Effective Business Process Communication Foundations
authors: Irfan Sophan Himawan; Astri Dwi Andriani; Denny Aditya Dwiwarman; Ira M. Ulfah; Khoiruddin Muchtar; Alda Chairani; Fitria Ayuningtyas; Karisma Rahayu
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid adoption of intelligent financial systems is reshaping accounting, with Business Process Management (BPM) providing the essential foundation for system design, implementation, and control. Using process and innovation theories, this chapter reveals that main obstacles are not technological, but stem from the lack of standardized, automated business processes. It examines BPM alignment with modern reporting data flows—focusing on process mining, Robotic Process Automation (RPA), alternative data integration, and ESG reporting—while addressing governance, change management, cyber risks, and hybrid competencies. Furthermore, it explores hyperautomation, generative AI, and blockchain as transformative forces. Ultimately, the chapter demonstrates that BPM is a critical necessity, rather than a preference, for successful intelligent accounting systems today.</jats:p>

title: Building Organizational Resilience Through Cultural Intelligence and Workforce Diversity
authors: Bryan Christiansen
abstract: <jats:p>The global business environment is shaped by geopolitical instability, technological disruption, demographic change, labor shortages, and evolving workforce expectations. These conditions require organizations to move beyond risk management toward organizational resilience, defined as the capacity to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, and recover from disruptions while sustaining performance. Research indicates that human capital factors, workforce diversity and cultural intelligence, are critical drivers of resilience in connected and hybrid workplaces. However, diversity alone does not guarantee effectiveness; without inclusive leadership, psychological safety, and culturally intelligent management, it can create communication barriers and conflict. This chapter argues that cultural intelligence and workforce diversity are complementary strategic resources that strengthen organizational resilience by fostering trust, organizational learning, and adaptive capability.</jats:p>
