title: C-LiTE: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Cellular feature learning in Histopathology
authors: Esha Sadia Nasir; Jiaqi Lv; Gozde N. Gunesli; Shan E Ahmed Raza
abstract: Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.

title: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
authors: Hao Wu; Sipeng Chen; Jingwen Fu; Yuwang Wang
abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.

title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
authors: Yimeng Liu; Eric Isbrandt; Felix Katzenburg; Kevin P. Greenman; Han Hao; Yang Cao; Varinia Bernales; Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
authors: Francesco Belardinelli; Flavio Corradini; Matteo Leonesi
abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
authors: DiffuSpace Technical Team
abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

title: CoachSI: Self-Improvement of Robot Policies with a Language Coach
authors: Jiachen Tao; Gengyu Zhang; Haoxuan Wang; Bing Liu; Yan Yan
abstract: Generalist robot policies execute atomic skills reliably but fail when the same skills are composed into long-horizon tasks. Self-improvement from the policy's own experience does not close this gap: experience collected by the policy alone stays within its own distribution and reproduces what it can already do. We show that what the policy lacks is not a skill but the next step. We present CoachSI, a self-improvement method in which a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) coaches the policy in language: it watches the robot and names the next step in the format of the policy's atomic instructions, and never outputs an action. Successful coached rollouts are relabeled in hindsight with the original task instruction and used to fine-tune the policy. The fine-tuned policy is then deployed on its own. On states where a World Action Model and a Vision-Language-Action model have stalled, naming the next step raises subgoal completion by 4.6x over the unchanged task instruction, and the frozen VLM supplies it from the same camera images the policy sees. After fine-tuning, unassisted success on long-horizon tasks in unseen scenes rises from 47.4% to 59.3%, 9.8 points above fine-tuning on human demonstrations and 7.3 points above fine-tuning on self-collected successes at an equal data budget. With a coach that sees only camera images, it reaches 56.8%, above both baselines. The gain is obtained with the action backbone frozen: language coaching teaches the policy what should happen next, and the skills it already has do the rest.

title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video
authors: Yiyan Ji; Qixun Wang; Yang Shi; Zhuoran Zhang; Yifan Xu; Tengfei Liu; Yuqi Tang; Xiaohan Zhang; Shujie Li; Jiafu Tang; Xuanyu Zhu; Xinyu Liu; Yan He; Yushuo Guan; Zihao Wang; Xianghua Ying; Shixuan Liu; Haotian Wang; Wenjing Yang; Zhaoxiang Zhang; Yuanxing Zhang; Pengfei Wan; Jiaheng Liu
abstract: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.

title: Coherent belief and opinion propagation produces more echo chambers: corrected version
authors: Hiro Kataoka; J{é}r{ô}me Euzenat; Koji Hasebe
abstract: The occurrence of echo chambers is a well-known phenomenon in social networks. Echo chambers are groups of agents satisfying three properties: homogeneity, i.e., sharing the same opinion, segregation, i.e., listening primarily to agents of the same group, and reinforcement, i.e., increasing opinion similarity over time. Opinion dynamics models have been used to explain how echo chambers occur through agents updating their opinions. However, social network users also exchange beliefs supporting their opinions. Here, we aim at identifying the effect of propagating beliefs together with opinions on the formation of echo chambers. For that purpose, we complement an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations. Beliefs and opinions are also maintained coherent guided by values that agents share. We introduce measures, applying to either beliefs and opinions, to identify echo chambers based on the three properties. This model is used to simulate opinion and belief propagation with varying initial conditions and agent tolerance for different opinions/beliefs. Results confirm the occurrence of echo chambers observed in previous opinion dynamics studies in a different setting and with a stricter measure. They also demonstrate the occurrence of echo chambers with belief propagation. Finally, they show that connecting opinions to beliefs and maintaining their coherence increases the number of belief echo chambers, but that they involve a reduced number of agents.

title: Collaborating With ChatGPT: Considering the Implications of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Journalism and Media Education
authors: John V. Pavlik
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is ushering in an era of potential transformation of journalism and media content. This essay considers one notable generative AI platform called ChatGPT made available to the public in 2022 for free use. ChatGPT allows users to enter text prompts and rapidly generates text responses drawn from its knowledge acquired via machine learning in engagement with the internet. This essay is coauthored by a human journalism and media professor in collaboration with ChatGPT. The essay demonstrates the capacity and limitations of ChatGPT and offers reflections on the implications of generative AI for journalism and media education.

title: Collective Emotional Intelligence as a Structural Foundation for Self-Organizing Corporate Cultures and Organizational Well-Being
authors: Venelin Terziev; Teodora Petrova; Marin Georgiev
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines emotional intelligence (EI) as a key factor in constructing resilient corporate cultures focused on collective socio-emotional health. The traditional rational management model is analyzed as insufficient for maintaining human sustainability in an era of digital acceleration. The research proposes a transition toward a new paradigm based on self-organization, self-development, and neuro-adaptive leadership. A central focus is an organizational-motivational mechanism prioritizing psychological safety, internal motivation, and shared values. By aligning organizational goals with personal values, enterprises foster a 'living ecosystem' that mitigates burnout. The study explores how collective emotional potential serves as a strategic resource for achieving operational excellence and well-being in the age of artificial intelligence. The chapter argues that the shift from hierarchy to self-organization is essential for the sustainable flourishing of individuals and organizations alike.</jats:p>

title: Collective Socio-Emotional Health in Organizations
authors: Sohom Saha; Mahendra Kumar Singh
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter describes the impacts of contemporary online workplaces on the emotional and mental health of the employees. It emphasizes that the current workplace, where technology is used all the time, may cause stress, burnout, and lack of concentration. The chapter presents a combined model of three main concepts of neuroadaptation (how the brain adapts to digital needs) and emotional intelligence (how individuals perceive and cope with emotions) and digital work settings. It demonstrates that well-being is not a personal problem but rather a shared phenomenon and is influenced by workplace culture, leadership, and technology utilization. Emotional intelligent leadership, psychological safety, and balanced digital practices are also highlighted in the chapter. On the whole, it gives effective advice on how to build better, healthier, and more productive organizations in the digital era.</jats:p>

title: Collision-Free Is Not Enough: Passage-Conditioned Navigation for Wheeled-Legged Robots
authors: Wai Ka Sun; Waiyiu Pong; Bowen Wang
abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10° off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang; Wendao Wu; Chenheng Zhang; Chunyuan Zheng; Yanyi Li; Cong Fang; Haoxuan Li; Zhouchen Lin
abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

title: ColorRef: Calibrating Verbal Feedback for Color Revision
authors: Pablo Loyola; Andres Hoyos-Idrobo; Edison Marrese-Taylor; Colin Rowat; Alfredo Solano
abstract: People rarely specify an exact color when asking someone to revise a design: they might say \textit{a little darker} or \textit{more blue} after seeing a proposal. A language-model assistant must then infer not only which way to change the color, but how far. We study this distinction with \textsc{ColorRef}, a color reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher, knowing a recorded target hidden from the guesser, supplies verbal corrections. On 1{,}000 crowd-sourced description--target pairs, three rounds of deterministic oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 $ΔE_{76}$. However, those corrections provide additional information, and improvement alone does not establish well-calibrated feedback following. A controlled Qwen3-14B diagnostic reveals a more specific failure: following a requested direction and ordering graded phrases do not guarantee a suitable step size; strong modifiers can induce excessive changes. We therefore measure each receiver's typical response to \textit{a little}, \textit{somewhat}, and \textit{much} on separate colors and select wording matched to its observed steps. On 128 held-out starting colors, calibration reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B against a fixed graded-wording rule. The benefit is concentrated on large corrections, with many unchanged cases and no consistent increase in threshold success. Our findings show that following the direction of feedback is not the same as making an appropriately sized revision.

title: Combining Human and Artificial Intelligence: Hybrid Problem-Solving in Organizations
authors: S. Raisch; K. Fomina
abstract: Organizations increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to solve previously unexplored problems. While routine tasks can be automated, the intricate nature of exploratory tasks, such as solving new problems, demands a hybrid approach that integrates human intelligence with AI. We argue that the outcomes of this human – AI collaboration are contingent on the processes employed to combine human intelligence and AI. title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
authors: Lirui Luo; Kelong Mao; Xinwei Yang; Rongqing Li; Luyu Chen; Kieran Wong; Yudong Guo; Xinrui Wang; Jiayin Zhu; Gu Simiu; Sulong Xu; Cong Fang
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
authors: Jiayi Chen; Lizhe Chen; Yujia Chen; Shihan Dou; Ming Zhang; Chendi Ge; Shiguang Ni; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xuanjing Huang; Maxm Pan
abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Ratio-Based MCDM Methods: Performance and Ranking Stability under DAM Weighting
authors: Mahardika Inra Takaendengan; Irma Anggraeni; Febri Dwi Irawati; Gde Brahupadhya Subiksa
abstract: Ratio-based Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) methods provide practical approaches for ranking alternatives, but differences in normalization and aggregation mechanisms can produce different rankings and levels of stability. This study comparatively evaluates ratio-based MCDM methods under a common Data Assessment Method (DAM) weighting framework, focusing on MOORA and ARAS for logistics hub location selection. The study uses a dataset comprising 12 candidate logistics hub locations and six criteria. DAM is first applied to derive criterion weights, after which MOORA and ARAS are implemented using the same decision matrix and weighting configuration. Ranking performance is examined through baseline ranking comparison, while robustness is assessed using systematic criterion-weight perturbations of ±0.05 and ±0.10. Kendall’s Tau is employed to measure ranking consistency, and Mean Absolute Rank Change (MARC) is used to evaluate ranking stability. The DAM results show a relatively balanced criterion-weight distribution, with CLH02 receiving the highest weight of 0.1932. Both methods identify LH6 as the best alternative and LH9 as the least preferred, although several intermediate alternatives exchange positions. MOORA achieves a Kendall’s Tau of 0.9163 and a MARC of 0.3715, whereas ARAS obtains 0.9674 and 0.1840, respectively. These results demonstrate that ARAS provides higher ranking consistency and substantially greater stability under weight perturbations. Therefore, ARAS is identified as the better-performing ratio-based MCDM method for the evaluated logistics hub location problem. The findings highlight the importance of assessing both ranking consistency and stability when selecting MCDM methods for robust decision support.

title: Comparing Each Generation with Independent Siblings Gives Video World Model Post-Training a Proper Objective for Outcome Frequencies
authors: Xin Li; Yiwen Chen
abstract: Video world models are used as simulators, so when a first frame leaves several physical outcomes open, repeated generations should produce each outcome as often as it occurs in the data. Physics post-training scores every generation against the single recorded future of its history, which makes single videos more faithful, but the expected score is linear in the model distribution and is maximized by always producing the most likely outcome. The log-likelihood of the recorded outcome is maximized by the data distribution, and its gradient weights agreement with the record by the inverse of how often the model produces the generated outcome, a frequency that other generations of the same history with independent noise, its siblings, can estimate. To train with this weight from a finite group, we propose SibPO, which performs Sibling-paired Policy Optimization: siblings estimate a truncated inverse-frequency weight for agreement with the record, and a second term subtracts the same weight times the agreement with the siblings, which makes the expected objective a strictly proper divergence over outcome cells at every group size. On PisaBench, SibPO lowers the KS distance to simulated landing times by 9.1-10.2% relative to the strongest method outside its reward family on three of four video models without degrading single videos, and it lowers the error of estimated robot policy success rates by 13%.

title: Comparison of the Accuracy and Efficiency of Linear Regression and Nonlinear Logit and Probit Models in Stock Price Forecasting
authors: Parasto Azami; Najmeh Kargar Kamour; Hoda Hemmati
abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to compare the accuracy and efficiency of linear regression with nonlinear Logit and Probit models in short-term stock price forecasting. The study uses daily stock data of Isfahan Steel Company from January 1, 2024, to November 19, 2025. After eliminating multicollinear variables, the closing price was considered the dependent variable, while the number of trades, price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), net percentage of retail trading, and per capita buy and sell values of individual investors were selected as independent variables. An out-of-sample forecasting approach was applied, reserving the last 30 trading days as the test set. The results indicate that although linear regression shows acceptable explanatory power, it underperforms in short-term forecasting. The Logit model achieved the lowest MSE, RMSE, and MAE values, followed by the Probit model. The findings confirm the nonlinear nature of stock price dynamics and highlight the superior predictive performance of probability-based nonlinear models, particularly Logit.</jats:p>

title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
authors: Shwetanshu Singh; Mark Keavney; Mathieu Duteil; Meriem Mehri; Scott Blain
abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
authors: Alper Kalle; Theo Rudkiewicz; Mohamed-Oumar Ouerfelli; Mohamed Tamaazousti
abstract: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

abstract: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.

title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
authors: Abbas Sani
abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model families and language directions, with a single worst case of 2.19 chrF; (iii) on consumer GPUs, INT8 and INT4 quantisation provide substantial memory savings (49-61% at INT4) but do not reduce inference latency relative to FP16 - in fact, latency increases by 1.3x to 5.3x; (iv) a clear performance gradient tracking training-resource availability is visible across languages (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba). These findings motivate a research agenda focused on hardware-aware compression and error-type analysis beyond aggregate metrics for low-resource deployment.

title: Computer Vision and Robotic Intelligence in Next-Generation Healthcare
abstract:
<jats:p>Book Description
Computer Vision and Robotic Intelligence in Next-Generation Healthcare
Technology like Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision, Deep Learning and Robotic Intelligence is transforming the healthcare industry. These technologies are revolutionizing the way in which diseases are detected, diagnosed, monitored and treated and enhanced the accuracy, efficiency, personalization, and patient-centeredness of healthcare systems. Computer Vision and Robotic Intelligence in Next-Generation Healthcare provides a comprehensive review of the most recent smart technologies, which are reshaping the provision of healthcare and clinical decision-making today. This edited book features invited papers from experts and researchers from different disciplines that address the latest developments in medical image analysis, computer vision for diagnostics, surgical navigation, rehabilitation robotics, medical robotics, cyber security in healthcare and intelligent clinical systems. The chapters emphasize pioneering applications of deep learning, convolutional neural networks, transformer-based models, visual tracking, robotic vision, and AI-driven rehabilitation tools, transforming patient care and healthcare outcomes. It provides an overview of different areas including assistive robotics for elderly care, multimodal medical image segmentation and classification, real-time image processing in medical diagnostic devices, robotic vision in minimally invasive surgery, AI medical robotics, intelligent intrusion detection for healthcare infrastructures, and predictive healthcare analytics. The course also addresses privacy concerns, the interpretability of models, cyber security, and ethical and regulatory aspects of smart healthcare systems. The book is a perfect mix of theory and application and has real-life examples to give a wonderful insight into the application of computer vision in a healthcare environment along with robotic intelligence. Brimming with valuable insights, it is a key source of information for researchers, healthcare practitioners, engineers, policy makers, and graduate students interested in the impact of intelligent technologies on the future of healthcare systems. title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
authors: Kevin Wardakhan; Marie Line Alberi-Morel; Jérémie Leguay; Afef Feki; Adrien Sardi; Sébastien Archeveque; Claudiu Mihailescu
abstract: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.

title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
authors: Abdul Qadir Ibrahim; Martin Burger; Abel Maviano Jonathan
abstract: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.

title: Conformal Selection for Hierarchical Streaming Data
authors: Zhenyuan Sun; Chengyao Yu; Ruixing Ming; Bingyi Jing
abstract: Many real-world tasks involve making sequential decisions about whether to select candidates before their responses of interest are revealed. In this work, we address the online selection problem in the context of hierarchical data, where candidates arrive sequentially from different populations. This extends existing online conformal selection frameworks beyond the standard i.i.d./exchangeable data assumption. The primary challenge lies in constructing valid statistics for each candidate sequentially under the hierarchical data structure. To this end, we first develop Online Hierarchical Selection (OHS), a distribution-free method that enables principled candidate selection for hierarchical data streams. Specifically, we introduce methods to construct rank-based e-values for both between-group and within-group samples, and apply averaged e-values to the online e-BH procedure. We then develop OHS with feedback (OHSF), which boosts the power of OHS by leveraging potential response feedback. Theoretically, the proposed methods achieve false discovery rate control under mild hierarchical exchangeability and data arrival assumptions at any time. We also generalize methods to broader settings, such as data with covariate shift and selection under effect-related responses. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

title: Connected and Automated Microbiology Laboratories for Real-Time Monitoring
authors: Vikas Sharma; Alekh Chaudhary; Tarun Kumar Vashishth; Nisha Nirola; Charul Tyagi; Vivek Kumar
abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation in microbiology laboratories is changing the generation, processing, and application of microbial data for research, diagnostics, and other industrial purposes. This chapter describes how IoT, Automation and digital workflow technologies have been integrated into this field (e.g. serverless computing platforms, electronic lab notebooks, wireless connectivity, connected sensors, automated instruments, cyber-physical infrastructure (CPI), etc.). It details how these technologies increase the accuracy, repeatability and efficiency of laboratory data and decrease human error and turnaround time. Additionally, the book details different system architectures, data interoperability, and cloud-based platforms that allow for seamless data acquisition and analysis throughout the microbiological workflow. The chapter examines challenges related to data security, standardisation, scalability, and regulatory compliance.</jats:p>

title: Constructing Dynamic Conversations with Neural Back-channel Generation and Voice-line Scheduling
authors: Yifang Pan; Chris Landreth; Karan Singh
abstract: We present a novel approach to the problem of combining two voice-line channels of dyadic conversational audio into a unified conversation with controllable back-channeling and turn-taking dynamics. In voice performances for the game industry, the two tracks of voice-lines are typically recorded or synthesized in isolation. Our method takes two such unsynchronized tracks and uses a neural scheduler to sequence them into a single dynamic conversation, modifying both tracks by inserting or removing pauses and introducing voice overlap as appropriate. We further propose a back-channel predictor that is able to predict opportunity for back-channels for a given conversational turn's audio and content, which the scheduler can then incorporate. We evaluate our scheduler and predictor independently and in combination by: various quantitative comparison; a qualitative and perceptual comparison to prior art and naive baselines; a compelling set of results showing animator control over the diversity, extent and nature of back-channeling and turn dynamics.

title: Consumer Engagement With the Metaverse and AI Chatbots for Women's Clothing Fashions
authors: Astri Dwi Andriani; Penpim Phuangsuwan
abstract: <jats:p>Consumer engagement with women's fashion is being transformed by the metaverse and AI chatbots, as brands create immersive virtual experiences where shoppers can try on outfits digitally, attend interactive fashion shows, and participate in style communities. AI chatbots offer personalized recommendations, instant styling advice, and all-time support, making the shopping journey smoother and more interactive. This integration of technology not only enhances convenience and personalization but also builds stronger brand loyalty and increases customer satisfaction within the female fashion sector.</jats:p>

title: Contactless Estimation of Respiratory Frequency Using 3D-CNN on Thermal Images
authors: Federica Gioia; Filippo Pura; Alberto Greco; Dario Piga; Arcangelo Merla; Marco Forgione
abstract: Monitoring physiological parameters such as respiratory rate ($f_R$) is essential for diagnosing and managing various pathological conditions. Thermal imaging offers a promising contactless alternative to traditional methods, which often rely on partially invasive sensors or obtrusive wearable systems. However, existing approaches for $f_R$ estimation from thermal signals typically require extensive pre-processing and manual or semi-automatic region-of-interest (ROI) tracking, limiting their practical applicability. This study proposes a deep learning-based method for estimating $f_R$ directly from thermal videos, eliminating the need for complex pre-processing and ROI tracking. A 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) is developed to operate on raw thermal video data. To address challenges related to small datasets, the model is trained using data augmentation and transfer learning from synthetic datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a validation $R^2$ score of approximately 0.61 on both pre-processed and raw thermal videos. By simplifying the workflow, this method holds promise for enhancing the feasibility of thermal imaging in real-world applications, such as remote healthcare and driver monitoring in automotive applications.

title: Context as a Resource
authors: Xufei Tian; Han Hu; Wenli Du
abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

title: ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds
authors: Runze Wang; Fei Zha; Bing He; Ke Xu; Zhongyuan Wu; Yuxuan Xie; Wenzheng Wu; Zhongyuan Liu; Youcheng Cai; Ligang Liu
abstract: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
authors: Jinbae Seo; Jungin Park; Hyunsung Jang; Namkoo Ha; Jiyoung Lee; Kwanghoon Sohn
abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
authors: An T. Le
abstract: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $Θ(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(Θ(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $αd$ coordinates, $0<α<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $Θ(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leqαd$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<α<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

title: Contrast Where It Matters: Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding for Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs
authors: Yiheng Li; Wenhao Wang; Xingyi Li; Mingda Jia; Zichang Tan; Yinhang Tang; Zhen Lei; Yang Yang
abstract: Despite strong multimodal capabilities, large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate when linguistic priors outweigh visual evidence or when predictions are grounded in irrelevant or misleading image regions. Training-free contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by contrasting the original prediction with an auxiliary one that exposes linguistic priors. Yet existing methods focus on altering the auxiliary input or computation and do not ensure that either branch uses query-relevant visual evidence during decoding. We propose Visual Evidence-Guided Decoding (VEGD), a training-free framework that identifies query-relevant visual evidence and guides its use throughout contrastive decoding. VEGD locates this evidence by aggregating localization heads with strong visual responses and coherent spatial structure, then selectively weakens it in the auxiliary image. During generation, VEGD directs visual-carrier heads in both branches toward the same evidence location, strengthening access to intact evidence in the main branch while anchoring the auxiliary branch to its weakened counterpart. An adaptive distribution fusion strategy then combines or contrasts their predictions according to distribution divergence. Experiments across diverse LVLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that VEGD consistently reduces hallucinations.

title: Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated Biologically Plausible Network
authors: Fatima Atwi; Constant Roux; Christian Bergaud; Olivier Stasse
abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.

title: Conversational AI Avatars in the Metaverse for Business-Driven Consumer Engagement
authors: Jakkrit Thavorn; Worasak Klongthong; Parichat Jaipong
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how conversational AI avatars can create business-driven consumer engagement in the metaverse. Using a narrative literature review supported by qualitative content analysis, it shows that avatar value does not arise from human-like appearance or automation alone, but from the alignment of immersive servicescapes, avatar design, trust mechanisms, engagement pathways, business outcomes, and responsible scaling conditions. Building on research on chatbots, digital humans, metaverse retailing, virtual influencers, and AI governance, the chapter develops a framework that positions AI avatars as trust-centered engagement infrastructure. It also maps avatar roles across the customer journey and offers managerial principles for creating measurable, responsible, and scalable business value.</jats:p>

title: Conversational AI in Healthcare
authors: Esther Besty Anaiye; Basil Osayin Daudu
abstract: <jats:p>Users use AI-based technologies such as conversational AI (chatbots) to access health information and gain healthcare support. This enhances the user-AI technology relationship, thereby addressing the traditional healthcare system. However, there are ethical and technical concerns about the use of AI-driven systems. Against this background, a qualitative approach, incorporating scholarly and authoritative literature, was adopted to meet the article's objectives of exploring conversational AI in healthcare, its evolution, technologies, applications, benefits, risks, and solutions to rising problems. The relevance of conversational AI agents in improving healthcare cannot be overemphasised, as effective mastery of conversational AI tools in accordance with robust AI regulatory policies ensures healthy and lasting patient-centred care.</jats:p>

title: CookieGuard: Automated Combinatorial Testing, Syntax Validation, and Fault Correlation for Cookiecutter Templates
authors: Authors, Anonymous
abstract: This artifact contains the datasets, scripts, and analysis notebooks used in our study of Cookiecutter template testing. It includes the collected Cookiecutter templates, the scripts used for processing and testing, and the notebooks used to analyze and summarize the experimental results. The artifact contents are organized as follows: Cookiecutter_templates_script.ipynbA Jupyter notebook collects Cookiecutter templates and performs initial dataset analysis. It provides statistics about the collected repositories, including programming language distribution, Cookiecutter variable types, and other dataset characteristics. process_all_templates.pyA script used to execute the proposed five-stage testing pipeline on the complete collection of target Cookiecutter templates. analysis.ipynbA Jupyter notebook analyzes the experimental results and extracts insights from the study, including detected errors, hook-related information, retired combinatorial test cases, and other findings. cookiecutter_templates_workspace.zipThe raw dataset containing the 1,304 collected Cookiecutter template repositories used in our study. cookiecutter_templates_workspace_*.zipThe resulting datasets after applying the testing pipeline to the collected Cookiecutter template repositories. The datasets contain the processed template repositories together with the generated testing results. Two types of algorithm runs are provided: Unranked runs: cookiecutter_templates_workspace_M*.zip, where M denotes the size (cap) of the configuration space explored by the run, ranging from M1 to M10000 configurations. For example, cookiecutter_templates_workspace_M1000.zip corresponds to an unranked run with a configuration space of 1,000 combinations. Randomized runs with fixed seeds: cookiecutter_templates_workspace_M*_R_S*.zip, where M denotes the size (cap) of the configuration space and S denotes the random seed used for selecting configurations. The provided randomized runs use seeds 7 and 42. For example, cookiecutter_templates_workspace_M1000_R_S7.zip corresponds to a run with 1,000 configurations using random seed 7, while cookiecutter_templates_workspace_M100_R_S42.zip corresponds to a run with 100 configurations using random seed 42. The filename convention is: M<N> → unranked run with a configuration space of N combinationsM<N>_R_S<K> → randomized run with a configuration space of N combinations using random seed K. This artifact enables replication of the dataset collection, testing process, and analysis presented in the associated paper.

title: Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach
authors: Jiahao You; Ziye Jia; Chao Dong; Qihui Wu; Zhu Han
abstract: The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

title: Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters
authors: Hantao Yang; Hong Xie; Defu Lian
abstract: We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.

title: Coordinated Use of Large Language Models in Academic Research
authors: Vladislav Marinov
abstract: This study proposes a methodological framework for the coordinated use of multiple large language models in academic research. Its central argument is that involving more models does not in itself guarantee more reliable results; what matters is how cognitive and verification operations are organised. The framework is based on seven principles (procedural independence, functional allocation, the diagnostic value of divergence, the diagnostic value of convergence, external verification, proportionality of checking, and human epistemic responsibility) and sets out a non-linear multi-LLM protocol in which independently obtained results are compared, critically examined and, where necessary, verified against external sources. The approach is illustrated through real-world cases drawn from research practice. The study concludes that moving from a single language model to a coordinated multi-LLM process represents a change in the organisation of research, in which the researcher makes the final decisions and bears scholarly responsibility.

title: Copilot or Culprit? How AI Is Changing Open-Source Bug Reporting and Maintenance
authors: Yinuo Liu; Yunlong Lyu; Zichao Luo; Tian Dong; Zian Luo; Peng Chen; Hao Chen
abstract: AI-generated bug reports have drawn criticism for unreliable claims and faulty reproducers that burden maintainers. However, as LLM capabilities improve, some maintainers have begun to express more positive views on AI use in bug reporting and maintenance. Understanding this evolution requires examining whether AI-involved reports are becoming more reliable, which uses of AI are associated with valid findings, and how maintainers investigate these reports and act on them. To this end, we conduct the first large-scale study of 120,918 bug reports from 101 open-source projects between January 2024 and September 2026, tracing AI involvement from discovery and reporting through validation and resolution. Our findings show that AI-involved reports become more complete over time, with a growing share of reports confirmed as valid. In bug reporting, AI for reproduction and diagnosis are associated with higher validity, whereas report writing is not. Extends into maintenance, maintainers increasingly use AI to investigate code and recommend fixes. However, they devote more effort to AI-assisted reports of human-discovered bugs than to reports of AI-discovered bugs. These findings highlight both AI's growing participation in bug investigation and the continuing need for verification and follow-up. Drawing on these findings, we provide practical guidance for turning AI-generated findings into verifiable reports: emphasizing reproducibility, verification, and accountability. We followed this guidance when submitting 53 reports on AI-discovered bugs, of which 69.81% were accepted by maintainers as of writing.

title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations
authors: Zhiwen Qiu; Daisy Lin; Diyu Zhou; Jialin Wu; Rosita Ji; Saleh Kalantari
abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.

title: Correcting Flows with Marginal Matching
authors: Meital Bojan; Nadav Bojan Sellam; Ev Zisselman; Aviv Tamar
abstract: Flow matching models, ODE-based generative models, generate samples by gradually morphing a simple source distribution into a target distribution. However, these models still face challenges in optimally balancing computational efficiency with generation fidelity. While predictor-corrector schemes have been proven to help address this issue in diffusion models effectively, their application to flow matching models remains under-explored. In this work we present a novel training-based predictor-corrector framework for flow matching, which exploits the fact that the ODE can be easily reversed. Our key idea, termed Marginal Matching, is to correct samples at a particular time step in the forward ODE towards a matching marginal distribution of the backward ODE. This scheme proves to reduce a bound on the distance between the data distribution and the learned distribution, motivating two different implementations for the correction function. We show that our proposed method improves sample quality on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, with minimal overhead in computation time.

title: CoScan: Multi-Scale Content-Adaptive Space-Filling Scans for Causal State-Space Image Restoration
authors: Wei Dong; Terry Ji; Yan Min; Shahram Shirani; Jun Chen; Han Zhou
abstract: Selective state-space models (SSMs) have recently shown strong potential for efficient image restoration. A central difficulty, however, is that a 2D feature map typically needs to be linearized into a 1D token sequence for causal state-space updates, making restoration performance highly sensitive to the imposed scan order. Existing deterministic scans follow space-filling principles but remain fixed and content-agnostic, and can yield fragmented or semantically inconsistent contexts under degradations. We propose \textbf{CoScan}, a \textbf{co}ntent-adaptive \textbf{scan}-order design for causal vision SSMs. CoScan learns image-dependent space-filling traversals via differentiable proxy supervision driven by \textbf{scan-quality objectives} that \textit{encourage short-range coherence and causal predictability, while preserving spatial adjacency}. To support hierarchical restoration backbones, we introduce an \textbf{efficient multi-scale scan construction by coarsening a fine-level minimum spanning tree}, producing coherent scans across feature resolutions. In addition, a \textbf{frequency-guided start selection strategy} is designed to \textit{place informative structures early in the sequence prefix to strengthen causal context formation}. Plugged into existing Mamba-based backbones, CoScan yields consistent improvements across several restoration benchmarks with minimal overhead and shows promising results on high-level vision tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/dongw22/CoScan

title: CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation
authors: Pengxin Wang; Nakjung Choi; Jingdi Chen
abstract: Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

title: Cosmetic Recontouring And Digital Planning: A Smart Strategy For Aesthetic Transformations
authors: Leandro da Mata da Costa; Luana Mendonça Dias; Janaína Emanuela Damasceno
abstract: Introduction: Cosmetic recontouring is a relevant technique in aesthetic dentistry, standing out for its conservative approach by correcting imperfections in anterior teeth without the need for significant tooth reduction. Digital planning has further enhanced these treatments, enabling greater personalization and precision in the restorative process. Objective: To present the treatment of an incisal edge fracture in anterior teeth using a minimally invasive approach. Case Report: This report describes the treatment of a dental polytrauma involving multiple incisal edge fractures, in which the planning was carried out virtually using the Digital Smile Design (DSD) protocol. Cosmetic recontouring was performed to restore the anterior teeth, using the silicone index technique as a guide. Conclusion: The application of a minimally invasive approach allowed for precise and efficient execution of the restoration, yielding satisfactory aesthetic results while preserving the original tooth structure to the greatest extent possible. Keywords: Esthetics, Dental. Health Sciences, Technology, and Innovation Management. Dental Impression Materials. Composite Resins. Dental Restoration, Permanent.

title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
authors: Chang Yang; Yao Xuan; Wendan Yan; Nhat Le; Jiang Liu; Longhao Jin; Zhen Peggy Yao; Alireza Vahdatpour; Djordje Gligorijevic
abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.
