title: Design and Evaluation of a Hybrid Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning Model for Economic News Sentiment Analysis to Predict Price Fluctuations in the Iran Mercantile Exchange
authors: Amin Jamali; Hamid Reza Jamali
abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to design and evaluate a hybrid Persian natural language processing and machine learning model for extracting economic news sentiment and predicting steel price fluctuations in the Iran Mercantile Exchange. This applied-developmental study employed a descriptive-analytical design based on secondary textual and time-series data. The dataset included 45,836 economic, industrial, and financial news articles published between January 2019 and January 2026 and 1,486 synchronized daily observations of steel billet and sheet transactions. A fine-tuned ParsBERT model classified news as positive, negative, or neutral, and a daily sentiment index was calculated using source credibility, publication timing, and news intensity. Numerical variables included closing prices, trading volume, supply, demand, the informal exchange rate, the global iron ore price, and technical indicators. Random Forest, LSTM, XGBoost, ParsBERT-LSTM, and ParsBERT-XGBoost were compared using walk-forward validation. ParsBERT achieved a sentiment-classification accuracy of 89.4% and an F1 score of 0.887. Granger causality analysis showed that the two-business-day lag of news sentiment significantly predicted price returns, with F = 8.75 and p = 0.003. ParsBERT-XGBoost produced the best performance, with an RMSE of 710 and an MAE of 520 Iranian rials per kilogram. Compared with numerical XGBoost, the hybrid model reduced RMSE by 27.6%. It also achieved a directional accuracy of 72.6%, a win rate of 67.4%, a Sharpe ratio of 1.76, and a maximum drawdown of 9.2%. The informal exchange rate, news sentiment index, and global iron ore price were the most influential predictors. Integrating Persian news embeddings with fundamental, transactional, and technical variables through the ParsBERT-XGBoost architecture improved forecasting accuracy and risk-adjusted performance and may provide an effective decision-support and early-warning tool for the Iran Mercantile Exchange.</jats:p>

title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
authors: Ishita Asnani; Shaghayegh Fazliani; Zachary Ryan; Kriyoshig Prasai; Chirag Kumar; Indra Gonzalez Ojeda; Marc Lipsitch; Madeleine Udell
abstract:
Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing.
  Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust.
  Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale.
  Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts.
  Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

title: Designing a Business Intelligence Model for Enhancing Brand Performance in the Food Industry of Tehran Province: A Grounded Theory Approach
authors: Arezoo Havaie; Seyed Ahmad Ghasemi; Nader Khalesi
abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to design and explain a context-specific business intelligence model for enhancing the brand performance of companies operating in the food industry of Tehran Province. This applied and exploratory qualitative study was conducted using the grounded theory methodology. The research population comprised senior managers and experts working in the food industry of Tehran Province, who were selected through purposive and judgmental sampling. Data were collected through in-depth, directed interviews with 12 participants who possessed relevant managerial experience and expertise in marketing, commercial planning, and the food industry. The data were analyzed according to the systematic approach of Strauss and Corbin through open, axial, and selective coding. Participant feedback and peer review were employed to establish the credibility of the findings. Recoding was also performed to assess reliability, producing an intercoder test–retest reliability coefficient of 0.83. The findings indicated that market competition, emerging technologies, organizational needs, and data quality constituted the causal conditions underlying the development of business intelligence. The central phenomenon was the analysis of data to generate valuable information, encompassing data collection, storage, analysis, application, and the monitoring of key performance indicators. Technological infrastructure, organizational structure, top management support, and regulatory requirements were identified as contextual conditions facilitating model implementation. Environmental turbulence, economic conditions, resistance to change, and government interventions functioned as intervening conditions. The principal strategies included data-driven analysis and decision-making, value creation and competitive advantage, organizational flexibility and responsiveness, intelligent supply-chain and production management, brand-value enhancement, and improved marketing communications. These strategies resulted in more accurate market and customer analysis, strategic brand decision-making, organizational innovation, greater brand value and differentiation, and enhanced brand sustainability and customer trust. Business intelligence represents a strategic and dynamic organizational capability through which market and organizational data are transformed into actionable knowledge. Its effective implementation can strengthen evidence-based decision-making, organizational adaptability, customer trust, brand differentiation, and sustainable competitive advantage in the food industry.</jats:p>

title: Designing a Model for Customer Behavior Analysis in Banking Using Artificial Intelligence
authors: Ali Rostami; Ahmad  Ghobadi Alvar; Mohammad Malekinia
abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to develop and validate a model for analyzing and predicting bank customers’ behavior using artificial intelligence. This research was basic-applied in terms of purpose, sequential exploratory mixed-methods in terms of data type, cross-sectional in terms of data collection time, and based on content analysis and meta-synthesis in the qualitative phase and descriptive-survey procedures in the quantitative phase. In the qualitative phase, the statistical population included all studies related to customer behavior in banking systems and the factors and indicators affecting its analysis and prediction, published in valid databases between 2000 and 2025. After screening through the PRISMA procedure, 84 studies were selected for final analysis. Extracted concepts were classified into components and broader dimensions. In the quantitative phase, combined data from banking customers, along with the views of banking experts and customer-relationship specialists, were used. A researcher-made questionnaire derived from the qualitative phase was applied to assess the model components. Customer behavior prediction was performed using decision tree, support vector machine, and deep learning based on Transformer architecture. The qualitative findings led to the identification of 49 concepts, 22 components, and 12 main dimensions. The identified components included individual characteristics, financial status, responsiveness, reliability, assurance, digital experience, in-person experience, transparency, security, service satisfaction, value satisfaction, offer characteristics, communications, campaign response, brand value, transaction patterns, consumption patterns, channel preference, cooperation continuity, brand advocacy, reduced use, and offer acceptance. In the quantitative phase, the decision tree model showed the strongest predictive performance, with an R² of 0.8327, MAE of 0.0421, and RMSE of 0.0532. The support vector machine model ranked second, followed by the deep learning model, although all three algorithms demonstrated acceptable predictive capability. The proposed model demonstrated that integrating demographic, financial, behavioral, experiential, transactional, and marketing-related data can provide a valid basis for analyzing and predicting bank customers’ behavior. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence algorithms, particularly decision trees, can support banks in identifying hidden behavioral patterns, personalizing services, reducing customer churn, improving campaign effectiveness, and strengthening managerial decision-making in customer relationship management.</jats:p>

title: DetailScale-SR: Decoupling Restoration and Continuous Detail Control for Real-World Super-Resolution
authors: Shengchuan Gao; Zhongjie Duan; Yingda Chen; Jingjing Chen
abstract: Real-world image super-resolution often seeks the most detailed plausible reconstruction, although more detail is not always desirable. The same degraded image may require restrained restoration, faithful reconstruction, or enhanced visual detail according to user intent. We present DetailScale-SR, a preference-conditioned framework that continuously controls reconstructed detail for a fixed low-resolution input without altering the scene being restored. Rather than relying on post-processing or repeatedly rewriting prompts, it learns a continuous family of reconstructions while separating content recovery from detail preference. This enables a smooth transition from conservative restoration to richly textured results under consistent input and semantic constraints. Its controllable range also extends beyond conventional restoration: DetailScale-SR can enhance high-frequency structures and generate perceptually richer textures than the paired high-resolution reference. Text restoration is another distinct strength. For text-rich scenes, especially Chinese posters and signs, it recovers more legible and character-faithful text than prior generative SR methods under matched textual guidance. DetailScale-SR therefore unifies continuous detail control, beyond-reference enhancement, and reliable recovery of semantically important content. Our model is available at https://modelscope.cn/models/DiffSynth-Studio/Qwen-Image-2.1-SR

title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
authors: Siquan Huang; Yijiang Li; Xingfu Yan; Ningzhi Gao; Leyu Shi; Ying Gao
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.

title: Detect What You Need: Chain-of-Causal Reasoning for 3D Intent Grounding
authors: Zihao Zhang; Aming Wu; Yang Li; Yahong Han
abstract: Accurately matching human intentions in 3D space is an important goal of artificial intelligence. Recently, 3D Intention Grounding (3D-IG) has emerged, aiming to localize target 3D objects given a natural-language intent. Unlike conventional visual grounding with descriptive referring expressions, 3D-IG intents are abstract and non-descriptive, making object localization substantially more challenging. This requires inferring latent functional requirements from non-descriptive intents and aligning them with object-level 3D representations. However, existing methods largely rely on implicit intent-object matching, leading to logical gaps and limited interpretability, robustness, and generalization. To address these challenges, we propose Chain-of-Causal Reasoning (CoCR), a causality-inspired functional dependency reasoning framework that explicitly bridges abstract intentions and candidate objects through intermediate functional requirements. Specifically, CoCR progressively decomposes complex intents into ordered functional requirements, thereby forming an explicit intent-function-object reasoning chain that links abstract intentions to object suitability. Building on this chain, we construct a causality-inspired functional dependency graph to model requirement-attribute relationships and introduce a causal-visual alignment module that aligns function-aware representations with the geometric-semantic features of 3D point clouds, enabling bidirectional verification between structured functional reasoning and visual evidence. Extensive experiments on 3D Intention Grounding and 3D Visual Grounding demonstrate that our method enhances intent-aware object localization. Our code is available at https://2490o.github.io/CoCR.

title: Deterministic Temporal Embedding for Calcium Imaging Trace Extraction
authors: Qi Gao; Julius Beichert; Miriam Ratliff; Karl Rohr
abstract: Reliable extraction of calcium-dependent fluorescence traces in calcium imaging sequences requires identifying pixels whose fluorescence intensity reflects the same underlying cellular activity. We present a deterministic temporal embedding framework that maps pixel-wise fluorescence traces to a low-dimensional representation in which temporally coherent sources form spatially coherent regions. Starting from a fuzzy-neighborhood graph and spectral initialization, we optimize a class-balanced cross-entropy objective using exact sparse attraction and a deterministic particle-mesh decomposition of the dense repulsive interaction with sparse edge compensation, avoiding stochastic negative sampling. The resulting latent representation is spatially decoded into reliable source supports for trace extraction without imposing an explicit cellular shape prior. Experiments on synthetic and in vivo two-photon calcium imaging data demonstrate robust recovery of irregular and spatially touching sources together with efficient deterministic embedding optimization.

title: Development of the Range of Value (ROV) Method Based on Dynamic Weighting for Decision Support Systems
authors: Erlin Windia Ambarsari; Muhammad Waqas Arshad; Gustian Rama Putra; Yuwan Jumaryadi; Febryo Ponco Sulistyo
abstract: Decision-making in complex environments requires an evaluation framework capable of integrating multiple criteria with different levels of importance and performance. This study proposes Dynamic-ROV, a modified Rank Order Value approach designed to evaluate alternatives through data-driven criterion weighting and utility-based assessment. The proposed procedure consists of decision matrix normalization, standard deviation-based criterion weighting, best and worst utility evaluation, final utility calculation, and ranking. The approach was applied to the selection of nine manager candidates using seven evaluation criteria. Its robustness was assessed through 28 sensitivity scenarios involving positive and negative changes in individual criterion weights, while its ranking consistency was further examined against SAW, MOORA, GRA, and SMART. The results show that Candidate M-02 achieves the highest final utility value of 0.3862 and obtains the first rank, whereas Candidate M-08 records the lowest utility value of 0.1179 and ranks ninth. The sensitivity analysis indicates that the principal ranking structure remains stable across all tested scenarios, with M-02 consistently occupying the first position and M-08 remaining in the last position. Comparative evaluation also demonstrates that Dynamic-ROV produces ranking patterns that are broadly consistent with the established MCDM methods. These findings indicate that Dynamic-ROV provides a reliable and stable framework for multi-criteria evaluation while offering a data-oriented mechanism for determining criterion importance and assessing alternative performance. The proposed approach can therefore serve as an alternative decision-support method for selection problems in organizational settings.

title: Deviations from the NTK Regime in CNNs under Joint Depth-Width Scaling
authors: Maria Matveev; Pascal Esser; Gitta Kutyniok; Mariia Seleznova
abstract: The concentration and training-time constancy of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) depend on the interplay between network width, depth, and initialization. While joint depth-width scaling has been studied in fully-connected, residual, and recurrent networks, its effects in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) remain less understood. We investigate these effects numerically in CNNs, examining NTK dispersion at initialization and kernel rotation during training. Let depth $L$ be the number of convolutional layers, and width $C$ the number of channels per layer. We find that NTK dispersion increases with $L/C$ in the critical and chaotic initialization regimes, but remains small in the ordered regime. At critical initialization, dispersion curves approximately collapse as a function of $L/C$, suggesting a nontrivial joint scaling regime. During training, kernel rotation generally increases with $L/C$, even in the ordered regime where initial dispersion is small. Together, these results suggest that $L/C$ may govern NTK deviations from the infinite-width limit in certain regimes, and that NTK concentration at initialization and stability during training exhibit different scaling behaviors.

title: DfD-GS: Defocus Image Prior for Metric-Scale Single-View Depth Estimation and View Synthesis
authors: Shiori Ueda; Rinto Yagawa; Hideo Saito; Shohei Mori
abstract: Recovering metric-scale geometry from observations at a single viewpoint remains fundamentally ill-posed, limiting the reliability of novel view synthesis. Recent methods rely on learned monocular depth priors, which provide strong structural estimates but can suffer from scale ambiguity and dataset-dependent biases. We propose DfD-GS, a feed-forward framework that predicts a metric-scale 3D Gaussian scene representation from a single-view all-in-focus--defocused image pair. The key idea is to exploit defocus blur as a physical metric depth cue. DfD-GS first estimates a defocus-based metric disparity map from the all-in-focus--defocused image pair and the corresponding defocus strength. This estimate is used to align and refine a monocular depth prior to metric scale. Visible and hidden 3D Gaussians are then predicted for occlusion-aware novel view synthesis. Experiments on synthetic-defocus datasets constructed from Booster and Middlebury show that DfD-GS outperforms single-image baselines in metric depth estimation and novel view synthesis. On WildRGB-D, DfD-GS achieves lower AbsRel and LPIPS but higher depth RMSE than the single-image baselines. Additional analyses show that DfD-GS maintains a more stable metric scale under field-of-view changes. Qualitative results on a real dataset show recovery of the main scene structure under optical defocus.

title: Diagnosis is not a policy: a state-transition audit of caoability-conditioned test-time inference
authors: Yuchong Hu; Zhao Zhang; Kainan Liu; Haoyu Wang; Siyan Zhang; Jing Xiao
abstract: Test-time actions can satisfy retrieval, state-realization, program-consistency, or rendering objectives without correcting an answer. Test-time Error Response and Realizability Audit (TERRA) is an evaluation/auditing protocol, not a new inference algorithm. It uses a unified decomposition of intervention outcomes into applicability, target-state realization, endpoint translation, harm, and resource/inference cost. Paired comparisons fix the incoming state and evaluation conditions; cross-model analyses vary the receiving configuration. Executable financial reasoning experiments yield three findings: the same context expansion can harm one configuration and benefit another; sufficient evidence does not ensure correctness because configurations differ in evidence-to-answer translation; and diagnostic headroom---accuracy attainable with idealized diagnostic information over the measured baseline---plus local consistency does not ensure practical gains. Action value is $V(a\mid x,m)$, not diagnosis alone; diagnosis is not a deployable policy $π(a\mid x,m)$.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
authors: Jonathan Lichtle; Aymen Meddeb; Antonin Birot; Ibrahima Niang; Lisa Gastaud; Riyad Hanafi; Sofiane Dujardin; Corentin Selomme; Guillaume Cachard; Aghiles Hamroun; Grégory Kuchcinski; Su Hwan Kim; Bastien Le Guellec
abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
authors: Mengxiao Gao; Elly K. H. Hung; Yuchen Wu; Yi Yu
abstract:
Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks.
  Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
authors: Ivan Lee; Xingyu Xu; Yuejie Chi
abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

title: Digital Environments, Social Media, and Student Psychological Well-Being
authors: Richa Kapoor Mehra; Ridwan Ishola Mogaji
abstract: <jats:p>Technology in itself is not dangerous, but its uncontrolled use is. If used mindfully, it yields positive consequences; however, an uncontrolled technological explosion has a negative impact on the psychological well-being of all beings. This chapter explores how overexposure to the digital environment has negative repercussions for individuals' psychological well-being, leading to the eruption of negative emotions, such as anger and distress, and, in turn, a violent society. The present chapter proposes that social well-being is impossible without subjective well-being. To achieve subjective well-being, the chapter provides two solutions: looking inward is imperative, and subjective well-being through physical activity. Thus, well-being is a holistic concept and comprises both mental and physical well-being as a way forward for psychological well-being.</jats:p>

title: Digital Forensic Microbiology
authors: Baljeet Yadav; Anurag Gupta; Kumudkant Awasthi; Garima Awasthi; Mahipal Singh Sankhla; Sameer Saharan
abstract: <jats:p>Digital Forensic Microbiology combines digital forensics and traditional microbiology, enabling contamination source attribution and outbreak reconstruction for foodborne pathogens and other microorganisms. Digital forensics track evidence from collection to analysis. The increasing digitization of microbiology, driven by metagenomics and genome sequencing, prompts consideration of pathogen-related evidence that spans computer-based, archival, and research microbiology. When digital microbiological evidence accumulates, rigorously tracing its chain of custody, documenting data provenance, and assuring integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation, and reproducibility within both regulatory and non-regulatory contexts become vital. Digital forensic microbiology, encompassing machine-learning source attribution, AI-aided outbreak reconstruction, and comprehensive evidence-integrity protocols, supports a diverse range of microorganisms, acts spanning foodborne contaminations to healthcare-associated infections, and broad traces across the contamination continuum.</jats:p>

title: Digitalizing Early Project Delivery: Machine Learning–Enabled Urban Regulatory Intelligence for Governance and Feasibility Decisions
authors: Caroll Francesconi; Eric Forcael
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Some of the most complex challenges in construction projects arise during the early stages of project delivery, where regulatory uncertainty and limited visibility of urban conditions often constrain feasibility assessments and delay coordination among project stakeholders. In this context, this study proposes a machine learning–based approach that enables the exploration, clustering, and classification of urban areas using structured and georeferenced data from construction permits issued by government agencies. A midsized Latin American city is used as a case study, drawing on official permit records collected over a 15-year period. Unsupervised learning techniques (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" alttext="k" display="inline" overflow="scroll">
                        <mml:mi>k</mml:mi>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    -means) were applied to identify latent urban development patterns, followed by supervised models [random forest and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)] to classify construction zones based on functional and morphological features. The findings demonstrate how automated urban analysis generates consistent and interpretable indicators related to building density, location, and construction typology, which are directly relevant to early project delivery decisions. Beyond predictive performance, the study demonstrates that machine learning–powered urban regulatory intelligence can aid early project governance by decreasing information asymmetry, providing regulatory insights upfront, and fostering earlier alignment among project owners, designers, and contractors. These features are essential for collaborative delivery methods like integrated project delivery and lean project delivery, where early coordination, transparent information sharing, and a common understanding of constraints are crucial for ensuring project success.
                  </jats:p>

title: Digital Literacy and Critical Thinking as Defence
authors: Tendai Charles; Jocelin Hattar
abstract: <jats:p>Deepfakes and other forms of synthetic media destabilise perceptual and institutional cues of authenticity, increasing both the risk of misbelief and the risk of corrosive scepticism. This chapter aims to articulate an educationally actionable Deepfake Literacy Framework (DLF) that supports trust-calibrated judgement in digital knowledge ecosystems. Methodologically, the chapter employs conceptual synthesis and theory-building, using Conceptual Framework Analysis to build a five-domain competency model: (1) synthetic media awareness across text, audio, image, and video; (2) epistemic judgement and argument literacy for evaluating claims, evidence, and warrants under uncertainty; (3) verification practices and provenance reasoning, including the interpretation and limits of authenticity signals; (4) socio-technical and civic literacy addressing platform amplification, persuasion strategies, and responsible sharing; and (5) ethical AI communication and educational integrity, including transparent AI use, assessment design, and institutional communication protocols.</jats:p>

title: Digital Marketing in Thailand's Faith Economy
authors: Yarnaphat Shaengchart; Pongsakorn Limna; Sutithep Siripipattanakul; Penpim Phuangsuwan; Parichat Jaipong
abstract: <jats:p>Thailand's faith economy has been transformed by digital technologies, social media, and AI-driven communication systems. This chapter reviews digital marketing trends within Thailand's faith economy, focusing on consumer engagement through metaverse technologies and AI chatbots. Using a systematic qualitative review guided by the PRISMA framework, the study synthesizes literature on digital spirituality, influencer marketing, Mutelu culture, online merit-making, immersive technologies, and AI-enabled communication. The findings show that social media platforms, spiritual influencers, and immersive technologies enhance visibility, personalization, and engagement within digital spiritual ecosystems. However, the commercialization of spirituality also raises ethical concerns related to misinformation, authenticity, and consumer vulnerability. This chapter contributes to the literature on digital religion and faith-based marketing by explaining how technology and spirituality intersect within Thailand's evolving digital faith economy.</jats:p>

title: Digital Microbiology in Clinical Diagnostics and Pathogen Surveillance
authors: Sylvester Chibueze Izah; Ayebapreye Kari; Matthew Chidozie Ogwu
abstract: <jats:p>Digital microbiology is transforming clinical diagnostics and pathogen surveillance by leveraging technological advancements that increase the speed, accuracy, and precision of microbial detection. This chapter, per the authors, examines the integration of artificial intelligence with real-time genomic surveillance, predictive microbiology, precision approaches, and digital twins for simulation-based modeling, highlighting their role in enhancing infectious disease management. These innovations facilitate rapid identification and monitoring of pathogens, improving clinical outcomes and public health responses. Implementation challenges, including infrastructure constraints, workforce training, equitable access, data privacy, validation, and regulatory considerations, are also addressed. Emphasizing collaborative research, strategic policymaking, and practical deployment, this chapter underscores the potential of digital microbiology to strengthen global health security and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>

title: Digital One Health Biosurveillance
authors: Godgift Nabebe; Ebinyo Rebecca Aseibai; Kingsley Excel Dunga; Sylvester Chibueze Izah; Vivian Ibienebakabobo Promise; Matthew Chidozie Ogwu
abstract: <jats:p>Digital transformation is reshaping microbiology from specimen processing and molecular diagnostics to population-scale biosurveillance. This chapter examines digital One Health biosurveillance as an integrated framework that connects microbial, clinical, veterinary, plant, food, wastewater, environmental, genomic, geospatial, and sensor data across human, animal, plant, and ecosystem interfaces. It focuses on smart laboratory automation, laboratory information systems, sequencing and metagenomics, GIS, remote sensing, Internet of Things platforms, machine learning, and AI-assisted early warning. Applications in zoonoses, antimicrobial resistance, food- and waterborne infections, wastewater surveillance, and climate-sensitive microbial risks are critically reviewed. Emphasis is placed on interoperability, data quality, validation, privacy, cybersecurity, equity, and human oversight. The chapter argues that digital One Health systems are most effective when technology is embedded in robust laboratory networks, standards-based data exchange, and actionable public-health workflows</jats:p>

title: Digital Predictive Microbiology and Quantitative Risk Assessment
authors: Matthew Chidozie Ogwu; Olugbemiga Ojo Aliu; Sylvester Chibueze Izah
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the evolution of predictive microbiology from classical growth models to modern digital predictive microbiology and positions predictive analytics as the critical link between microbial data ecosystems and evidence-based decision support. It reviews the foundations of digital predictive microbiology, including data acquisition, integration, model development, validation, uncertainty analysis, and decision translation, and synthesizes major modeling approaches encompassing mechanistic, statistical, Bayesian, machine learning, hybrid, and digital twin frameworks. The chapter further explores the integration of quantitative microbial risk assessment with AI-enabled predictive systems and highlights applications across food safety, healthcare, wastewater surveillance, environmental monitoring, agriculture, industrial biotechnology, and One Health. Ethical governance, model transparency, explainable AI, and regulatory considerations are discussed as essential requirements for responsible implementation.</jats:p>

title: Digital Transformation and Accounting Information Quality: The Moderating Role of Environmental Uncertainty
authors: mehdi Maranjori
abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to explain the moderating role of environmental uncertainty in the relationship between digital transformation and accounting information quality among firms listed on the Tehran Stock Exchange. This applied study employed a descriptive-correlational and ex post facto research design based on panel data. The statistical population consisted of all firms active on the Tehran Stock Exchange from 2020 to 2024. After applying systematic elimination criteria, 106 firms were selected as the final sample. Accounting information quality was measured through discretionary accruals using the Jones model. Digital transformation was operationalized as a dummy variable indicating whether the firm had invested in technology and digitalization, and environmental uncertainty was measured based on sales fluctuations. The research hypotheses were tested using multivariate regression analysis with panel data and fixed-effects estimation in EViews 8. The first regression model was statistically significant, with an F-statistic of 14.536 and a significance level of 0.000. The coefficient of determination and adjusted coefficient of determination were 0.425 and 0.421, respectively. Digital transformation had a positive and statistically significant effect on accounting information quality, as indicated by a coefficient of 0.596, a t-statistic of 3.857, and a significance level of 0.001. The second regression model was also statistically significant, with an F-statistic of 15.251 and a significance level of 0.001. The adjusted coefficient of determination was 0.382. The interaction effect between digital transformation and environmental uncertainty was positive and statistically significant, with a coefficient of 0.251, a t-statistic of 2.221, and a significance level of 0.034. The findings indicate that digital transformation enhances accounting information quality by improving transparency, reducing information asymmetry, and limiting opportunistic managerial behavior. Environmental uncertainty also significantly moderates this relationship, highlighting the importance of digital technologies for maintaining accounting information quality under unstable business conditions.</jats:p>

title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
authors: Erico Kayumba Mutonkole; Olasupo Ajayi; Omowunmi Isafiade
abstract: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.

title: DiLE: Discrimination-Aware Latent-Space Learning for Universal Multimodal Embeddings
authors: Ben Kang; Junda Wang; Yuxuan Yuan; Hang Li; Yuhan Liu; Xin Chen; Wanting Geng; Tong Lin; Pei Fu; Dong Wang; Jian Luan; Huchuan Lu
abstract: Multimodal large language models have greatly improved input understanding in universal multimodal embedding models. However, this understanding does not ensure that their embeddings preserve the evidence needed to distinguish relevant items from confusable alternatives. To preserve essential discriminative evidence in embeddings, this paper proposes DiLE, a discrimination-aware latent-space learning framework that combines task guidance with on-policy retrieval feedback. Specifically, a few learnable queries are used to encode task-relevant information in a compact latent space. Reasoning instructions and auxiliary answer-generation supervision shape these representations to support both task understanding and retrieval discrimination. To address task-specific discriminative needs, we design shared-private expert adaptation that integrates cross-task knowledge sharing with task-specific representation learning. Building on this, the on-policy hard-negative distillation is introduced: the student retrieves confusable candidates, and a reverse KL divergence objective aligns its embedding-based similarity distribution with the teacher's fine-grained relevance distribution over these candidates. Candidates are periodically refreshed using updated student snapshots, tying teacher supervision to the student's evolving retrieval behavior and confusions. Across four model configurations that span two backbone generations, DiLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MMEB-v2, UVRB, and MRMR, demonstrating its effectiveness across modalities and tasks.

title: Dimension-Free Buffer Bounds for Compressed-Momentum Error Feedback
authors: Alireza Moayedikia
abstract: Analyses of error feedback bound the memory buffer through a compressor contraction constant -- $r/p$ for the best rank-$r$ approximation of a $p$-dimensional spectrum -- which survives into the rate. We show it need not appear at all. When the compressed momentum is re-injected into the pre-compression accumulator, the previous compressed momentum $β_1 M_{t-1}$ is an admissible competitor in the projection, and the buffer obeys $\|E_t\|_F \le (1-β_1)\|G_t\|_F + γ\|E_{t-1}\|_F$, free of the dimensions $m,n$ and of the rank $r$. The argument uses only that the compressor is a metric projection onto a closed cone, so it covers top-$k$ selection as well as truncated SVD, holds for every selection from the projection set with no condition on singular-value crossings, and in its trajectory-tracking form assumes nothing about the gradients. In the two-stage template of the standard analyses it replaces a Stage-2 constant of order $p^2/r^2$ by one of order $1$, against $Θ(p/r)$ for the sharpest contraction-based bounds. Transferring the full rate costs a leakage term, which we bound by the step-weighted gradient mass $\sum_{u\le t}η_u\|G_u\|_F$ and show tight up to a factor $\sqrt{2}$; the price is an additive $O(\log^2 T)$ floor, not a slower rate. On BERT fine-tuning at rank ratio $32/768$ the feedback decay costs under $0.008$ validation $F_1$.

title: Direct3D-V3: Latent-Free Diffusion Transformers in the Native Voxel Domain
authors: Shuang Wu; Jiachen Qian; Youtian Lin; Feihu Zhang; Philip Torr; Yao Yao; Xun Cao
abstract: Native 3D generation has largely been built around latent diffusion, with recent advances concentrating on stronger variational autoencoders (VAE) and increasingly elaborate latent representations, from vecset and triplanes to structured sparse voxels. Despite their architectural differences, these methods all share the same premise: geometry is first compressed into a latent space and only then modeled by the generator. We take a different route and propose Direct3D-V3, a latent-free diffusion transformer (DiT) framework that discards the VAE altogether and operates in the native voxel domain, directly modeling raw SDF voxel grids during both training and sampling. To make this direct voxel formulation geometrically reliable, we introduce an implicit manifold regularization over neighboring voxels to suppress non-watertight surfaces, and convert predicted SDF grids into meshes via Marching Cubes so that rendered normal losses can supervise the model directly from its predicted SDF. To improve alignment between the conditioning image and generated geometry, Direct3D-V3 also predicts the camera parameters of the conditioning image as an auxiliary task, encouraging the DiT to learn the mapping from image observations to 3D shape. This latent-free design removes the reconstruction bottleneck, brings training under an objective in the native voxel domain, and yields meshes with substantially richer local detail. The predicted camera and native SDF voxel output further make Direct3D-V3 extensible to generative reconstruction, where diffusion is interleaved with normal-guided refinement to improve alignment with the observed view while the generative prior completes unseen regions. Project page: https://dreamtechai.github.io/Direct3D-V3.

title: Discovering Superior Intelligence
authors: Alexander Wendt
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter distinguishes unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) from extraterrestrials, reviews official recognition of UAP, and frames the extraterrestrial hypothesis as a realistic but unproven explanation. It traces the shift from extraterrestrial to nonhuman intelligence, introduces superior intelligence to highlight asymmetry and vulnerability, and explains how the ultra-terrestrial hypothesis reshapes debates about distance and evidence. The chapter evaluates physical evidence, testimonial evidence, and behavioral evidence; argues that anomalous UAP performance implies advanced technology and intentional agency; and rebuts claims that the hypothesis lacks evidence. It challenges distance and irrationality objections through technological, temporal, and interest-based reasoning; situates the debate within the Fermi paradox; and preserves analytic agnosticism while sustaining explanatory plausibility. Finally, the chapter presents discovery as a protracted scientific process shaped by inference, secrecy, politics, and consensus formation rather than a single revelatory event.</jats:p>

title: Disentangling Monitor Hardware Artifacts and Smoothing Lag for Shift-Robust Intraoperative EEG and Hemodynamic Risk Calibration
authors: Zeyu Jia
abstract: Commercial intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) and blood pressure monitors introduce cyclic impedance pulses, smoothing delays, direct-current (DC) drift, and cuff holds that confound risk forecasting and uncertainty calibration. We developed a causal signal-conditioning and shift-robust conformal calibration framework across 5,439 public anesthesia procedures. Streaming filters blank 10.13-min 64-Hz impedance checks, apply unclipped post-notch conditioning, separate 63-s suppression-ratio lag, and distinguish three-channel cuff inflations from dropouts across propofol-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA; N = 3,214), volatile anesthesia (N = 2,046), European endoscopy sedation (N = 171), and DC-coupled surgery (N = 8). De-impedanced cortical tree ensembles were compared against deep sequence models, paired with patient-cluster Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted Conformal Risk Control (CRC) and lag-buffered online Conformal Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) tracking. Pre-filter blanking removed 97.90% and 97.60% of false flatline conflicts while preserving 99.23% and 98.96% of deep suppression. On unseen TIVA surgeries (N = 525), cortical features achieved area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) 0.3135 (1.94% prevalence) and 0.1627 (0.82% lag-free prevalence), with no detectable difference from deep encoders (p >= 0.36) and no cortical gain for hypotension (0.3432 vs. 0.3437, p = 0.784). Zero-retraining volatile transfer (N = 1,048) showed no detectable difference from an end-tidal gas oracle on lag-free suppression (0.0820 vs. 0.0736, p = 0.472). Subgroup-Covariate-Weighted CRC bounded all 70 TIVA shift cells at <= 4.38% (alpha = 5.0%) in 66.32 ms per 30-s epoch. Causal artifact disentangling and shift-aware conformal calibration support reliable real-time intraoperative risk bounds within explicit physiological observability limits.

title: Dissecting the Relationship Between Emotional Intelligence and Job Performance Using PLS-SEM
authors: Shamli Sharma; Kamal Preet; Neema Gupta; Neha Verma
abstract: <jats:p>Emotional Intelligence (EI) is progressively regarded as a key aspect in determining how well employees perform, especially in service-focused fields like banking. The paper explores how EI affects the Job Performance (JP) of personnel working in public sector banks in India. To investigate this, a descriptive research method is used and gathered primary data from 400 employees at branches of SBI and PNB in Himachal Pradesh, utilizing a structured questionnaire. Using SmartPLS 4 for PLS- SEM, measurement model and structural linkages are assessed. Results demonstrate that various dimensions of EI have a statistically significant and positive impact on JP. This highlights value of emotional skills in fostering employee adaptability, resilience, and productivity. The study expands present literature by presenting a multi-faceted view of linkage between EI and JP in realm of public banking. Additionally, it presents practical recommendations for HR management, highlighting need to incorporate EI into training, performance management, and organizational policies to maximize efficiency.</jats:p>

title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
authors: Aviv Yossef; Or Patashnik; Or Zamir
abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence
authors: Mariya
abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days null. Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, yet the day-to-day variance of the fraction of cells covered is roughly 3 to 10 times what independent cells would give, and misses cluster in time; both effects grow with lead time for the CNN, also appear for HRES, and are shared by all methods. An oracle that divides each day's normalised errors by that day's mean removes 81 to 92 percent of the excess dispersion for the CNN and 93 to 98 percent for HRES, so days of large errors across much of the grid account for most of it. A day-scale predicted from seasonal terms and already-verified errors lowers the overdispersion index without widening intervals but improves interval score by at most 0.6 percent; on HRES from 12 hours to 3 days it has the lowest overdispersion index while ACI or season-conditional calibration has the best interval score, so no method is best on both. The study covers one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters.

title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
authors: Fernando Berzal
abstract:
Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not).
  However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well.
  Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Montúfar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

title: dLoop: Looped Diffusion Language Models via Recurrent Latent Refinement
authors: Handa Li; Pengxiang Li; Mingyu Cao; Xilu Wang; Li Shen; Da Li; Lu Yin
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support parallel generation, yet they often require many denoising steps because only a fraction of token predictions are sufficiently reliable to be committed at each step. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize confidence learning or commitment policies. However, these approaches operate on the outputs of a single denoising forward pass, in which information from the prompt, previously committed tokens, and uncommitted positions may not yet be fully integrated. Consequently, some predictions remain under-refined when the commitment decision is made, and modifying the commitment policy alone cannot improve their underlying representations. We introduce dLoop, which restructures a pretrained diffusion language model into a Prelude-Loop-Coda architecture and recurrently applies a parameter-shared intermediate block to the same partially masked state. Rather than advancing the denoising process, each additional loop provides further latent computation, allowing information distributed across uncommitted positions to continue interacting and become more fully integrated before commitment. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval show that dLoop achieves the highest or tied-highest accuracy on every benchmark. With tokens per forward pass (TPF) adjusted for loop computation, it outperforms Fast-dLLM in both accuracy and TPF on all four benchmarks and dParallel on three, and is more accurate than d3LLM on all four, while d3LLM attains higher TPF; no compared method surpasses dLoop in both. Mechanistic analyses show that extra loops mainly help on slow, unstable trajectories and that updates at uncommitted positions drive changes in token decisions and later generation. Pre-commitment latent computation thus makes predictions more reliable, offering a route to DLM acceleration distinct from forcing confidence through the training loss.

title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies
authors: Jun Xia; Shangwen Wang; Jun Ma; Ruichao Ren; Zhouyang Jia; Xin Zhao; Huijun Liu; Jie Yu
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
authors: Abdiaziz Muse; Jiju Poovvancheri
abstract: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
authors: Pengju Liu; Caiwen Ding
abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

title: Do Deep Stereo Models Learn Shape Priors?
authors: Linbo Tang; Aneel Damaraju; Todd Zickler
abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.

title: Does It Depend on the Split? Frozen Satellite Features vs. Fine-Tuned CNNs for Tree Species Mapping
authors: Dharani Deivasihamani; Nandakishore Puttashamachar
abstract: Self-supervised foundation models are often said to need fewer labels than supervised training. We test this on a forestry task: classifying 20 tree species classes in 0.2 m aerial images from the TreeSatAI dataset. We compare a frozen DINOv3 model pretrained on 493 million satellite images, with only a linear classifier trained on top, against an ImageNet ResNet-50 that is fine-tuned end to end. On the official split, fine-tuning wins clearly (macro F1 0.764 vs. 0.685). However, 28.8% of the official test patches overlap a training or validation patch, and copying the label of the nearest such patch is correct for 83.6% of them. We therefore build a spatial split that holds out whole 2 km squares with a 200 m buffer. On this split the comparison becomes inconclusive (0.648 vs. 0.640, paired 95% CI of the difference [-0.054, 0.016]), and the learning curves of the two models overlap at every label budget from 343 to 33,126 training patches. On the five rarest classes, the frozen model achieves a higher mean F1 (0.566 vs. 0.445), although the confidence interval for this difference includes zero ([-0.05, 0.23]). Diagnostics show that the frozen features mainly miss differences between closely related species, such as the two native oaks. Choosing the input size and layer on validation data (224 px, block 16) raises the frozen model to 0.662 on the spatial split. A comparison that looks decisive on the official split is thus inconclusive under geographically separated evaluation. We release the spatial split and our code.

title: Does the Action Matter? Probing Action-Conditioned Semantic Forecasting as a World Model for Autonomous Driving
authors: Binay Kumar Singh; Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
abstract: World models are increasingly used in autonomous driving to predict how a scene evolves under the ego vehicle's actions, supporting counterfactual reasoning and model-based planning. However, existing evaluations focus on prediction fidelity and planning performance, and rarely verify that the predictions depend on the conditioning action. In this paper, we study action dependence in action-conditioned semantic forecasting, which predicts future semantic segmentation from past segmentations and the ego action. We compare a forecaster with feature-wise and input-level action conditioning against an identical model without action input, and measure action dependence with test-time action interventions scored by standard segmentation metrics. The evaluation is validated in a synthetic environment with known action-dependent dynamics and applied to Cityscapes and BDD100K, both within each dataset and across the two vehicle platforms. Experiments show that the executed action improves mid-term mIoU by at most 2.5 points on Cityscapes and 0.6 points on BDD100K, whereas a wrong action reduces it by up to 23.2 and 7.0 points, below the model without action input. On real data, feature-wise conditioning depends 1.6 times more on the action than input-level conditioning at similar accuracy, whereas both depend on it equally in the synthetic environment, where the history does not determine the action. These results show that an accuracy gain indicates that a driving world model uses its action, but not how strongly its forecasts depend on it. Code is available at https://github.com/binayksingh/does-action-matter.

title: Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model
authors: Diaoxuan He; Linqian Wu
abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.

title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
authors: Biswa Sengupta
abstract: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.

title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
authors: Shobhita Sundaram; Cansu Sancaktar; Phillip Isola
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

title: Domain-Aware Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Spacecraft Pose Estimation under Sim-to-Real Shift
authors: Nidhal Eddine Chenni; Arunkumar Rathinam; Djamila Aouada
abstract: Autonomous rendezvous and proximity operations require not only an accurate estimate of the pose of the target spacecraft, but also a reliable indication of when this estimate can be trusted. Conformal prediction provides such an indication with a formal guarantee, by producing pose uncertainty sets that contain the true pose with a specified probability. Such a guarantee, however, assumes that calibration and test data follow the same distribution, an assumption that is violated in orbital perception, where labelled calibration images are available only from synthetic renderings while operational images are real. In this work, we show on the SPEED+ dataset that conformal pose estimation calibrated on synthetic images loses its coverage guarantee on real images, and that many of the resulting failures are silent: the predicted pose set appears valid but excludes the true pose. To address this, we calibrate on synthetic images translated to the appearance of real images. Since translation alters appearance while preserving geometry, the synthetic pose labels remain valid and no labelled real images are required. Experiments with two translation models show that this calibration restores coverage above the specified level for miscoverage levels of 0.1 and above, and reduces silent failures from up to 43.5% to at most 3.3% of the test images, bringing conformal pose estimation a step closer to trustworthy deployment in space.

title: Don't Lose the Future: Latent-Aware 4-Bit Quantization of World Action Models
authors: Yichen Guo; Yanlong Chen; Xinyue Zhang; Mohan Liu; Song Zhang; Yawei Li
abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict how a scene will evolve and condition their actions on this predicted future. Deploying them on a robot's onboard computer calls for 4-bit weights, activations and key-value caches (W4A4KV4). Existing 4-bit quantizers for WAMs preserve the generated action, and estimate sensitivity one denoising step at a time. However, they fail to preserve the fidelity of the predicted future: once the action pathway is protected, the remaining action error enters mostly through a degraded future that none of them deliberately protects. We propose LAQ, a latent-aware quantization framework that preserves the predicted future where it is written, stored and read. Specifically, we introduce a reader metric, which measures future error by its effect on the action, and a read count, which weights each rounding error by the number of denoising steps that read it. Together they give the allocation of precision over activations and caches a closed-form solution. We further develop gaze-guided refinement, which gives the tokens the action attends to a second 4-bit pass in the denoising loop and in the cache. All weights stay at 4 bits, with no high-precision branch and no per-task recalibration. On the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, LAQ reaches 76.4% and 83.3% average success on Fast-WAM and Cosmos-Policy, within 1.2 percentage points of the 16-bit models and all above the baselines with 16-bit KV caches. It compresses the model by 3.8x, reduces the peak GPU memory of the whole policy by 2.3x, and runs 1.66x faster than the 16-bit model. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, it reaches 47.0% average success over three tasks, against 52.0% for the 16-bit model and 30.0% higher than QuaRot.

title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
authors: {'_id': '6aff64f38c0c69ddd0a947d5', 'user': {'_id': '655ce1466a37ab8e1c3de260', 'avatarUrl': '/avatars/853c77029662b91108d0392fa95ca8a8.svg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'sadeghi', 'user': 'afshinsadeghi', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'afshinsadeghi'}, 'name': 'Afshin Sadeghi', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-19T21:34:09.306Z', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6aff64f38c0c69ddd0a947d6', 'name': 'Daniel Becker', 'hidden': False}
abstract:
A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator.
  The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

title: DORMS: Image Segmentation via Depth-Ordered Region Merge Trees
authors: Furkan Mumcu; Yasin Yilmaz
abstract: We introduce DORMS (Depth-Ordered Region Merging for Segmentation), a purely algorithmic approach to image segmentation from monocular depth maps, requiring no neural networks or learned parameters in the segmentation process. An off-the-shelf monocular depth estimator provides the input depth maps. Our method constructs depth-ordered merge trees through a deterministic union-find sweep, combining component area, depth persistence, and spatial contact constraints to guide region merging.
