title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
authors: Sikha O K; Abdollah Moslemi; Elham Alizadeh; Ludovic Humbert; Miguel A. Gonzalez Ballester; Jerome Noailly
abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
authors: Zihan Wang; Jianzhe Li; Zhenyi Zhang; Peijie Zhou
abstract: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

title: Embedding Happiness at Workplace for Quality of Work Life: Challenges and Opportunities
authors: Randa El Bedawy
abstract: ‘Quality of Work Life’ has become progressively a popular concept recently, as it reflects the means that an organization can apply to safeguard the inclusive well-being of its employees instead of concentrating just on the job aspects. The ‘Happiness at Workplace’ is a concept that got as well the attention of various researchers and practitioners lately in particular after pandemic of COVID -19, to find out its best practices and importance at various contexts to avoid the stress of employees. In fact, happiness is a leading concern that all people aim to acquire along life, including employees as well as a main driver to succeed at workplace. This chapter discusses happiness at workplace as evaluated between theory and practice, as well its challenges and opportunities, adding to shedding the light on required pillars and its impact on employees’ performance as a reflection of a quality of work life. The chapter proposes as well the organizations’ role to embed employees’ happiness at workplace.

title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search
authors: {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebdc', 'name': 'Siqiao Xue', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebdd', 'user': {'_id': '6430bdd8cd31d174a9f900fb', 'avatarUrl': 'https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/noauth/Y9SPnRfpKSbYc7MhNdP-H.jpeg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'Ziyin Zhang', 'user': 'Geralt-Targaryen', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'Geralt-Targaryen'}, 'name': 'Ziyin Zhang', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-20T08:45:05.151Z', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebde', 'name': 'Zihan Liao', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebdf', 'name': 'Jin Qin', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebe0', 'name': 'Yixiang Mu', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afd490243cedf0e6abcebe1', 'user': {'_id': '6837243353739ee0d588d04c', 'avatarUrl': 'https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/6837243353739ee0d588d04c/QY5Rt6vrt36pxNrwAi9yx.jpeg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'Hang Yu', 'user': 'fhlyhv', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'fhlyhv'}, 'name': 'Hang Yu', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-21T16:45:04.673Z', 'hidden': False}
abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
authors: Zongyuan Wu; Xin Wang; Tongtong Feng; Yuan Meng; Zeyang Zhang; Ling Feng; Wenwu Zhu
abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

title: Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence and Their Implications in Materials Engineering
authors: Satyam S. Sahay; Joshua Stuckner
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) has seen accelerated maturity with diverse industrial applications during the last decade. This article explains machine learning in materials engineering. It discusses causal inference and its opportunities in materials engineering. The article describes physics-informed neural networks and their application in materials engineering. It presents AI applications in additive manufacturing. The article provides an overview on generative AI and its near-term applications in materials engineering.</jats:p>

title: Emotion-Aware Interventions
authors: Nadya Nurzahida Gusti
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how emotion-aware computing moves from psychological theory into measurable signals an AI-enabled wellness system can sense, interpret, and act on. Psychological theory and the field's computing history set up a review of the wearable, facial, vocal, and behavioral sensing methods now capable of reading emotion in real time. Personalization engines take over next, using dynamic user profiles, reinforcement learning, and context-aware delivery to turn a sensed emotional state into a tailored response rather than a one-size-fits-all script. Applications in mental health, chronic illness, and everyday well-being supply the evidence, showing where the approach already helps and where support remains thin. The chapter closes by weighing the privacy and fairness risks of sensing and acting on someone's emotions against the benefits, and argues that such systems should extend human care and clinical judgment, not replace them.</jats:p>

title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
authors: Jiakun Li; Eric F. Lock
abstract: Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.

title: End-to-End Landsat Land Surface Temperature Reconstruction with AlphaEarth Embeddings
authors: Shengjie Liu
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) data at Landsat's 30 m resolution is important for many applications, but cloud contamination prevents its spatially continuous observations. Here, we propose A$^2$E$^2$, an end-to-end U-Net that integrates annual temperature cycle (ATC), coarse LST from Earth system modeling, and AlphaEarth embeddings for Landsat LST reconstruction. The ATC supplies a physics-guided thermal prior, the coarse LST provides a temporal background, and the U-Net converts the embedding field into day-specific fine-scale correction using observed pixels. Experimental results on four seasonally distributed Landsat 8/9 scenes over New York City in 2022 show that A$^2$E$^2$ achieves 0.78 K mean absolute error and 1.01 K root mean squared error, reducing error by 60.1% relative to baseline method without spatial correction and by 3.7% relative to the same U-Net guided by annual mean spectral reflectance. Sensitivity analysis shows stable performance regardless of distance to clear pixels and percentage of blocked pixels. Independent validation with ECOSTRESS LST shows that Earth foundation model embeddings have better performance than annual mean spectral bands for LST reconstruction.

title: Energy estimates of open-weight large language models across stated food weights: a dose-response evaluation
authors: Donato Riccio; Fabrizio Maturo; Iulia Brezeanu
abstract: We tested whether energy estimates of open-weight large language models (LLMs) scale proportionally with an exactly stated food weight, and whether computing energy density times weight removes the error. Under a prespecified protocol, seven open-weight LLMs estimated the energy of 168 randomly drawn foods from the USDA Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies at nine stated weights, from 0.25 to 4 times the default amount. The primary outcome was the elasticity of the estimate with respect to weight (1: proportional scaling). A two-step estimate multiplied each model's own stated energy density by the weight in code. All seven models compressed their estimates, with elasticities from 0.548 to 0.979 (every 95% CI below 1); four compressed severely (0.548 to 0.709). These four overestimated a quarter of the default amount by 47% to 130% and underestimated four times it by 20% to 34%. Supplying the density restored near-proportional scaling in three of the four, and the two-step estimate cut the typical error factor at these extremes from 1.47-2.43 to 1.20-1.38. Compression persisted at full precision and grew in five of seven models under a plain question. The models hold the energy densities needed for proportional scaling and answer near a typical serving, reproducing the flat-slope syndrome of dietary recall. Accuracy at usual portions does not reveal it. Food-logging tools should compute the energy of weighed entries as density times weight, and evaluations should test fixed foods across stated weights.

title: Engineering Human-in-the-Loop Control for Agentic AI
authors: Ganesh Harke
abstract: <jats:p>The transition from Predictive to Agentic AI transforms investment management systems from linear decision pipelines into recursive orchestrators, creating a governance deficit at the intersection of Models, Markets, and Mandates. Unlike passive predictive models, autonomous agents possess actionable intelligence that challenges the non-delegable nature of fiduciary duty. This chapter proposes an engineering-led framework to bridge this accountability gap by replacing manual oversight with a rigorous Control Plane architecture. It develops a taxonomy of Human-in-the-Loop designs, including the Centaur (Signal Generation), Governor (Execution), and Risk Crew (Incident Response) models, mapped to specific latency and risk profiles. By synthesizing recent engineering patterns such as defense prompts and state-aware kill switches, the chapter shows how to impose deterministic constraints on probabilistic planners. Finally, it reframes Chain-of-Thought logging as a structural mechanism for process auditability, ensuring that autonomous investment decisions meet the regulatory standards.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Active Learning Performance with Initial Data Selection Based on Foundation Models
authors: Mohammad Mirzaee; Mehrshad Fallah Estalkhzir; Mohammad Reza Mohammadi
abstract: In active object detection, selecting the initial labeled pool is essential, especially in complex datasets with expensive labeling and low resource budget. This study presents an active learning framework designed to optimize the initial training cycle of active learning for the object detection task. Our approach diverges from traditional methods by utilizing feature-based clustering from the YOLO-World model and refining images based on objectness scores rather than relying on uncertainty sampling in the initial cycle. This approach focuses on finding samples with various features and emphasizes training in areas where the foundation model is most confident. Doing so helps the model better understand different types of objects. For subsequent cycles, we employ a consistency-based sampling technique to maintain the robustness of the training process. To evaluate our method, we use two complex datasets called Aquarium and NWPU VHR-10, which are well known for their diverse object sizes and challenging conditions. In the NWPU dataset, our method increases mAP50 by an average of 6.6% in image-based evaluation. Moreover, the image refinement method shows an improvement of approximately 11% in object-based evaluation. The results show improvements in model performance and labeling time, demonstrating the advantages of using foundation models in early cycles of active learning. An implementation of the algorithm is available at https://github.com/Mhrshd-fllh/ALBoost-FM

title: Enhancing Consumer Engagement in Sustainable Wellness Tourism Through Metaverse and AI Chatbot Integration
authors: Supakorn Suradinkura; Tanpat Kraiwanit; Chanin Amornbuth; Kanin Khaniyao; Rosatorn Toobunterng
abstract: <jats:p>Wellness tourism is central to Thailand's service economy and requires digital engagement strategies that preserve trust, cultural authenticity, safety, and sustainability. This chapter uses an empirical-to-conceptual approach, integrating survey evidence with emerging metaverse and artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot applications. A cross-sectional survey using convenience sampling of 542 Thai wellness tourists in Bangkok found very high perceptions of sustainable wellness tourism. Destination image and identity, activity diversity and quality, and safety, cleanliness, and accessibility significantly influenced perceptions. Based on these findings, a conceptual framework proposes AI chatbots and metaverse technologies to enhance immersive, personalized, and sustainable wellness tourism experiences. The metaverse–AI chatbot component is a theory-informed design extension, not a test of technology effects, as the original survey did not measure technology use. It bridges destination evidence with digital engagement design and proposes testable hypotheses for future research.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Mental Health with Artificial Intelligence: Current Trends and Future Prospects
authors: D. Olawade; O. Wada; A. Odetayo; A. C. David-Olawade; Fiyinfoluwa Asaolu; J. Eberhardt
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in various fields

title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
authors: Jingyi Sun
abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

title: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients for Stable Feature Attribution
authors: Rukmangadh Sai Myana; Sumit Kumar Jha; Yanzhao Wu
abstract: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) are widely used to interpret neural networks, yet imperceptible input perturbations can drastically alter their attribution maps while leaving model predictions unchanged. We introduce Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG), a path-based attribution method that intrinsically attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path using maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature parameter $τ$. We quantify the effect of the entropy-regularized weighting on attribution stability by using the Lipschitz properties of the model and its gradients. We decompose the attribution change under an input perturbation into a model-response term, whose bound is $τ$-independent, and a weight-variation term, whose bound decreases at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/(2τ))$. Their ratio $R(τ)$ characterizes the trade-off between gradient information and attribution stability. We further add a new dimension to attribution evaluation by adapting classical noise estimators into two metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P, that quantify attribution noise. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet datasets, our experiments show that, relative to the next-best method, ERIG remains comparable on ranking-based fidelity metrics while improving localization by approximately 24% and attribution stability by approximately 47-fold on average, reaching up to four orders of magnitude improvement over IG, all at negligible additional computational cost.

title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
authors: Biswa Sengupta; Jinhua Wang; Léo Maxime Brunswic
abstract: Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $σ^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically principled changes that do not act on the measured miscalibration, namely exact polar factors, steepest-descent input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.

title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
authors: Michael Liaofan Liu; Joe Kileel
abstract: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.

title: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings
authors: Haijun He; Fei Li; Donghong Ji; Junjun He
abstract: Medical-image embeddings are increasingly shared in place of raw images for authorized downstream tasks, yet they may reveal sensitive attributes. Standard concept-erasure methods target population-level guardedness. However, we prove that, when binary task and sensitive labels are associated, global and task-conditional linear guardedness cannot both hold while a nonzero linear task signal is preserved, so global erasure must either eliminate that signal or retain task-conditional linear leakage. We further show how global erasure affects linear readers' discrimination between positive and negative samples with different sensitive attributes, deriving an approximate closed-form prediction of its utility cost from pre-erasure statistics. Motivated by this conflict, we introduce Task-Conditional LEACE (TC-LEACE), a closed-form variant of LEACE that enforces linear guardedness within each task stratum of its fitting data. We evaluate four vision foundation models on 85 CelebA attribute pairs spanning a broad range of associations. After LEACE, conditional leakage persists across all four encoders, the discrepancy between marginal and conditional audits increases with association strength, and predicted utility costs track observed losses. We then examine hospital chest radiographs using three foundation models, including two biomedical models, in which chest-tube status is strongly associated with diagnosis. Although a marginal attack on LEACE-erased embeddings underperforms a diagnosis-only reference, chest-tube status remains detectable within diagnosis strata. TC-LEACE recovers most of LEACE's linear task-utility loss while keeping task-conditional leakage within a prespecified margin of LEACE's.

title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
authors: George Giapitzakis; Ankur Moitra; Andrej Risteski; Dhruv Rohatgi
abstract:
Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path.
  In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$.
  We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

title: Ethical Considerations in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Design
authors: Qian Jiang; Kin Wai Michael Siu
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied in various scopes. Ethical issues related to this field, such as privacy breaches, data bias, etc., have been brought to the forefront. In the field of design, there are challenges in defining the originality of AI works and the role of human beings. how to cultivate future designers with good moral character and behavior in the age of AI is a key topic of discussion for design education. This paper addresses the rapid adoption of AI into design, which focuses on the ethical considerations in Asia. Using the historical review and comparison, the core principle of ethics in Asian context is analyzed. Current views of Chinese designers and educators on the integration of AI and design are found out by questionnaire. In the end, an ethical framework is proposed. The paper advocates the need for culturally sensitive ethical frameworks in Asian design practices.</jats:p>

title: Ethical principles for artificial intelligence in education
authors: Andy Nguyen; H. Ngo; Yvonne Hong; Belle Dang; Bich-Phuong Thi Nguyen
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has the potential to transform the educational landscape and influence the role of all involved stakeholders. In recent years, the applications of AIED have been gradually adopted to progress our understanding of students’ learning and enhance learning performance and experience. However, the adoption of AIED has led to increasing ethical risks and concerns regarding several aspects such as personal data and learner autonomy. Despite the recent announcement of guidelines for ethical and trustworthy AIED, the debate revolves around the key principles underpinning ethical AIED. This paper aims to explore whether there is a global consensus on ethical AIED by mapping and analyzing international organizations’ current policies and guidelines. In this paper, we first introduce the opportunities offered by AI in education and potential ethical issues. Then, thematic analysis was conducted to conceptualize and establish a set of ethical principles by examining and synthesizing relevant ethical policies and guidelines for AIED. We discuss each principle and associated implications for relevant educational stakeholders, including students, teachers, technology developers, policymakers, and institutional decision-makers. The proposed set of ethical principles is expected to serve as a framework to inform and guide educational stakeholders in the development and deployment of ethical and trustworthy AIED as well as catalyze future development of related impact studies in the field.

title: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence
authors: M. Rege; H. K.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
authors: Dowling Wong
abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: Evaluating invariance training with certified answer-changing controls in neural graph algorithms
authors: Zhe Dong; Fang Qin
abstract: Invariance training aims to make neural algorithmic reasoners robust to answer-preserving input changes and is judged by accuracy and by how rarely such edits change predictions. We ask whether this evaluation detects lost sensitivity to answer-changing edits on minimum spanning trees of synthetic graphs, where both directions can be certified. Attaching a subgraph through one bridge provably preserves every original label. Attaching it through two edges, oracle-selected to change a label, and lowering one weight inside the graph serve as answer-changing controls; a response is a changed prediction on an edge whose label changes. A reproduced graph transformer (GDT) within its published accuracy range changes a provably fixed label on 53.3-65.9% of the 64-vertex graphs it solves exactly after a 64-vertex bridge attachment; removing the connecting edge changes little. With 16-vertex graphs and attachments, three invariance objectives lower GDT violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at essentially unchanged accuracy. Training also lowers the response to two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%, while the response to in-base weight edits stays near 99.5%. At 64 vertices accuracy also falls, but on 16-vertex bases only the attachment control reveals the loss. A message-passing network loses some attachment response at small penalty weights but gains little invariance. Running the conventionally trained GDT on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations and keeps accuracy and both responses, so the task does not force the trade-off. Sensitivity checks for trained invariance should include certified answer-changing edits that attach material as the training edits do.

title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
authors: Charlotte Peart; Franziska Sofia Hafner; Luc Rocher
abstract: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
authors: Christian Lange; Oisin Mac Aodha
abstract: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.

title: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
authors: Yu Yuan; Ruizhou Ding; Shaoheng Fang; Stanley H. Chan; Zhuo Chen
abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

title: Event-Based Dynamic Lip Region Estimation During Speech
authors: Hamze Hammami; Omar Eldardeer; Francesco Rea
abstract:
Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. These include automatic lip reading, audiovisual speech analysis, and human-robot interaction, particularly in challenging environments characterized by low illumination or high dynamic range. Event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and voice activity detection, however, mostly operate on a cropped region of interest (ROI), by hand or by the dataset, and no event-based method supplies that ROI as a spatial region; existing event-based face analysis gives the mouth as landmarks, which presents a mismatch between application and localization. The present work predicts a dense heatmap over the lip region from the full event "frame". Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed at every location by a two-pathway continuous-time recurrent network (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on the real elapsed time of each bin: a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway, utilised for refining and anchoring the prediction. The model reaches 69.5% on lips on four unseen speakers and switches target only 2.1 times per second, against 8.9 and 11.0 for convolutional baselines with
  more parameters. Adding a spatial encoder improves precision but fails on a new face scale. On a real event sensor, trained only on simulated events, the proposed model reaches 58.0% on lips against 43.2% for the CNN, with fewer than half its target switches.

title: Event-Based Person Detection for Maritime UAV Search
authors: Zijie Ning; Patrick Vandewalle
abstract: Maritime search and rescue requires locating people in the water quickly, motivating the use of UAVs to survey the search area. During flight, camera motion and the longer exposures used in low light can blur small targets and hinder person detection. Event cameras record brightness changes as they occur, reducing the motion blur associated with longer exposure times. We investigate their use for maritime person detection by generating synthetic events using the v2e event simulator from public MOBDrone rescue videos and retaining the existing annotations. We compare the recurrent vision transformer model RVT-T with YOLOv8n and RT-DETR-R18 trained on exposure-matched images. On 843 test samples from held-out recordings, RVT-T achieves 15.63% person AP50:95, compared with 6.89% for YOLOv8n and 9.44% for RT-DETR-R18 under 100 ms synthetic exposure. Increasing exposure times from 50 to 200 ms progressively reduces frame-based detection accuracy, widening the gap to the event model. To evaluate the feasibility of on-board processing, we deploy our detector on a Jetson Orin Nano platform. The RVT-T model retains its accuracy and requires approximately 136 ms and 2.02 J per sample, allowing real-time processing on the UAV.

title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
authors: Fangrui Huang; Bingyang Wang; Chuhan Li; Yijiang Li; Arpandeep Khatua; Austin Shen; Riki R Z Choi; Cuiyuanxiu Chen; Jin Huang; Zachary Robertson; Kate Lin; Akshay Paruchuri; Sijun Tan; Xin Liu; Zhengmin Ni; Sanmi Koyejo; Ehsan Adeli
abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.

title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention
authors: Zhen Huang; Shuwei Li; Ruizhe Yao; Xinrui Chen; Danyi Liu; Haoyuan Liang; Zhiyu Ye; Qiuyan Sun; Bingwei Chen; Yiyuan Li; Xu Zhou; Haohuan Fu
abstract: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.

title: EVF-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for E-commerce Visual Effects in Video Generation
authors: Run Ling; Ke Cao; Runze He; Jie Gao; Ao Ma; Wei Feng; Zhanjie Zhang; Hao Wang; Jinghe Hu; Guibing Guo
abstract: E-commerce visual effects (EVF) are dynamic, product-centered visual presentations in e-commerce videos, often accompanied by promotional text. They play an important role in attracting viewer attention and conveying product information. However, general measures of visual quality and text relevance alone do not establish whether generated videos preserve product appearance, maintain readable text, and produce coherent, contextually appropriate effects. To address this issue, we introduce EVF-Bench, a dedicated benchmark spanning six evaluation dimensions: visual quality and text relevance as general dimensions, and motion, product consistency, text stability, and creative rationality as EVF-specific dimensions. To complement the benchmark and support task-aligned research and model adaptation, we further construct EVF-32K, a dataset of over 32000 curated image-text-video triples tailored to e-commerce scenarios. Using this suite, we systematically evaluate representative video generation models and their domain-adapted variants. The results reveal complementary strengths, with no evaluated configuration leading all six dimensions. Together, EVF-Bench and EVF-32K provide a task-oriented evaluation framework and a supporting data resource for e-commerce video generation.

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
authors: Wen Wang; Jindong Wang; Jiahua Bao; Tu Yongsiqi; Yihao Liu; Junwei He; Wenkui Fan
abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

title: Evidence from a Multi-Regime Causal Discovery Benchmark: UCMT Algorithms, Comparative Performance, and Controlled Ablation Studies
authors: Mahyar Eslami
abstract: We present an internal, pre-registered evaluation of the UCMT causal discovery algorithm family alongside established alternatives across heterogeneous benchmark regimes, complemented by a separately pre-registered, controlled study of UCMT v2 Global components. The contribution is both empirical and methodological: a family-stratified comparison of three actively developed algorithm configurations and targeted evidence about which internal stages affect their outcomes. In the main benchmark, UCMT v2 Global has higher directed F1 than NOTEARS and DAGMA in selected real, semi-synthetic and Gaussian-network comparisons at the paired-run level, while trailing leading permutation-search methods in other settings. The BOSS-based UCMT v4 produces a CSuite-specific directed-F1 improvement over BOSS (mean paired difference +0.279; pair-level Holm p < 0.001), but the dataset-level adjusted result is not significant (p = 0.188). In a separate fixed-skeleton ablation, UCMT v2 Global exceeds an adapted R^2-SortnRegress orientation baseline on standardized iSCM data (directed F1 0.537 vs 0.468, dataset-level Holm p = 0.031); absolute orientation accuracy is 0.563 and there is no established broad advantage over RESIT, ANM or DirectLiNGAM. Controlled ablations show that sparsity and BIC-based refinement materially affect some outcomes, whereas the examined arbitration and automatic regime-selection mechanisms do not yield confirmed general improvements. We report performance shortcomings, multiple-testing correction, runtime costs, evaluation limitations and reproducibility checks. The results support UCMT as an implemented and empirically investigated algorithm family, not a claim of overall superiority, independent validation or demonstrated commercial impact.

title: EviScope: Evidence-Conditioned Sampling for Long-Range 3D Detection
authors: Mingyang Lyu; Yinqian Sun; Gongce Cao; Chujie Tang; Yuhao Zhang; Lu Jia; Qian Zhang; Bo Wang; Pin Lyu
abstract: Query-based camera-radar detectors choose where and over which frames each object query samples from the query's position or feature. We test whether radar evidence around the query should also set these choices at the 150 m range of MAN TruckScenes, where recall differs across object-level radar-return counts within every range band. EviScope is a minimal test: the current frame's returns form a non-learned bird's-eye evidence field, which each query reads at its decoded centre to scale its radial sampling extent and to weight eight frames. It adds 5,450 parameters (0.009%) to RaCFormer, with no latency increase in our timing. Our module-free recipe exceeds the published TruckScenes mAP (25.9 over seven runs against 24.1), so we measure the module only against its own baseline at matched seeds. The evidence a query reads rises with its object's return count (Spearman 0.51) but captures zero-return objects only in part, and the learned radius tracks it ($ρ\approx-0.91$ in four runs). Over seven four-epoch pairs the module changes NDS by $+0.31\pm0.36$ and mAP by $-0.27\pm0.22$ (mean $\pm$ SE). Against a geometry-only conditioner with the same parameter count, trained at three matched seeds, it is higher by $+1.25\pm0.72$ NDS and $+0.87\pm0.21$ mAP, on mAP in every pair, and the control's mean NDS is near the baseline's. An exploratory far-range gain failed an internally pre-specified held-out test, and large inference-time substitution penalties also occur without query-local evidence: neither learned allocation nor inference-time dependence substitutes for matched end-to-end comparisons.

title: EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
authors: Zhouhan Qian; Sicheng Chen; Chad Wong; Tianyi Zhang; Enhui Chai; Zeyu Liu; Fei Xia
abstract: Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.

title: Evolve Where It Matters: Coverage-Guided Self-Evolution of Agent Skills
authors: Boyin Tan; Jiadong Zhang; Xiaosong Ma; Chun Jason Xue; Xiaowei Huang; Youcheng Sun
abstract: Agent skills package procedural knowledge as natural-language instructions, and a skill helps only when its instructions are correct and properly followed by the agent. Self-evolving agents revise their own skills from the runs they make, but existing methods judge each run as a whole, by its outcome or by where it went wrong, and cannot tell whether a failure comes from a wrong instruction or from one the agent did not follow. Instruction-level coverage was introduced to test skills and labels each instruction of a run as follow, not-follow, or not covered, which separates these causes. We leverage it for skill self-evolution with SkillPlumber, a framework in which an agent evolves its own skills where coverage shows they fall short. A persistent root cause analysis agent turns each label into a revision question and checks each revision against the next run, while a maintainer distills investigations across tasks into a shared strategy library. Across three benchmarks and three executors, SkillPlumber solves 64.7% to 70.5% of the tasks, 25.6 to 30.4 percentage points higher than the initial skill and 8.7 to 14.0 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline, and removing coverage reduces recovered failures by 20.8% on SkillsBench with GPT-5.5.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Eduardo Dueñez; Edgar Said Hernandez Sanchez; Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán; Suzanne Sadedin
abstract: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: EvoMem: Self-Evolving Skills for Time-Aware Long Video Memory Agents
authors: Yutong Guan; Meixing Shi; Haoran Sun; Bing Sun; Yuxiang Cai; Yankai Jiang
abstract: Although memory-augmented architectures have expanded the ability of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to process long videos, existing retrieval processes still largely rely on global semantic matching and lack state-driven temporal control, often returning fragmented or redundant evidence and failing to maintain a coherent evidence chain. To address this challenge, we propose EvoMem, a time-aware long-video memory agent guided by self-evolving retrieval skills. EvoMem constructs a hierarchical time-indexed memory, where different types of evidence are aligned onto a unified video timeline; during retrieval, temporal cues from acquired evidence are further converted into explicit signals that constrain subsequent memory access. To address recurring procedural errors in long-video question answering, such as unclear retrieval targets, improper memory access paths, or premature stopping, EvoMem introduces retrieval skills to provide process-level guidance, enabling the agent to dynamically adjust retrieval content, memory operations, and target temporal ranges according to the current evidence state, while deciding when to stop. Furthermore, inspired by reinforcement learning, we formulate skill evolution as a reward-guided policy improvement process. Each candidate skill is treated as an external policy patch, and rewards are assigned according to answer-correctness state transitions on the validation set. In this way, effective skills are accepted and low-quality skills are rejected without updating model parameters. Experiments on four long-video question answering benchmarks show that EvoMem significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average accuracy of 60.1% and an average improvement of 8.6 percentage points over the previous best methods, demonstrating its effectiveness for long-video reasoning.

title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
authors: William H. W. Thompson; Guillaume St-Onge; Laurent Hébert-Dufresne; Jean-Gabriel Young
abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.

title: Examination of the Operational Capacities and Challenges of Integrating Artificial Intelligence Technology into Different Stages of Criminal Proceedings
authors: Nejat Alipour
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has attracted considerable attention in judicial and legal domains in recent years. This technology possesses the potential to accelerate judicial processes and enhance accuracy within criminal proceedings. The present study was conducted with the aim of examining the operational capacities and identifying the challenges associated with integrating artificial intelligence across different stages of criminal adjudication. The research adopts a descriptive–analytical method and, through the review of scientific, judicial, and experiential sources, analyzes the opportunities and limitations related to the application of artificial intelligence in criminal justice processes. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence can play an effective role in data analysis, predictive assessment, and facilitating decision-making by judges and attorneys. However, significant challenges remain, including concerns related to privacy protection, data security, the risk of algorithmic errors, and public as well as judicial acceptance of decisions influenced by automated systems. Furthermore, in complex and sensitive cases, the role of human judges remains irreplaceable, and continuous human oversight over artificial intelligence systems is essential. Artificial intelligence may therefore be employed as an assistive tool within criminal proceedings, yet the complete replacement of human judicial reasoning is presently infeasible. Successful integration of this technology requires an appropriate legal framework, sustained human supervision, and specialized user training.</jats:p>

title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
authors: G. Cooper
abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential in the field of education. The study explores three main areas: (1) How did ChatGPT answer questions related to science education? (2) What are some ways educators could utilise ChatGPT in their science pedagogy? and (3) How has ChatGPT been utilised in this study, and what are my reflections about its use as a research tool? This exploratory research applies a self-study methodology to investigate the technology. Impressively, ChatGPT’s output often aligned with key themes in the research. However, as it currently stands, ChatGPT runs the risk of positioning itself as the ultimate epistemic authority, where a single truth is assumed without a proper grounding in evidence or presented with sufficient qualifications. Key ethical concerns associated with AI include its potential environmental impact, issues related to content moderation, and the risk of copyright infringement. It is important for educators to model responsible use of ChatGPT, prioritise critical thinking, and be clear about expectations. ChatGPT is likely to be a useful tool for educators designing science units, rubrics, and quizzes. Educators should critically evaluate any AI-generated resource and adapt it to their specific teaching contexts. ChatGPT was used as a research tool for assistance with editing and to experiment with making the research narrative clearer. The intention of the paper is to act as a catalyst for a broader conversation about the use of generative AI in science education.

title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation
authors: Maxx Richard Rahman; Prakhar Kumar; Wolfgang Maass
abstract: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.

title: Experimental Data Generation and Ground-Truth Assignment
authors: Björn-Ivo Bachmann; Marie Stiefel; Martin Müller; Dominik Britz
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article explores deep learning (DL) approaches in depth by examining the experimental generation of such high-quality data and, especially, the creation of objective and correct ground-truth annotations as a fundamental step in the development of supervised machine learning (ML) models. In particular, the challenges and strategies associated with annotating complex microstructures and how these challenges and strategies influence the success of ML-based analysis techniques are discussed. The article mainly focuses on two-dimensional metallographic investigations. However, the concepts listed can be applied analogously to three-dimensional (3D) approaches, such as serial section tomography.</jats:p>

title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence
authors: Shakked Noy; Whitney Zhang
abstract: We examined the productivity effects of a generative artificial intelligence (AI) technology, the assistive chatbot ChatGPT, in the context of midlevel professional writing tasks. In a preregistered online experiment, we assigned occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks to 453 college-educated professionals and randomly exposed half of them to ChatGPT. Our results show that ChatGPT substantially raised productivity: The average time taken decreased by 40% and output quality rose by 18%. Inequality between workers decreased, and concern and excitement about AI temporarily rose. Workers exposed to ChatGPT during the experiment were 2 times as likely to report using it in their real job 2 weeks after the experiment and 1.6 times as likely 2 months after the experiment. Description Editor’s summary Automation has historically displaced human workers in factories (e.g., automotive manufacturing) or in performing routine computational tasks. Will generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT disrupt the labor market by making educated professionals obsolete, or will these tools complement their skills and enhance productivity? Noy and Zhang examined this issue in an experiment that recruited college-educated professionals to complete incentivized writing tasks. Participants assigned to use ChatGPT were more productive, efficient, and enjoyed the tasks more. Participants with weaker skills benefited the most from ChatGPT, which carries policy implications for efforts to reduce productivity inequality through AI. —EEU The assistive chatbot ChatGPT raises productivity in professional writing tasks and reduces productivity inequality.

title: Explainability of genotype embedding models through observed cohort paths
authors: Amashi Niwarthana; Aloysius Tan; Jagath C. Rajapakse
abstract: Deep learning models that combine genotypes with neuroimaging predict neurological diseases more accurately than either modality alone. Their clinical use, however, requires identifying which genetic variants a prediction is based on. Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients address this by integrating the model's gradient from a baseline to the input. These methods assume the model accepts any point along that path as a valid input. Genotype models violate this assumption. They map the three discrete allele dosages \{0,1,2\} to vectors through a learned embedding defined only at those values, so a straight line passes through fractional genotypes at which no embedding, and therefore no gradient, exists. Attribution must therefore proceed in embedding space where the choice of path can affect the resulting attribution. We show that the commonly used per-variant estimator does not generally satisfy completeness. Additive separability guarantees completeness for this estimator, but interactions between variants generally break that property. Instead, we integrate along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths connecting genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. Each path satisfies completeness in the continuum although the interiors of its segments are not necessarily observed. Our method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations, and is competitive with a support-background Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations. It also shows higher seed stability and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.

title: Explainable AI and Blockchain for SOC Analysts
authors: Darshana Shah; Bhavik Pandya; Antura Akter
abstract: <jats:p>The increasing complexity of cyber threats has created significant challenges for Security Operations Centers (SOCs), particularly in managing large volumes of alerts, ensuring timely responses, and maintaining trust in automated systems. This chapter presents a human-centric approach to cybersecurity by integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), Explainable AI (XAI), human decision-making, and blockchain technologies. AI enhances threat detection and response efficiency, while XAI improves transparency by providing interpretable insights into model decisions. Human-in-the-loop mechanisms ensure oversight and accountability, and blockchain enables secure, immutable logging of system activities. The chapter further proposes an integrated framework and demonstrates its practical application through real-world SOC scenarios. Implementation challenges and future research opportunities are also discussed. Overall, this work highlights the importance of combining explainability, human oversight, and governance to build trustworthy and effective AI-driven cybersecurity systems.</jats:p>

title: Explainable AI and Digital Twins for Intelligent Microbial Laboratories
authors: Anmol S Budhewar; Aman Suresh Tharayil; Balkrishna Keshavrao Patil; Adinarayana Andy; Sayali K. Somwanshi
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of microbiology has led to unprecedented laboratory automation, generating vast data and advancing analytical capabilities. However, integrating complex artificial intelligence models with high-throughput systems introduces challenges in understanding system functions, ensuring reproducibility, and maintaining trust in automated outputs. This chapter presents a framework that integrates Explainable Artificial Intelligenceand Digital Twin technologies to create intelligent microbial laboratories. Through real-time automation, sensor-based data acquisition, computational modeling, and interpretable AI methods, the system continuously monitors, simulates, and optimizes microbial experiments. This approach improves experimental reliability while supporting human decision-making in clinical microbiology. The chapter further outlines practical workflows, architectural designs, and use cases demonstrating how explainable digital twins transform automated laboratories into adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy platforms for scientific discovery.</jats:p>

title: Explainable AI for Solar PV Power Forecasting: From Model Selection to Trustworthy, Reproducible Deployment
authors: Nuzhat Khan; Muhammad Paend Bakht; Ab Al-Hadi Ab Rahman; Fabiano Pallonetto; Amy Fahy; Mohamed Khalafalla Hassan; Paul Stynes; Muhammad Anique Aslam; Terence O Donnell; Mohammad Riadh
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is now a standard tool for forecasting the output of solar photovoltaic (PV) plants, yet published accuracy figures are often hard to compare and harder to trust. Many studies validate with random splits, report no reference forecast, and present feature attributions without saying what they can and cannot show. This paper reviews the main families of ML methods for PV power forecasting and resource assessment, from tree ensembles to deep and foundation models, and sets out a reproducible workflow that combines automated model search with explainable AI. The workflow is then tested on an openly available dataset: a 16.32 kWp plant in Porto, Portugal, forecast one day ahead from a 4 km numerical weather prediction grid. Over a full test year, the best models reach a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) of 11.6% of installed capacity, about half the error of smart persistence. The choice of input features changed accuracy far more than the choice among strong algorithms, and shuffled cross-validation was mildly optimistic. After conformal calibration, the nominal 80% prediction intervals covered 81.7% of observations, against 64.5% before. SHAP rankings stayed stable when the model was retrained on different periods but shifted when correlated inputs were removed, so attributions should be read as properties of a model rather than of the plant. The paper closes with practical lessons and open problems, including deployment on edge hardware and the effect of a changing climate.

title: Explainable AI for Sustainable Finance, ESG, Sentiment, and MCDM
authors: Lucas Werneck Louzada; Bruno Tonioni Cunha; Francisco Bruno Ribeiro Fernandes; Osvaldo Luiz Gonçalves Quelhas
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is reshaping sustainable finance by integrating financial, ESG, and textual data. Yet predictive sophistication intensifies opacity when decisions rely on complex models. This article develops an architecture connecting ESG analytics, sentiment analysis, machine learning, explainable AI (XAI), and multiple-criteria decision-making (MCDM). The framework distinguishes prediction, explanation, and decision across six layers: data, analytics, explainability, decision intelligence, outcomes, and governance. Drawing on literature and applications, it shows how XAI and MCDM transform heterogeneous sustainability data into auditable decision support. The architecture emphasizes traceability, uncertainty, and competing priorities, recognizing differences across ESG providers, sustainability narratives, and sentiment limits. XAI supports model scrutiny and human oversight, while MCDM translates predictive outputs into transparent rankings under preferences, constraints, and uncertainty. The framework identifies governance requirements, risks, and future research.</jats:p>
