title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
authors: Mohammad Meymani; Roozbeh Razavi-Far
abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

title: On the Informativeness of Structural Stability Bounds for GNNs: GINs versus GATs
authors: Alan Gany; Paul Landrier; Bogdan Cautis; Laks V. S. Lakshmanan; Silviu Maniu
abstract: Stability bounds for graph neural networks limit how much node representations can drift when the graph changes, but they are rarely compared with the simplest alternative: a bound on the distance between any two outputs, whatever the graph. We derive structural stability bounds for Graph Isomorphism Networks (GINs) and single-head GATv1 networks under deterministic edge perturbations that need not be small, and compare each with such a perturbation-independent diameter bound. For GINs, we characterize exactly when the stability bound is tighter, through a condition linking perturbation size, depth and maximum degree; it holds with a wide margin on Cora, but fails beyond a few layers on the low-degree MUTAG graphs. For GATv1, the bound is never tighter, which calls for analyses based on attention masses.

title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
authors: Ivano Lodato; Simran Hiranandani; Aditya Varna Iyer
abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

title: OpenGNS: An Open Dataset of the Gradient Noise Scale across Vision, Language, and Diffusion Models
authors: Marcel Aach; Jiangtao Wang; Stefan Kesselheim; Andreas Lintermann
abstract: The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/olympique-marcel/OpenGNS

title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
authors: Alexander Boesgaard Lorup
abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
authors: Wenhao Yuan; Longhui Yuan; Zexi Jia; Ningzhe Shi; Jingwei Li; Shipeng Cen; Pengcheng Luo; Jie Zhou; Jinchao Zhang
abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

title: Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Deployments in Metallurgical Industries
authors: Satyam S. Sahay
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article discusses the opportunities for artificial intelligence (AI) deployments in metallurgical industries. The unique requirements for industrial deployment of AI models along with the underlying subtle complexities in an industrial environment are detailed. Furthermore, the article also outlines considerations for AI leverage in an industrial environment. This article is a companion to the article titled Applications of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Metallurgical Industries in this Volume, in which specific industrial-use cases are presented for four significant industrial processes: alloy design, metal refining, casting, and heat treatment, which this article also discusses.</jats:p>

title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
authors: Shi-Yuan Ma; Xingjian Bai; Ryan Hamerly; Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad
abstract:
Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy?
  This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics.
  While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
authors: Christopher Chukwuemeka; Andreas Mang
abstract: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.

title: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
authors: Jiaxin Shi; Ziyuan Chen; Jian Huang; Hansheng Wang
abstract: Stability under input perturbations is necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. Weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. However, existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are insufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. In this paper, we establish a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint. This theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as the network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed. We then propose a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, we establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and provide robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies show that the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to that of classical deep network methods.

title: Optimizing Smart Grid Energy Control With Deep Q-Networks
authors: Omar Nejjarou; Mohamed Lahby; Said Aqil
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents an in-depth study of energy management optimization in smart grids using deep Q-networks (DQN). The objective is to address the growing complexity of modern energy systems, driven by the integration of renewable energy sources, dynamic changes in demand, and the need for real-time decision-making. We will present the fundamental concepts of smart grids and formulate the energy management problem as a Markov decision process. We then explore the principles of reinforcement learning and detail the DQN approach, including its architecture and learning mechanisms. Practical applications, comparative analyses with traditional optimization methods, and key challenges are also discussed. Finally, this chapter highlights recent advances and future research directions in the field of intelligent energy management systems.</jats:p>

title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
authors: Prashank Kadam
abstract: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.

title: ORGANIC3D: Grounding 3D CT Vision Language Models in Organ Level Image Text Coupling
authors: Zelong Liu; Hamza Ahmed; Wynn Wingyi Lee; Mickael Torjman; Alexander Dimitrakakis; Jiahua Lu; Timothy Deyer; Bachir Taouli; Zahi A. Fayad; Xueyan Mei
abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.

title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
authors: Jacek Karolczak; Jerzy Stefanowski
abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

title: PAD: Policy-Aware Data Valuation for Autonomous Driving
authors: {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d2', 'user': {'_id': '6ab7d214f32cad26a0dcfbdb', 'avatarUrl': '/avatars/32ce8b96eb248c6fe0f311eca21270f7.svg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'Chengkai Xu', 'user': 'ChengkaiXu', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'ChengkaiXu'}, 'name': 'Chengkai Xu', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-20T16:45:04.876Z', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d3', 'name': 'Yicheng Guo', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d4', 'name': 'Jiaqi Liu', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d5', 'name': 'Yiming Cui', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d6', 'name': 'Shiyu Fang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d7', 'name': 'Peng Hang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d8', 'name': 'Hao Zhang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0053f1ecb204ffe44e69d9', 'name': 'Jian Sun', 'hidden': False}
abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving increasingly depends on scaling training demonstrations, yet data growth does not guarantee proportional gains. However, additional data do not guarantee better policies: a demonstration that benefits one planner may be redundant or harmful to another. Existing curation methods typically infer data value from intrinsic sample properties or training-dependent proxies that do not measure downstream policy utility. To address this, we introduce Policy-Aware Data Valuation (PAD), a framework that assigns each candidate demonstration a utility specific to the target driving policy. PAD combines scene-level calibration feedback with projected policy gradients and a regularized approximation of local training geometry, producing scalable influence-based values for the policy. A controlled group-removal study establishes the directional fidelity of these values, while cross-planner analysis shows that the same candidate pool induces markedly different rankings across planner families. On DiffusionDrive, PAD improves EPDMS over real-only training by 3.5 points on NavTest and 5.0 points on NavHard. Policy-specific curation consistently outperforms real-only and full-pool training across diffusion-, regression-, and flow-matching-based planners while substantially reducing scene-level regressions. These results establish policy-aware data valuation as a basis for replacing indiscriminate data accumulation with targeted policy improvement, enabling more efficient and reliable scaling of autonomous-driving systems.

title: PAIR-MED: Policy-reward Alternation for Iterative Refinement in Multilingual Medical Reasoning
authors: Fan Gao; Xiaohang Xu; Lang Huang; Nan Lu; Irene Li
abstract: Large language models demonstrate strong medical question-answering capabilities, yet reasoning performance remains uneven across languages. Process reward models (PRMs) provide step-level feedback for improving reasoning, but a fixed PRM may become increasingly misaligned with the trajectory distribution of an evolving policy during reinforcement learning, thereby reducing the reliability of its supervision. We propose a policy--reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a medical PRM and optimizes a multilingual reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, the current policy generates multilingual trajectories to update the PRM, which then provides process-level rewards for the next policy update. Medical step supervision maintains the PRM's medical foundation, while process, outcome, and language-related rewards guide policy learning. We develop multilingual medical PRMs (PAIR-PRM) and reasoning models (PAIR-MED) at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages. On the medical subsets of Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX, our models improve average accuracy by 3.01--7.47% over their corresponding Qwen backbones. On CUREMED-BENCH, PAIR-MED-9B improves the joint language consistency and logical accuracy metric by 12.88% and 7.45% over baselines for in-domain and out-of-domain languages. Further analyses examine PRM adaptation, multilingual reasoning quality, and the contributions of individual training components.

title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
authors: Mario Franco; Carlos Gershenson
abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
authors: Mayukh Debnath; Manan Roy Choudhury
abstract: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
authors: Keryan Chelouche; Petr Dobias; Nistor Grozavu; Olivier Romain
abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.

title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
authors: Aabhash Dhakal; Tim Lachner
abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

title: Pareto-Optimal and Strategyproof Data-Sharing Between Competitors
authors: Morgan Colin-Mourre; Felipe Garrido-Lucero; Patrick Loiseau
abstract: We study data-sharing among firms competing in the same market through the quality of their predictive models. We model firms' profit through two main components, precision and market share, where the former depends on the firm's own number of datapoints and the latter depends on the endowments of all firms. We characterize Pareto-optimal contracts as those in which at least one firm receives all of the other firms' datapoints. We then propose a parametric family of data-sharing contracts and show that, under any of them, the relative market shares of all firms remain constant, eliminating the negative effect of sharing data with competitors and equalizing all firms' gains relative to the no-sharing scenario. We further show that one contract within this family satisfies both Pareto-optimality and strategyproofness against firms attempting to under-declare the size of their initial endowment. Finally, using a real-world dataset, we empirically test the gain in profit for all firms under the contract described above, and show that data-sharing is particularly beneficial when the machine learning task is harder or when firms' initial endowments are closer to homogeneous.

title: PatchAdaNet: Unsupervised class incremental learning using local patches and global adapters
authors: Kamel Aouaidjia; Yanchao Duan; Zihui Zhen; Xin Li; Yongfei Lv; Chongsheng Zhang
abstract: Biological learning systems acquire knowledge incrementally through broad, reusable representations established early and kept largely stable, while integrating new experience with minimal interference with previously learned knowledge. Replay-based methods approximate this by storing samples or features from previous tasks and mixing them into the current task. However, memory buffers grow with the number of tasks and may retain task-specific noise that reduces generalization. To address these limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network), an unsupervised class-incremental learning method for image classification that continually updates feature representations using autoencoders. Since images share structural features such as edges, corners, and shapes, we first divide each image into patches and train independent autoencoders on external data to reconstruct each patch. The layers of all patch encoders are aggregated into global frozen layers that generalize across tasks and remain fixed throughout learning. Learnable adapters then build global image representations from these features to reconstruct the entire image. To prevent feature drift without storing data, we introduce the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a fixed-size running average of adapter outputs updated after each task to penalizes representation drift. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is applied to the learnable layers to preserve previously learned features by constraining important weights. Finally, a linear classifier is trained on the frozen latent representation and GFC for class-incremental evaluation. We evaluate PatchAdaNet in both CNN and Vision Transformer settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets, providing a comparative study of the two architectures under identical class-incremental settings. Code is available.

title: PaveSplat: Resolution-Robust Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting with Residually Corrected Surface-Aligned Covariances
authors: Janghun Kim; Hyun-Cheol Kim; Eunbin An; Myeonghun Oh; Hyon-Gon Choo
abstract: We present PaveSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting method that adds a learned residual to the analytic surface-aligned covariance, keeping surfels paving the visible surface across rendering resolutions. Pixel-aligned feed-forward Gaussian splatting predicts one primitive per pixel from a few images in a single pass, and its rendering quality depends on how well these primitives cover the surface. Recent surfel-based methods compute the surface-aligned covariance analytically from predicted depth. However, this covariance has no way to correct the surfel orientation where the depth-derived frame is ill-posed. The surfels then cover the surface loosely; at the training resolution each surfel's one-pixel minimum footprint covers the gaps, but they show up as holes when the same prediction is re-rendered at a higher resolution. To address this, we keep the analytic covariance as an initialization, with its axes aligned to the surface tangents, and add an identity-initialized unit-quaternion residual that reorients a surfel only where this improves rendering, turning surfels that the analytic frame mis-aims back onto the surface. On RealEstate10K, PaveSplat achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among single-Gaussian-per-pixel methods at every scale (1x-8x). The native-resolution gain is small; the benefit appears when the same prediction is rendered at higher display resolutions without re-running the network. On zero-shot DL3DV, it leads PSNR within this group at every scale and ranks first or second on SSIM/LPIPS. A coverage-hole analysis shows fewer uncovered pixels than both baselines under high-resolution re-rendering.

title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Farzana Yasmin; Ricardo Vilalta
abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

title: Peeking Inside the Black-Box: A Survey on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
authors: Amina Adadi; M. Berrada
abstract: At the dawn of the fourth industrial revolution, we are witnessing a fast and widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in our daily life, which contributes to accelerating the shift towards a more algorithmic society. However, even with such unprecedented advancements, a key impediment to the use of AI-based systems is that they often lack transparency. Indeed, the black-box nature of these systems allows powerful predictions, but it cannot be directly explained. This issue has triggered a new debate on explainable AI (XAI). A research field holds substantial promise for improving trust and transparency of AI-based systems. It is recognized as the sine qua non for AI to continue making steady progress without disruption. This survey provides an entry point for interested researchers and practitioners to learn key aspects of the young and rapidly growing body of research related to XAI. Through the lens of the literature, we review the existing approaches regarding the topic, discuss trends surrounding its sphere, and present major research trajectories.

title: Pengaruh Literasi Digital terhadap Etika Penggunaan Artificial Intelligence pada Mahasiswa Perguruan Tinggi
authors: Yusuf Unggul Budiman; Ahmad Jurnaidi Wahidin; Daz Vholasky Anggraini
abstract: <jats:p>The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has transformed the way students seek information, complete assignments, and understand academic materials. However, AI use also raises ethical issues, including plagiarism, overreliance on instant answers, and a lack of transparency in acknowledging AI assistance. This study aims to analyze the effect of digital literacy on the ethical use of AI among university students. A quantitative survey method was employed. Data were collected using a 1–5 Likert-scale questionnaire from 125 respondents, with 119 complete responses analyzed. Digital literacy was measured using 12 items, while ethical AI use was measured using 12 items. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity testing, reliability testing, correlation, and simple linear regression. The results show that digital literacy has a positive and significant effect on ethical AI use. The correlation coefficient of 0.638 indicates a strong relationship, while the coefficient of determination of 0.406 indicates that digital literacy explains 40.6% of the variation in ethical AI use. The regression equation is Y = 1.196 + 0.706X. These findings indicate that students with higher digital literacy tend to use AI more ethically, responsibly, and transparently. This study recommends strengthening digital literacy programs with an emphasis on AI ethics in higher education.</jats:p>

title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation
authors: Zhiwei Li; Yuhao Zhou; Yikai Yang; Haonan Wang; Qing Ye; Jiancheng Lv; Kazunari Matsuda
abstract: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.

title: PeriaTrace: Tooth-Level Grounding Diagnosis and Patient-Facing Explanations from Periapical Radiographs
authors: Zhenhuan Zhou; Yuchen Zhang; Jingbo Zhu; Shiqing Ma; Yanlin Wu; Tao Li
abstract: Periapical radiographs (PRs) are central to endodontic diagnosis, but interpreting them and preparing reports are time-consuming. Technical language can limit patients' understanding, while existing automated methods often lack tooth-level links between findings and image evidence. We present PeriaTrace, a three-stage framework integrating tooth-level diagnosis, visually grounded report generation, and patient-friendly explanations and care recommendations. PeriaTrace was developed and evaluated using 12,877 PRs from an internal dataset and two external clinical cohorts. In internal evaluation, it achieved a macro Dice coefficient of 85.35%, BLEU-4 of 0.6504, an F1 score of 94.37% for joint tooth localization and Fédération Dentaire Internationale (FDI) identification, and a grounding-tag F1 score of 77.93%. In the two external cohorts, senior endodontists considered 91.16% and 84.52% of reports suitable for retention or revision without complete rewriting. Generation averaged 4.41 seconds per PR, several tens of times faster than manual drafting. Among 196 survey participants without medical backgrounds, 96.4% preferred reports with plain-language explanations and care recommendations, and 84.7% found visual localization cues helpful. PeriaTrace may enable faster, evidence-traceable reporting while supporting clinical review and patient communication. (Abridged version)

title: Persistent Identity in Person Tracking: Online Enrollment and Registered Recognition
authors: Ratha Siv; Matei Mancas; Bernard Gosselin
abstract: We extend PoseTReID with online appearance-bank matching (Gallery) and a residual-conflict guard for registered SVM recognition. All methods use supplied ground-truth (GT) person boxes. We average all-box assessment IDF1/HOTA equally across videos. On six SportsMOT clips, StrongSORT leads standalone trackers (79.44/84.72%) and exceeds both Gallery variants. Over eleven videos, Gallery AIN (83.29/85.44%) and COPE (84.66/86.38%) exceed standalone trackers with complete results. This lead depends on two retrospectively added GTA development compilations and is absent on the original nine videos. Registered SVMs lead both cohorts among complete results, with AIN at 95.72/94.82% over eleven videos. They use every GT crop from approximately 20% of frames, including future appearances. On MOT20-03, registered AIN reached 96.80% IDF1 and assigned the correct enrolled name to 90.72% of assessment GT observations. Gallery and standalone trackers receive no per-video labelled enrollment. Both identity routes restore identities across internal title cards, but Gallery trails SORT on three videos (four in HOTA) and both SVMs trail SORT on MOT16-04/MOT20-03. Under six-clip persistent-only scoring, native Gallery gains 2.39 percentage points in mean IDF1 over a matched control, with lower correct-P coverage and 5.02 times as many encoder attempts. Pose gating is mixed; the guard's metric effect is not isolated.

title: Persona Lenses: What Makes a Vision-Language Model See Through Its Persona's Eyes?
authors: Yoonho Shin
abstract: Vision-language models have been used to simulate where a user looks on a web page. However, a persona in the prompt reaches the simulated gaze only partly. We measure this reach as the difference in one model's gaze between two MatrAIx personas that differ in a single attribute. We introduce persona lenses, which place the persona between the model and the page: a text lens (a two-step prompt in which the model first writes what the persona would look at), a pixel lens (marks on the region matching the persona's interests) and a weight lens (a dwell reward gated to keep the scanpath natural). Using Qwen3-VL (4B and 32B) and Qwen3.5-9B on generated and live pages, we compare the lenses with one another and with scale, the 32B model with no lens. It has been confirmed that the text lens separates the personas strongly but is not robust to profile changes that should not move gaze. The pixel lens separates the personas less but is unaffected by attributes unrelated to gaze. At 4B and 9B, the weight lens separates the personas on interests held out from training, with no extra step on a new page. The 32B model separates the personas with the base prompt alone. Therefore, the choice of a lens depends on cost and model size.

title: PGU-Decoder: Prior-Guided Unified Decoding for Industrial Road-Network Map Updating
authors: Yuguang Ning; Bingbing Kang; Nan Zhao; Zhixuan Li; Ze Zhao; Dongdong Liu; Wenjian Zhu; Zekai Liu; Junhui Wang
abstract: Timely road-network map updates are essential to navigation and autonomous driving. Three key tasks are intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, covering topology, geometry, and attributes, respectively. Separate pipelines duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification, increasing operational costs. We propose PGU-Decoder, a production-grade unified decoding framework for semantic prediction across these tasks. A Prior Query Module (PQM) constructs point-level prior queries from sampled locations on road-network geometries. Fixed reference points preserve positional priors throughout decoding, allowing the model to focus on surrounding context. Point-level representations are aggregated into instance-level representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) captures inter-instance dependencies. Task-specific heads then generate predictions. We validate PGU-Decoder in large-scale automated road-network map updating across more than 360 cities in China, where it consistently outperforms seven baselines. Following deployment at AutoNavi Map, it achieves quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective industrial solution for road-network map updating.

title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Kai Lu; Chenyang Ma; Ioannis Havoutis
abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

title: Phantom of the Masquerade: Graph Neural Network-Based Detection of Masquerade Attacks in Controller Area Networks
authors: Nehal Ameen; Pablo Moriano; Irfan Ahmed
abstract: The lack of built-in security in controller area networks (CANs) exposes modern vehicles and industrial systems to masquerade attacks that can compromise safety and reliability. These attacks inject malicious messages that mimic legitimate communication patterns, making them difficult to detect using existing intrusion detection systems (IDS). Prior graph-based IDS approaches often rely on shallow embeddings that decouple representation learning from classification, which may limit their ability to fully exploit structural and signal-level information. In this paper, we propose PhantoMasq, a graph neural network (GNN)-based framework for detecting masquerade attacks in CAN systems. PhantoMasq models CAN traffic as message sequence graphs enriched with lightweight statistical features derived from signal behavior, enabling joint learning of structural dependencies and temporal characteristics. The detection task is formulated as a graph-level classification problem and solved using graph convolutional networks (GCNs). We evaluate PhantoMasq on the ROAD dataset under a protocol that prevents overlapping windows from spanning training and test data. Across five masquerade attack types, PhantoMasq achieves mean AUC-ROC between 0.831 and 0.999, with performance depending on the transmission rate of the targeted identifier and the magnitude of the induced signal deviation. Against a state-of-the-art graph-embedding baseline evaluated on the same sliding-window configurations, PhantoMasq achieves higher AUC-ROC on all five attack types, by 0.13 to 0.36, and is less sensitive to window configuration. Window-processing latency ranges from 2.33 to 5.94 ms per window on CPU, corresponding to a throughput of 168 to 429 windows per second. We make our implementation and experimental artifacts available to support reproducibility.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
authors: {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd2', 'name': 'Zirui Song', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd3', 'name': 'Jiadong Zhang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd4', 'name': 'Zheng Lu', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd5', 'name': 'Xiaosong Ma', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd6', 'name': 'Xiaojun Chang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b004007521eceac6cdcffd7', 'name': 'Xiuying Chen', 'hidden': False}
abstract: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.

title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks
authors: Zirui Song; Jiadong Zhang; Zheng Lu; Xiaosong Ma; Xiaojun Chang; Xiuying Chen

title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
authors: Yilong Dai; Yiming Sun; Shengyu Chen; Jiaqi Gong; Xiaowei Jia; Runlong Yu
abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.

title: Physical Laws without Physics Loss? Probing Learned Dynamics in Video World Models through Forced Response
authors: Yutao Li; Chen Wang; Wangmeng Zuo; Hui Li
abstract: Do video world models learn physical laws without a physics loss, or merely imitate motion? Overall motion and appearance scores cannot settle it. We investigate this through nonlinear forced response: an excitation shakes the support of a suspended object. We introduce dual visual-numeric conditioning and adapt six image-to-video backbones to predict this motion using only the flow-matching loss. Wan predicts motion accurately and generalizes to unseen excitations, objects, poses, and scenes. Counterfactual tests suggest capabilities beyond replaying training videos. But what laws have they learned? We design three tiers of tests using Taylor expansions of the dynamics and geometry. All six reproduce the linear response, including resonance; five capture higher-order dynamics, including nonlinear softening. Remarkably, softening is barely present in training: only 0.74% of the swing's squared displacement. Extensions to a double pendulum and a rocking block show sustained dynamics are learned more faithfully than brief impacts. Yet learned dynamics may fail to appear when state estimation or propagation goes wrong. We turn these tests and findings into strategies to improve video training and generation.

title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
authors: Stefan Martin; Jakob Schattenfroh; Patrick Schuenke; Felix Frederik Zimmermann; Ingolf Sack; Christoph Kolbitsch; Andreas Kofler
abstract: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.

title: Physics-Informed Feature Representations and Pretrained Tabular Foundation Models for Generalizable Melt Pool Geometry Prediction
authors: Rafid Enayet; Imtiaz Ahmed; Md Habibor Rahman
abstract: Developing generalizable, data-efficient machine learning (ML) models for advanced manufacturing remains challenging because experimental datasets are limited and process-property relationships vary across materials and operating conditions. In laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), melt pool width, depth, and melting mode (conduction, transition, or keyhole) govern process stability and defect formation. Conventional ML models typically use dimensional process parameters, which represent laser-material interactions only implicitly and may limit cross-material transfer. This study evaluates whether two physics-informed dimensionless features, normalized enthalpy and Peclet number, combining laser processing conditions with material thermophysical properties, improve melt pool prediction over raw process parameters. We systematically benchmark seven models: four classical ML methods (Gaussian process, support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) and three pretrained tabular foundation models (TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICLv2). Experiments span 316L stainless steel, IN625, IN718, and combined-material datasets, covering regression of melt pool width and depth and classification of melting modes. Dimensionless features yield comparable or superior predictive performance in most settings, with the largest gains in cross-material depth prediction (R^2 = 0.96). Tabular foundation models generally achieve stronger classification performance than classical baselines, particularly for multi-material datasets. These findings indicate that combining physically meaningful dimensionless representations with pretrained tabular models can improve data-efficient melt pool modeling and support more transferable process-window identification in LPBF.

title: PhysResponse: Probing the Physics of Video Generation with Controlled Interventions
authors: Yuhan Li; Shuran Zhang; Haixin Tian; Baonuo Rao; Weipeng Li; Yujia Hou; Zhenyu Wang; Zijun Wang; Luoyang Lin; Lijing Luo; Jiehui Huang; Kaiyuan Yang; Jingbin Tan; Panwen Hu; Xiaodan Liang
abstract: Video generation models are increasingly viewed as world simulators, which requires not only plausible motion but dynamics that respond correctly to specified physical parameters. Existing models, datasets and benchmarks, however, largely target physical plausibility, leaving this physical parameter responsiveness insufficiently explored. We introduce PhysResponse, a benchmark that measures it at two levels: scene-conditioned simulator inversion recovers the effective gravity, friction and initial speed of generated motion, and event evaluation tests outcomes near and across critical transitions. Evaluating ten image-to-video models, we find that even the lowest parameter errors exceed those of physically correct videos by over an order of magnitude, that models rarely reproduce both outcomes of a transition pair, and that the two levels expose complementary failures that visual metrics such as PSNR miss. To supply the missing training signal, we construct 72,000 simulated videos of 20 multi-object interaction types with controlled parameters; fine-tuning on them lowers parameter errors, even on held-out interaction types, and transfers to real videos and an external physics benchmark. Continued training with a numerical encoder further lowers all three errors on held-out types. PhysResponse provides a foundation for world simulators that follow physical conditions, not just appearances.

title: PhysScope: Agentic Multimodal Physics Reasoning with Grounded Visual Memory
authors: Haoyang Liu; Kecheng Liang; Xinyu Li; Weixing Chen; Yang Liu
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can correctly interpret physics diagrams yet apply constraints outside the states or conditions in which they hold, causing premise errors to propagate through subsequent calculations. We introduce PhysScope, an inference-time visual harness that supports self-correction of these scope mismatches without updating model weights. PhysScope enables the model to link physical scopes directly to its visual observations and explicitly constructs derived views to support reasoning. The harness imposes explicit constraints on state distinctions, conditions, and physical scopes during model reasoning, and checks agent-proposed revisions against sources and scopes. Accepted revisions invalidate registered dependents, thereby maintaining scope-aware working memory. On PhysAlign, PhysScope achieves higher solving scores than direct solving across all six evaluated VLMs. With Gemini-3.8-flash, it outperforms Canvas-CoT by 9.34 percentage points and substantially improves solving accuracy on the out-of-distribution (OOD) PhysUniBench benchmark. Ablation studies support explicit scope management and dependency maintenance as design principles for multimodal physics reasoning agents.

title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Zhenqing Ling; Qirui Jiao; Daoyuan Chen; Cheng Chen; Xinji Mai; Haowen Gao; Zhuo Zhang; Xuchen Pan; Mengsu Ding; Jiaji Deng; Yuexiang Xie; Xiaoming Qin; Weirui Kuang; Zhaoyang Liu; Yaliang Li; Bolin Ding; Jingren Zhou
abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.

title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings
authors: Jiani Cao; Anna Korhonen; Chen Cecilia Liu
abstract: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.

title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
authors: Lipeng He; Yihan Wang; Jiawen Zhang; N. Asokan
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

title: Pixel2Perspective: A Benchmark for Multi-Modal and Multi-View Generalization in Vision-Language Models
authors: Aditya Gandhamal; Aniruddh Sikdar; Arya Kishor; Suresh Sundaram
abstract: Embodied AI systems, such as drones and autonomous vehicles, improve navigation by enhancing perception in environments containing unseen objects. While Visual Language Models (VLMs) offer strong image understanding, their real-world application is underexplored. For effective deployment, open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) models, leveraging models like CLIP to assign pixel-level labels from text, must be robust to outdoor conditions, adverse weather, and varying viewpoints. Despite their potential, these models encounter significant challenges in cross-domain generalization, hindering their practical use in embodied AI applications. In this work, we present Pixel2Perspective, a benchmark for multi-angle object localization and open-vocabulary segmentation across both aerial and ground perspectives. This benchmark supports thorough evaluation across different viewpoints and sensor modalities. We assess foundational models like CLIP and advanced OVSS models using a curated dataset that spans varied outdoor conditions, sim-to-real scenarios, and multiple sensors, including infrared, to support the development of robust and generalizable perception systems. We also present a novel framework, Multi-Source RGB-IR Uncertainty Quantification (MSRIQ), which jointly models aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties across RGB and infrared imagery. This approach supports robust evaluation of open-vocabulary segmentation models across diverse environmental conditions. Our work sets a robustness-driven benchmark, providing key insights and laying the foundation for future research in open-world embodied AI perception. The benchmark and project page are available at https://aniruddhsikdar1.github.io/publications/pixel2perspective/

title: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds
authors: Hangwei Zhang; Rujing Dang; Ruimin Lin; Jiahong Wu; Xiangxiang Chu; Chuanxia Zheng
abstract: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project

title: Planning Width Is Hard to Approximate Even Given the Unique Optimal Plan
authors: Viet Bac Nguyen
abstract: For each fixed $k$, iterative-width search finds optimal plans in polynomial time on tasks of bounded tuple-chain width, but the approximability of planning width has remained open even when an optimal plan is supplied. When all optimal plans visit the same state sequence, we characterize set and chain width as hitting numbers of competing states. We construct positive-precondition STRIPS tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan, a single reachable goal state, binary branching, and constant-size actions. Every reachable state lies on a goal-reaching execution at most one action longer than optimal, yet distinguishing width $1$ from $Θ(N)$, where $N$ is the number of atoms, is NP-hard for set, chain, and goal-admissible width. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves a one-sided approximation factor $o(N)$ or a symmetric factor $o(\sqrt{N})$, and simple estimates attain both orders. For positive-precondition tasks with a supplied unique optimal plan of length at least two, testing set or chain width against a threshold $k\geq 1$ is coNP-complete for each fixed $k$ and $Σ_2^{\mathrm{P}}$-complete when $k$ is part of the input. Both results also hold for goal-admissible width if only one goal state is reachable. On an explicit state graph, a greedy algorithm approximates set width within a logarithmic factor even when optimal plans branch. Thus, knowing an optimal plan does not eliminate the difficulty of certifying substantially smaller width.

title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
authors: Gustavo Rezende Silva; Tobias John; Francisco Martín; EinarR Broch Johnsen
abstract: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
authors: Weihao Cheng
abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.
