title: Represented but misread: Post-training changes how language models read out what they represent
authors: Jochen Laubrock
abstract: Does post-training change what a language model represents, or how this representation is read out into an answer? We compared linear probes with the models' own answers, analyzed with signal detection theory, in six open-weight base models and their post-trained versions. For judgments of whether German texts were written by a human or an AI, probes and word n-gram classifiers separated the classes well, but the answers did not and often ordered the texts inversely. Post-training lowered the sensitivity of the answers on average ($Δd' = -0.34$ across model families; -0.29 across three prompts). It also changed the use of a stated base rate: Base models shifted their log-odds by less than the stated change in prior odds, most post-trained models by more. In two models with stage-wise checkpoints, the change occurred during supervised fine-tuning, model stitching implicated the early layers, and from mid-depth on internal states at positions after the text, not those of the text, transferred the change between checkpoints. Our corpora cannot be shared, so we add a case reproducible from public data, the truth of negated statements. Here, post-training acted in the opposite direction: Probes decoded truth at or near ceiling in every model, the answers of several base models did not use it, and post-training repaired them; by mid-depth the repair resided at the positions after the statement; below it, the representation of the statement contributed, strongly in one of four models. In a training study, adding 2,000 correctly labeled authorship judgments of news texts to otherwise identical fine-tuning data improved the answers on our newspaper and textbook corpora and inverted them on the chats, where they followed a news-trained probe of the base model. Post-training thus changed how a judgment is read out of what a model represents, and a small training signal can set its direction.

title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
authors: Siqi Xiang; Zhipeng Xu; Shengrui Liu; Zulong Chen; Chunyan Miao; Shijian Lu
abstract: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

title: Resolving the global forest fragmentation paradox
authors: Jiaxin Wu
abstract: This dataset contains sixteen landscape metrics calculated for global forest landscapes in 2000 and 2020 using non-overlapping 6 km × 6 km grid cells. The metrics characterise multiple dimensions of forest spatial configuration, including patch aggregation, isolation, edge, density, connectivity and shape complexity. Undefined values generated for the mean Euclidean nearest-neighbour distance (ENN_MN) and normalised landscape shape index (NLSI) were assigned a value of zero, corresponding to the minimum level of inter-patch isolation and shape complexity represented by each metric, respectively.

title: RespCCT and FreqCCT: Compact, Explainable and Cost-Aware Convolutional Transformers for Multi-Class Respiratory Disease Classification
authors: Auntor Chakma; Mst. Farhana Akter; Abu Henaf Rashid Ahmad Mufti; Asmana Yasmin
abstract: Chest auscultation depends on the listener, and software that classifies lung sounds could give a second reading where trained listeners are scarce. The most accurate published classifiers fine-tune large pretrained networks, and their accuracy is rarely reported with running cost or paired statistics. This study makes three contributions. (i) It proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers of 173,187 and 124,999 parameters that learn from random initialization on mel, constant-Q and cepstral images of 5 s frames from three public databases, ICBHI, KAUH and RD@TR, with 1,665 audio files in seven classes. (ii) It compares both models with five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants on one test set, using paired bootstrap intervals. (iii) It measures the cost of every pipeline stage on one CPU thread, tests whether attribution maps depend on the trained weights, and probes whether the learned features reveal the recording source. On the test fold, RespCCT reaches an accuracy of 98.13% and a macro F1 of 0.970, and FreqCCT reaches 97.58% and 0.951. Over five folds, RespCCT with three seeds reaches 97.65% and 0.959, and FreqCCT with one seed reaches 96.95% and 0.941. The two strongest pretrained networks reach a macro F1 of 0.984, whereas RespCCT needs 2.0 to 64.6 times less weight storage. Computing the three input images takes longer than running either model, and a linear probe identifies the source database with 0.958 accuracy. A team can weigh accuracy against storage and time before device testing.

title: Responsible AI Governance in Iran: A Program-Theory Evaluation of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
authors: Mohammad Masoumi Godarzi; Amin Poyanrad
abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence has become a strategic technology whose development requires coordinated institutional, regulatory, ethical, and infrastructural governance. This study evaluated the capacity of Iran’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy to support responsible AI governance by reconstructing its underlying program theory and examining the coherence of its implementation architecture. The research adopted a qualitative, theory-based case-study design. Data were obtained through documentary analysis of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy and related policy materials, together with semi-structured interviews with 12 experts from academic, research, policy, and industrial backgrounds. The data were coded and thematically analysed using MAXQDA, after which an integrated theory of change and theory of action was developed and applied to the national strategy. The findings indicated that responsible AI governance in Iran depends on sustained political commitment, a legally empowered and agile coordinating institution, equitable access to high-quality data and computational infrastructure, interdisciplinary human capital, effective university–industry collaboration, risk-based regulation, and continuous policy evaluation. The strategy provides an important normative foundation by emphasizing human dignity, national values, scientific development, priority sectors, and the participation of knowledge-based firms. Nevertheless, its implementation architecture remains insufficiently specified. Major weaknesses include ambiguity regarding institutional authority, sustainable financing, data classification, access to computational resources, legal liability, regulatory instruments, measurable indicators, and mechanisms for periodic revision. The analysis also identified major policy dualities involving open versus sensitive data, centralized versus networked governance, strict versus adaptive regulation, domestic versus international standards, state versus private investment, and problem-oriented versus technology-oriented development. The study concludes that the effectiveness of the strategy depends on translating broad objectives into an explicit, funded, accountable, and adaptive program of action. Responsible AI governance requires not merely ethical declarations, but a coherent causal chain connecting institutions, resources, activities, outputs, societal outcomes, and mechanisms of accountability.</jats:p>

title: Responsible AI in Forensic Accounting
authors: N. Sathyanarayana; Raji Rajan; G. Laxmana Rao; N. V. Vinutha; Shefali Shukla
abstract: <jats:p>The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into forensic accounting has significantly enhanced the detection of fraud, financial manipulation, and anomalies in corporate reporting. However, the increasing reliance on AI systems raises critical concerns related to governance, ethics, and regulatory compliance. This chapter examines the concept of responsible AI within the domain of forensic accounting, focusing on transparency, fairness, accountability, and data integrity. It proposes a governance framework that aligns AI deployment with ethical auditing practices and evolving regulatory standards. By analysing global developments and practical challenges, the chapter highlights the risks of algorithmic bias, opacity, and misuse of automated systems. It offers strategic recommendations for ensuring that AI-driven forensic practices remain reliable, auditable, and aligned with sustainability and ESG objectives.</jats:p>

title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Frameworks for Trustworthy Enterprise Decision-Making
authors: Amol Murgai; Kingshuk Srivastava; S. Rani; Ashish Kumar Anand; Samariddin Elmirzaev; Shaik Balkhis Banu
abstract: <jats:p>The convergence of enterprise artificial-intelligence governance is around three points: Most importantly, tier systems by their risk level, then implement proportionate controls, and finally document it in an attestation. This chapter concludes that the architecture has three points at which it fails to meet measurable objectives, and quantifies each. A portfolio simulation of 40 cases demonstrates that a categorical tiering introduces 14.5 to 24.7 per cent more residual risk, compared to a continuous allocation of the same set of assurance budget, as in the case of the range-compression defect for risk matrices. Tail risk increases by 84 per cent as dependency concentration increases at constant budget, a level of exposure that is not covered by any per-system control in enterprise systems, due to the fact that all of these systems share foundation models, vendors and data pipelines. a pass/fail attestation conveys only 0.069 bits of mutual information, marginally reducing the posterior probability of non-compliance from 0.150 to 0.108.</jats:p>

title: ResVision: Spectrum-Matched Resizing and Context-Preserving Inspection for Visual Reasoning
authors: Guojian Zhan; Jiahao Xu; Yahui Liu; Yao Hu; Chuan Mu
abstract: Agentic visual reasoning improves vision-language models by selectively enlarging evidence without adding new scene content, but the benefit depends on whether fine structure remains accessible and whether local observations stay grounded in the full scene. We identify three recurring bottlenecks: high-frequency detail can be attenuated during visual-token formation; spatially distributed evidence can remain encoded yet difficult for the language model to retrieve; and isolated crops can weaken whole-detail correspondence through scale and positional mismatch. ResVision addresses these limitations with two complementary components. Spectrum-Matched Resizing (SMR) estimates image complexity and selects an adaptive global sampling scale, avoiding unnecessary enlargement on simple inputs while allocating more visual tokens to detail-rich images. Context-Preserving Inspection (CPI) returns each inspected crop together with the complete working view, preserving local detail and global context across tool turns. We evaluate Direct and Agentic variants on four frontier VLMs and 29 benchmarks spanning six visual-reasoning families. Complete ResVision (Agentic Base plus SMR plus CPI) is best for every model, improving by 3.36 to 4.94 points over Direct Base and 1.87 to 2.94 points over Agentic Base. These results show that adaptive visual sampling and context-preserving inspection address distinct, complementary constraints in multimodal reasoning.

title: ReSynth: Constructing Synthetic Supervision for Multi-Image Understanding
authors: Yilin Wang; Xin Yu; Xinyi Guo; Xiangxi Zheng; Dongxing Mao; Linjie Li; Zhengyuan Yang; Alex Jinpeng Wang
abstract: People often understand the world by comparing different views of it. Vision-language models (VLMs), however, receive these views as separate images and still struggle to relate them. One problem is data. Training on these tasks requires groups of images with a known relationship: the same object from different viewpoints, or the same scene before and after a change. Such examples are hard to collect at scale from existing photo collections. We introduce ReSynth, which turns single-image perception and controllable image generation into cross-image relational supervision. Localized editing produces before-and-after pairs, viewpoint generation produces multiple views of the same instance, and verified scene contents support comparisons of counts and attributes. ReSynth combines Qwen3-VL-8B's captioning, grounding, and counting capabilities with Qwen-Image-2.1's generation and editing capabilities. It verifies single-image facts such as object counts and attributes, then combines these facts to construct multi-image QA. Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.

title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
authors: Yunhe Gao; Ashwin Kumar; Jiaming Liu; Chong Wang; Maya Varma; Fuying Wang; Stefania L. Moroianu; Louisa Fay; Sergios Gatidis; Akshay S. Chaudhari; Curtis Langlotz
abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.

title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
authors: Tianxiang Chen; Jingyuan Zhou; Weiming Yang; Kaidi Yang
abstract: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.

title: ReTouchGS: Ultralight Render-free Aesthetic Color Enhancement and Transfer for 3D Gaussian Splatting
authors: Chuanzhi Xu; Boyu Wei; Chengkun Yue; Xuanhua Yin; Yiyang Li; Haodong Chen; Qiang Qu; Weidong Cai
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic scene reconstruction. Existing 3DGS color transfer and interactive editing methods are guided by reference images and user-specified color adjustments. However, in many applications, users simply want aesthetically guided color enhancement that automatically makes the scene more visually appealing while maintaining consistent colors and tones across viewpoints. We present ReTouchGS, to our knowledge the first framework for reference-free aesthetic color enhancement of pretrained 3DGS models. It predicts a scene-level color lookup table (LUT) from the model and its associated camera parameters. ReTouchGS also supports reference-guided color transfer by fitting a scene-level LUT using one edited view of the same scene and its corresponding original render. A shared blend-aware color refinement network with only 44.7K parameters refines an analytic color update to realize either color mapping without rendering. It preserves geometry and delivers standard 3DGS assets in seconds. We also design the ReTouch3D benchmark to support the evaluation of aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer across viewpoints. Experiments demonstrate high color accuracy and strong generalization to unseen scenes in both aesthetic color enhancement and reference-guided color transfer.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Vincenzo Marcianò; Xiaoming Zhang; Michela Antonelli; Sebastien Ourselin; Maria A Zuluaga
abstract: Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace

title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
authors: Lena Pickartz; Philipp Schaer; Phillip B. Ströbel
abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

title: Retroactive Concept Bottleneck Models for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
authors: Yang Ji; Ying Sun; Yuanxin Zhuang; Yuting Zhang
abstract: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning (EFCIL) requires models to learn new classes sequentially without retaining training samples from previous tasks. Continual concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make their predictions interpretable by identifying visual concepts in an image and using them to score each class. However, these methods typically focus on preserving learned concepts or approximating past classes with generated features, which can leave new concepts underused in old-class predictions. We propose RetroCBM, which retains a small set of vocabulary-independent statistics relating frozen visual features to the embedding space of a pretrained vision-language model. Even after earlier training images have been discarded, we can use these statistics to supervise new concepts. To do so, we develop a retroactive regression rule that yields the same predictor for each new concept as class-balanced ridge regression on all images seen so far. We then reproject the stored statistics to recover the full-history squared classification loss and thus learn how much each new concept should contribute to old-class predictions. Since the classifier may use systematic concept errors to distinguish nearby classes, we further introduce a graph-weighted penalty on the margin shifts caused by those errors. Across six datasets, RetroCBM outperforms state-of-the-art interpretable methods in all class-incremental settings, with an 18.1\% relative gain in mean average incremental accuracy over the strongest exemplar-free baseline.

title: Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution
authors: Shenghua Liu; Youssef Faragalla; Surya Ganguli; Stephen A. Baccus
abstract: Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.

title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
authors: Y. -H. Taguchi
abstract:
For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $Δ= [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not.
  We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $π$ to $π\circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $Δ(π) = -Δ(π\circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in.
  The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $σ$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.

title: Revised Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guideline: An update for the age of Artificial Intelligence
authors: Ahmed Kerwan; A. Al-Jabir; Ginimol Mathew; C. Sohrabi; Rasha Rashid; T. Franchi; M. Nicola; M. Agha; R. Agha
abstract:
Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare and scientific publishing. Reporting guidelines need to be updated to take into account this advance. The SCARE Guideline 2025 update adds a new AI-focused domain to promote transparency, reproducibility, and ethical integrity in surgical case reports involving AI.

Methods: A Delphi consensus exercise was conducted to update the SCARE guidelines. A panel of 49 surgical and scientific experts were invited to rate proposed new items. In round 1, participants scored each item on a 9-point Likert scale and provided feedback. Items not meeting consensus were revised or discarded.

Results: A 94% response rate occurred amongst participants (46/49) in the first round. Ratings were analysed for agreement levels, and consensus was reached on all six proposed AI-related items. A revised SCARE checklist is presented which incorporates these new AI related items. Authors are now expected to disclose AI involvement not only in patient care but also in manuscript preparation, as exemplified by this paper.

Conclusion: The SCARE 2025 guideline provides an up-to-date framework for surgical case reports in the era of AI. Through a robust consensus process, we have added specific reporting criteria for AI to ensure that any use of artificial intelligence in a case report is clearly documented, explained and discussed including with respect to bias and ethics. This update will help maintain the quality, transparency, and clinical relevance of case reports, ultimately improving their educational value and trustworthiness for the surgical community.

title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
authors: Shuroug A. Alowais; S. Alghamdi; N. Alsuhebany; Tariq Alqahtani; Abdulrahman I. Alshaya; Sumaya N. Almohareb; Atheer Aldairem; Mohammed A. Alrashed; Khalid bin Saleh; H. Badreldin; M. Al Yami; S. Al Harbi; A. Albekairy
abstract: Introduction Healthcare systems are complex and challenging for all stakeholders, but artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed various fields, including healthcare, with the potential to improve patient care and quality of life. Rapid AI advancements can revolutionize healthcare by integrating it into clinical practice. Reporting AI’s role in clinical practice is crucial for successful implementation by equipping healthcare providers with essential knowledge and tools. Research Significance This review article provides a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of the current state of AI in clinical practice, including its potential applications in disease diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and patient engagement. It also discusses the associated challenges, covering ethical and legal considerations and the need for human expertise. By doing so, it enhances understanding of AI’s significance in healthcare and supports healthcare organizations in effectively adopting AI technologies. Materials and Methods The current investigation analyzed the use of AI in the healthcare system with a comprehensive review of relevant indexed literature, such as PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE, with no time constraints but limited to articles published in English. The focused question explores the impact of applying AI in healthcare settings and the potential outcomes of this application. Results Integrating AI into healthcare holds excellent potential for improving disease diagnosis, treatment selection, and clinical laboratory testing. AI tools can leverage large datasets and identify patterns to surpass human performance in several healthcare aspects. AI offers increased accuracy, reduced costs, and time savings while minimizing human errors. It can revolutionize personalized medicine, optimize medication dosages, enhance population health management, establish guidelines, provide virtual health assistants, support mental health care, improve patient education, and influence patient-physician trust. Conclusion AI can be used to diagnose diseases, develop personalized treatment plans, and assist clinicians with decision-making. Rather than simply automating tasks, AI is about developing technologies that can enhance patient care across healthcare settings. However, challenges related to data privacy, bias, and the need for human expertise must be addressed for the responsible and effective implementation of AI in healthcare.

title: Reward misalignment as an opportunity for materials discovery
authors: Ryotaro Okabe; Shoki Kishida; Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk; Dominic Bollettieri; Takuya Isogawa; Yongqiang Cheng; Mingda Li; Masaki Adachi
abstract: Reward misalignment is usually regarded as a failure of artificial intelligence. In materials discovery with generative AI models, however, disagreement between predefined rewards and expert judgment may reveal materials that the rewards overlook. We investigate this possibility using electronic flat bands as a prime example. Experts mostly agree with a numerical bandwidth score, but their disagreements are systematic and cannot be explained by an estimated 5% rate of mistaken labels. We learn the experts' preferences from pairwise comparisons and use them to guide a crystal diffusion model. The learned preferences and numerical score agree on the flattest bands but diverge elsewhere. For example, the preferences favor KCo2As2 and CoGa, reported compounds with partially flat bands that the score would discard. The framework also extends to synthesizability and phonon properties. Our findings suggest that reward misalignment can expose opportunities for materials discovery beyond what fixed rewards are designed to find.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
authors: Jiarui Cui; Boxun Yan
abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
authors: Jiarui Guo; Saining Zhang; Jiaying Wan; Jiawei Weng; Junhao Chen; Rui Zhang; Yuanbo Lyu; Zhiheng Lee; Peishuo Li; Jingrun Du; Weiqing Xiao; Weiyi Lin; Zenan Meng; Hu Wei; Lin Qu; Zongzheng Zhang; Hao Zhao; Chaojian Li
abstract: Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.

title: Rheological Performance and Predictive Modeling of Waste Toner–Modified Asphalt Binders Using an Artificial Neural Network
authors: Rahul M. S.; Krishna A.; Udaya Bhanu V.; Pavan T. S.; Suresha S. N.
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The use of waste toner (WT) as an asphalt modifier supports sustainable pavement design, but its performance under construction-level thermal exposure remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluated the effect of extended rolling thin-film oven (RTFO) aging on the rheological and thermorheological behavior of VG10 binders modified with 8%–14% WT. Binder performance was assessed through Superpave grading, multiple stress creep recovery (MSCR), linear amplitude sweep (LAS), and time–temperature superposition (TTSP) analyses. WT improved high-temperature stiffness and rutting resistance up to a 12% dosage, increasing the performance grade from PG 58 to PG 70. At 14%, the improvements diminished and deviations from thermorheological simplicity appeared under prolonged aging, indicating limited compatibility at higher dosages. Fatigue evaluation showed that although WT generally reduced fatigue life, the 8% dosage provided the most balanced response. A predictive framework was developed, and a feedforward artificial neural network (ANN) outperformed multiple linear regression in predicting complex modulus and phase angle. The results demonstrate that WT can serve as an effective modifier when used within optimized dosage limits.</jats:p>

title: Rigel-Ladon: An Option-Count Law for a One-Pass Decision Encoder, Tested on Held-Out Option Counts and Held-Out Schemas
authors: Mohammed Nayeem Khan; Vrishank Tiwari; Navin Kumar R
abstract: Laya is a small neural network that reads a text, a question and K written options, and returns one probability per option in a single pass. We ask how its accuracy falls as K grows from 2 to 35 and whether that can be predicted. We score nested option sets (every K-option question contains the smaller ones) on four question pools, for the released model (Base) and our fine-tune (FT), and score every item against each single rival. FT trained on one 12-option topic question (in-family); a 12-option HR (department-routing) question is out-of-family. Logit accuracy (the log of correct over incorrect answers) is linear in log(K-1) with slope 0.68 to 0.88. Fitted on K up to 6, the law predicts K=7 to 12 within 0.6 points and K up to 24 within 1.2 (a log-linear rule: 1.6 and 6.7). Taking the slope from the topic question and measuring only two-option accuracy on HR predicts its other K within 0.3 points (FT) and 0.7 (Base). On a 35-label pool of five schemas the law fails (5 to 11 points). Independence of irrelevant alternatives is rejected: the gold-versus-rival log-odds shifts by +0.24 to +2.07 nats per doubling of K, yet pairwise answers reproduce K-way accuracy within 4.7 points. Order averaging (averaging over several orderings of the options), shortlists, a temperature law and calibrated prediction sets did not transfer (FT's 90% sets cover 84% on HR). 2 of 10 predictions made in advance held. Caveats: one model family and LLM-labelled synthetic text.

title: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities
authors: Hoang Pham Cong; Long D. Nguyen; Ho Viet Duc Luong; Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat; Binh P. Nguyen; Huynh Thi Thanh Binh
abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

title: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zixuan Liu; Hashem Haghbayan; Zizhan Zheng; Siavash Khajavi
abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.

title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
authors: Fariborz Setoudehtazangi; Geoffrey J. McLachlan
abstract: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.

title: Risk-Triggered Search: Behavior-Preserving Safe Control
authors: Xinyu Deng; Bohao Lan; Kunpeng Li; Mingkai Yuan; Weihang Pan; Binbin Lin
abstract: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.

title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
authors: Ruben Sanchez-Corcuera; Unai Zulaika; Aritz Bilbao-Jayo; Miguel Fernandez-de-Retana
abstract: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The count holds for new and repeated problems and for groups of 4 to 256 attempts, and across learning rates, optimizers, GRPO variants and model sizes from 1.3M to 85M parameters, which move the threshold but not what is counted.

title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
authors: {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6a9f', 'user': {'_id': '64f8b03f83807928d25e766f', 'avatarUrl': '/avatars/56f0588d02b7db419ce8eed9b0cdf701.svg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'Tuna Han Salih Meral', 'user': 'tmeral', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'tmeral'}, 'name': 'Tuna Han Salih Meral', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-21T00:45:04.531Z', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6aa0', 'name': 'Kaan Oktay', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6aa1', 'name': 'Alec Helbling', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6aa2', 'name': 'Atakan Kara', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6aa3', 'name': 'Duen Horng Chau', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b0092e7ecb204ffe44e6aa4', 'name': 'Pinar Yanardag', 'hidden': False}
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral; Kaan Oktay; Alec Helbling; Atakan Kara; Duen Horng Chau; Pinar Yanardag
