title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
authors: {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b91', 'name': 'Zheyuan Liu', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b92', 'name': 'Chuhan Wang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b93', 'name': 'Jinduo Guo', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b94', 'name': 'Yue Huang', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b95', 'name': 'Xiangchi Yuan', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b96', 'name': 'Ningshan Ma', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6b00f0ffecb204ffe44e6b97', 'name': 'Meng Jiang', 'hidden': False}
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

title: Technico-Economic Analysis of Solar Tracking (Tracker) and Fixed Photovoltaic Systems: Case Study in Conakry
authors: Ansoumane Sakouvogui; Wogbo Dominique GUILAVOGUI; Yacouba Camara; Saïdou Barry; Nènè Aïssata Baldé
abstract: Background and Aim: The addition of solar tracking systems (trackers) allows for an increase in photovoltaic energy production under tropical climates, as demonstrated in Conakry. However, this performance increase comes with increased mechanical and electronic complexity. Method: This article presents a comparative techno-economic analysis between a fixed system and a single-axis tracker system (60 Wp), integrating capital expenditures (CAPEX), operational and maintenance costs (OPEX), as well as the parasitic consumption of the tracking system. Results: Experimental results show a gross production gain of 40.2%, which reduces to a net real gain of 31.2% once parasitic consumption is deducted. Economically, for a micro-generation application, the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) in an off-grid site is 0.25 USD/kWh for the fixed system compared to 0.45 USD/kWh for the tracker, with a payback period for the latter exceeding 21 years. These results reveal that while the tracker is technically superior, it is only economically viable for installations with a capacity greater than one kilowatt-peak (kWp), due to the incompressible fixed cost of control electronics at a small scale. Conclusion: The study concludes with a recommendation against using trackers for small solar lamps or domestic kits, but advocates for their deployment in rural mini-grids and industrial installations.

title: Technological impact on work life through integration of workplace learning and higher technical education learning: Stakeholders’ perspective
authors: James Elikana Mmari
abstract: This chapter aim at presenting stakeholders’ perceptions of the integration of workplace learning and higher technical education using technology and how it affects their working environment and in turn their work and study life altogether. The chapter provides stakeholders’ understanding of the key concepts; their understand of the impact of technology in working and learning environment, the integration of the two learning modes, the factors affecting this integration, the role of policies and how they affect the success of this integration. This empirical research focuses on the higher technical education–an area which is under researched when it comes to the topics related to vocational education and training in connection with the workplace environment. Furthermore, the study has also looked at the developing countries environment, where adult learning education perspective is still limited in the very early definitions and understanding, thus; the support to adults who could not succeed in the main stream educational system of that particular country, and the focus has been to help them from reading and writing illiteracy, however, many advancement has been done in this area, especially in developed countries, where, adult learning is no longer bounded in those constrains. Technological advancement, the need for further education and contemporary theories of adult education and learning, in connection with the workplace learning, requires variety of changing in education systems, policies and curriculum development processes so as to make the educational sector as inclusive as possible. With reference to these reasons, authors of this chapter discussed on the matters in depth with the empirical references from the main stakeholders in this area. It is with good hope that, the shared experience and the perspectives discussed will bring constructive insights to readers and other researchers who have interests in these topics. The complexity and yet uniqueness of these topics, especially when are being subjected into one umbrella of discussion and researched, make them worth reading. The empirical data used from this study were collected via a semi-structured interview protocol, this was due to the exploratory nature of investigation, that’s the study lies under a qualitative paradigm. Interviews were conducted with the main stakeholders of the study, who were (N = 4) students , (N = 4) employers from various business sectors, (N = 4) educators from higher educational institutions and (N = 3) policy makers from the policy development bodies. Applying the bottom-up content analysis method, the transcribed interviews were analyzed to identify themes. Atlas.ti, a qualitative content analysis software was used to aid the authors discover and organize themes and their categories to answer the research questions based on perceptions, challenges, and experiences of the stakeholders. Various categories and codes were discovered and used in discussing the results for an easy understanding of the subject matter. The findings from this research have also provided a good ground for further discussion and research in the subject matter, so as to bring and contribute valuable literature in the area of higher technical education, workplace learning and work life in general in connection with technological interventions. It is from this piloted study that researchers where able to run main, wide study in the subject matter to raise a doctoral thesis manuscript. With this short discussion and introduction of the core coverage of the topic, it is the hope of the authors that they have brought a valuable discussion and contribution that is worthy reading and included in this book. Authors, believe that this topic will open eyes and bring more in-depth research in this subject matter. We encourage and welcome further collaboration as well as comments, suggestions and questions concerning this study.

title: Technological Readiness and Data Analytics Adoption in Auditing Firms
authors: Suchita Gera
abstract: <jats:p>The movement of audit firms into digital modes has changed the way they provide assurance services, detect fraud, and assess risk in an increasingly adaptive financial environment. This research will evaluate how technology readiness affects the adoption of data analytics by auditing firms through constructs: perceived utility, perceived ease of use, organizational support, data analytic self-efficacy, behavioural intention, and actual use. To accomplish this, a quantitative research strategy was used in conjunction with conclusive surveys with 278 audit professionals. SEM were used to assess both the relationships between proposed variables. Results showed that organizational support was the best predictor of behavioural intention regardless of audit type; however, behavioural intention was shown to have a direct effect on the actual use of analytics tools in audit procedures. Mediation analysis had confirmed that behavioural intention serves as a significant mediator between dimensions of technology readiness and practical analytics adoption.</jats:p>

title: Technology Adoption in Retail Supply Chains
authors: Aafreen Shah; Aparna Jain
abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Blockchain technologies in retail supply chains through the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework, focusing on emerging economies such as India. As supply chains face increasing pressure to enhance efficiency, transparency, and sustainability, traditional systems are becoming inadequate in addressing demand volatility and operational complexities. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study combines qualitative insights from 40 organized retailers with quantitative data from 350 organized retailers, analyzed using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM). The findings reveal that technological factors such as perceived value and compatibility, organizational factors including top management support, and environmental factors such as external support and trading partner readiness significantly influence adoption. The results show that AI enhances forecasting and inventory optimization, while blockchain strengthens traceability and transparency, acting as complementary enablers of sustainable supply chains.</jats:p>

title: Tell Me How Sure You Are: Communicating Uncertainty in Auxiliary Evidence to Foundation Models
authors: Soumyajit Chatterjee; Baturalp Buyukates; Abhirup Ghosh
abstract:
In many queries, the context information provided to generative foundation models, such as LLMs and VLMs, is inherently uncertain, including its representations of the physical world. While conventional prompting discards the associated uncertainty, this paper, for the first time in the literature, systematically demonstrates that communicating such uncertainty in context provides useful additional cues for downstream decisions and yields improvements across a wide range of settings.
  We formulate the decision-making problem as a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task supported by auxiliary text-based characteristics. We choose this due to the availability of well-defined auxiliary properties, associated uncertainty, and unambiguous task correctness. Using five downstream foundation models across three datasets, we extensively evaluate uncertainty arising from both humans and learned models when observing or predicting auxiliary evidence. Across all settings, we find that communicating uncertainty substantially improves downstream LLM classification performance: macro-F1 improves up to $26.18$ percentage points compared to when the uncertainty information is not communicated.
  We further observe how the foundation models process such uncertainty information and find that auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive information about the correctness of downstream decisions. Together, these results establish uncertainty as useful contextual information and motivate more systematic consideration of uncertainty communication in future foundation-model inference pipelines.

title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
authors: Dibyajyoti Nayak; Yuze Pu; Kami Mohammadi; Somdatta Goswami
abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

title: Temporal Image Representations for Mouse Dynamics Authentication
authors: Junyi Li; Charles Devlen; Daqing Hou
abstract: Mouse dynamics authentication has traditionally relied on handcrafted features or time-series representations that capture both spatial and temporal characteristics of mouse movements. More recent approaches have modeled mouse data as images, enabling the use of powerful pretrained computer vision models. However, prior work primarily focuses on spatial-only representations where the cursor coordinates are plotted as a trajectory image. These representations discard the temporal characteristics which can help discriminate users. In this work, we propose image representations that incorporate speed and velocity information for mouse dynamics authentication. We investigate two mouse data representations, a XYPlot representation that intuitively shows the path of movement, and a Pairwise Distance (PWD) representation that utilizes the entire image canvas to encode relationships between mouse events. Both representations are evaluated under both location-aware and location-free settings using pretrained 2D-CNN and ViT architectures. We found that the incorporation of temporal information improved performance over spatial representations alone, and that the location-aware variants generally outperformed the location-free. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on two datasets, Balabit and TWOS, and extend our evaluation to two other datasets. We found that in general, location-aware PWD with temporal encoding combined with the 2D-CNN architecture provided the best results, with mean EERs of 5.21% and 12.70% on the Balabit Test-1 and Test-2 sets, respectively, 4.94% on TWOS, 6.16% on ChaoShen, and 0.59% on DFL.

title: Temporal Rank in Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Leo Dobson; Anton Ragni
abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a natural framework for temporal modelling, yet are often dismissed due to their sequential, non-parallelisable computation and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies, typically attributed to vanishing and exploding gradients. We identify a distinct and under-explored limitation: an information bottleneck induced by rank-constrained hidden state dynamics, which limits the number of independent input directions that can be preserved over time, as reflected in the rank of the input-to-state mapping. We show that this constraint restricts temporal capacity independently of gradient stability. To address this, we introduce structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal separability and prevent saturation of the input-to-state Jacobian over time. On controlled sequence tasks, the resulting model exhibits rapid learning despite remaining strictly within a standard RNN formulation. Our results demonstrate that RNN performance is governed by the evolution and preservation of temporal rank, and suggest that mitigating gradient pathologies alone is insufficient without explicitly maintaining temporal capacity.

title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
authors: Behrooz Tahmasebi; Melanie Weber
abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.

title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents
authors: Meghana Aparna Sistla; Alaia Solko-Breslin; Somesh Jha; Aditya Kanade; Krishnamurthy Dj Dvijotham
abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.

title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
authors: Ziqing Yang; Yixin Wu; Michael Backes; Yang Zhang
abstract: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

title: Text Lives in the Guidance: Preventing Silent Text Rewriting in Cached Diffusion Transformers
authors: Kun Zhou; Wenmian Yang; Zhensheng Wang; Weijia Jia
abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) now render long, legible text in images, and feature caching is a standard way to accelerate them. Caches are judged by image-level metrics, which do not check whether the rendered text is still correct. We find that caching silently rewrites this text. On Z-Image, TaylorSeer at 2.9x fewer FLOPs lowers word accuracy from 62% to 46%, while ImageReward and CLIP Score barely change. Sampling with fewer steps at the same compute keeps almost all of this text, so the loss comes from how the cache predicts the skipped steps. Decomposing the cache error along classifier-free guidance (CFG), we trace this loss mainly to the guidance term, the difference between the conditional and unconditional predictions, which caches extrapolate worst on text. Correcting the guidance inside the text alone recovers most of the lost text. We therefore propose GuideCache, which recomputes both CFG branches only on the tokens with the largest predicted guidance error, using the guidance terms that the cache already stores. At 2.4x fewer FLOPs, GuideCache restores full-compute prompt fidelity on Z-Image and Qwen-Image, and on Z-Image it renders text as well as or better than ToCa, TeaCache, and FasterCache while staying much closer to the full model's output. GuideCache works with caches of any order, and on top of fewer sampling steps it keeps more text than step reduction at a higher speedup. These results suggest that acceleration methods for text-rendering models should be evaluated on the text they render.

title: TextSphere: Efficient Text-to-Image Generation via Shared Hyperspherical Alignment and Uniformity
authors: Yixia Zhang; Girish A. Koushik; Xilu Wang; Wenwu Wang
abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image generation have substantially improved image quality, particularly through diffusion-based methods that require multiple inference steps. In contrast, Sphere Encoder offers an efficient generative framework capable of producing images with fewer forward steps. However, extending it to free-form text is nontrivial, because its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose TextSphere, an efficient text-to-image generative framework that extends Sphere Encoder with language conditioning and cross-modal alignment. We incorporate pretrained CLIP text embeddings through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to guide image generation while retaining the original spherical sampling mechanism. To bridge the cross-modal representation gap, we introduce a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) objective that jointly promotes semantic alignment and representation uniformity on the hypersphere. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k demonstrate that TextSphere consistently reduces generation FID (gFID) over the text-conditioned baseline while achieving reconstruction FID (rFID) below 1.0. With only 4 and 6 sampling steps, TextSphere achieves lower gFID than the compared diffusion- and GAN-based models trained from scratch on CUB-200-2011 and MS-COCO-2014, respectively. We further observe that improved reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily yield better generation quality. In addition, we use Partial Least Squares Singular Value Decomposition (PLS-SVD) to analyze cross-modal alignment and modality gap, offering insight into the effectiveness of our approach.

title: The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
authors: Tobias Ladner; Konstantin Kaulen; Stanley Bak; Julien Girard-Satabin; Taylor T. Johnson; Edoardo Manino; ThanhVu H Nguyen; Ben Wooding; Haoze Wu
abstract: This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.

title: The Blurring of Truth in the Post-Truth Era
authors: Elif Ateş; İdil Sayımer; Recep Yılmaz
abstract: <jats:p>The Post-Truth era, which postmodernist thinkers laid the foundation for, is a term used to describe the time and way of thinking we are in. While postmodernism questioned the social transformations experienced in the light of economic, social, and technological developments in the world from a critical point of view, it also put forward the idea that reality and its representation are problematic. As a matter of fact, in line with these ideas, the blurring of truth in the post-truth era and the idea that there can be no single thing that can be called truth have begun to prevail. The change and transformation of forms of communication have made it easier to manipulate, create perception, and change and rebuild the truth according to power relations. Qualitative research method was used in the study, and discourses in which the truth was distorted or blurred in line with power and ideology were analyzed using Teun van Dijk's critical discourse analysis framework.</jats:p>

title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
authors: Andrew W. Lo; Chaoyi Zhao
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

title: The Connection Between Emotional Intelligence, the Level of Loneliness and Characteristics of Attitudes towards Parents in Adolescence
authors: A.V. Degtyarev; S.D. Chivileva; D.M. Kuptsova
abstract: <jats:p><p style="text-align: justify;">This article examines the connections between emotional intelligence, the level of loneliness and the characteristics of adolescents&rsquo; relationships with their parents. Adolescence is characterized by significant emotional changes that affect adolescents&rsquo; social relationships and self-esteem. The study is based on theoretical concepts of emotional intelligence, the phenomenon of loneliness and child-parent relationships, developed by both domestic and foreign psychologists. In the empirical part of the work, methods of psychodiagnostic research and correlation analysis were used to identify relationships between the parameters under study. The study involved 76 people aged 12 to 16 years. The results show that high levels of emotional intelligence in adolescents are associated with low levels of loneliness and positive relationships with parents. There is also a positive correlation between subjective feelings of loneliness and the hostility of both parents, and a negative correlation between subjective feelings of loneliness in adolescence and parents&rsquo; positive interest in their children.</p></jats:p>

title: The Coverage Selection Gap: Ranking, Not Generation, Limits LLM Rubric Construction
authors: Ali Karkehabadi; Jamshid Hassanpour; Rafael E. Banchs
abstract: Task-specific rubrics are increasingly used to evaluate open-ended language-model outputs, yet constructing comprehensive evaluation criteria from complex source documents remains challenging. We study automatic rubric construction in professional mergers and acquisitions (M&A) due diligence, where evaluation criteria must be inferred from task instructions and supporting documents without access to an expert-authored reference rubric. We introduce a multi-axis generation framework that explores complementary structural and free-form views of the source evidence to construct a broad pool of candidate evaluation criteria. To distinguish failures of criterion discovery from failures of candidate selection, we introduce the coverage-selection gap, which measures the difference between reference-free ranking and a reference-informed greedy diagnostic under a fixed selection budget. Developed on 16 tasks and evaluated on four held-out tasks, our framework achieves 0.876 macro recall against senior-authored reference rubrics under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Ablation studies further show that introducing new structural search axes improves recall by 6-10 percentage points, whereas increasing generation volume along existing search directions yields at most 1.5 points. These findings suggest that, once a high-coverage candidate pool has been constructed, effective reference-free selection becomes a substantial bottleneck in document-grounded rubric construction.

title: The Delayed Societal Cost of Unfairness
authors: Giovani Valdrighi; Isabel Valera; Marcos Medeiros Raimundo
abstract: Fair machine learning typically evaluates the societal costs of a decision policy -- the loss incurred by the decision-maker (DM) and the unfair distribution of costs among demographic groups of decision-subjects (DS) -- on static data, where reducing one often comes at the expense of the other. Yet decisions change the populations on which they act, and prior work has shown that fairness interventions designed on static data may fail to benefit, or even harm, the disadvantaged group over time. We investigate a complementary question: When can a policy that is Pareto-optimal on pre-deployment data be outperformed by a fairer policy once each is evaluated on the population it induces, reducing costs for one stakeholder without increasing them for the other? In a setting where qualification scores evolve in response to binary decisions and their outcomes, we show that under Rawlsian fairness, which never lowers any group's acceptance rate, placing sufficiently high weight on fairness reduces societal costs whenever accepting disadvantaged DS at the DM's break-even point leaves them in a state less costly to the DM than rejecting them. Under egalitarian fairness, which may lower the advantaged group's acceptance rate, this additionally requires the reduction in DM loss on the disadvantaged group to outweigh the increase on the advantaged group. Under both fairness notions, however, when DM loss is accuracy-based, improvements in the post-deployment population may arise from declining DS qualification, revealing that gains for the DM do not necessarily translate into better outcomes for DS. Our results show that policy-induced population dynamics can overturn apparent performance-fairness trade-offs, allowing fairer policies to reduce the delayed societal costs of decision-making.

title: The Depth of a Prediction: Where Language Models Resolve a Word Predicts Human Reading Time
authors: Donato Riccio; Fabrizio Maturo
abstract: Surprisal from a language model's final layer predicts how long people read a word, yet the model computes its prediction across many layers. We read each word's prediction at every layer with the tuned lens and summarize this layerwise surprisal trajectory by its resolution depth, the depth around which its change is centered. On eight English eye-tracking and self-paced reading corpora (81,957 words) and ten GPT-2, OPT and Pythia models, words that a model resolves later, and the words after them, are read more slowly than equally surprising words. Resolution depth improves held-out prediction beyond final-layer surprisal, entropy and the best single layer by 0.26 millinats per word (pooled p = 0.001), about a third of entropy's gain, and each model family gains, GPT-2 and Pythia through one corpus each. The net gain varies between corpora (random-effects mean 0.07, p = 0.37); against layer-shuffled depth, which adds as many coefficients, it is positive in seven of eight corpora (random-effects mean 0.23, p = 0.016), and untrained networks show no gain under the logit lens. Pooled over corpora, the effect holds with corrected word probabilities and beyond first-to-last-layer divergences, and a whole-trajectory functional regression adds no significant information beyond resolution depth.

title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
authors: Tobias Braun; Marcus Rohrbach; Lorenzo Cavallaro
abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.

title: The Evolution of AI in Turkish Academic Discourse
authors: Tugay Sarıkaya
abstract: <jats:p>Despite growing Turkish social science literature on artificial intelligence (AI), few studies systematically examine how AI discourse has evolved or how trust is constructed. This study addresses this gap by analyzing Turkish open-access articles (n = 451) from TR Dizin (2004-2025) using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Five major themes emerged: ethics and human rights; legal accountability; transparency and explainability; media ecosystem and disinformation; and user acceptance. Findings show that Turkish academic discourse has shifted from technical performance questions ("What does AI do?") to multi-dimensional trust concerns ("Under what conditions is AI trustworthy?"), encompassing technical, institutional-regulatory, and societal dimensions.</jats:p>

title: The Evolution of Artificial Intelligence in the Digital Society
authors: I. S. Pypenko; Y. B. Melnyk
abstract: <jats:p>In merely a few years, humanity has transitioned from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) to autonomous artificial intelligence agents and quantum computing applications. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly capable of resolving Millennium Prize Problems and autonomously engineering its subsequent model iterations without human intervention. The contemporary stage of AI development is distinctively characterized by model unpredictability and emergence, wherein latent capabilities frequently transcend the comprehension of their developers. The ubiquitous integration of digital products alongside the emergent nature of this process inevitably converges toward the realization of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Consequently, identifying mechanisms for secure societal alignment and interaction with these novel technological systems has become paramount. At this stage, the focus of the international community is on setting up regulatory bodies and systems to monitor AI, as well as on the ethical implications of its implementation. The aim of the study is to identify the key evolutionary trends in artificial intelligence within contemporary society, and to forecast its technological and social implications. The present study establishes the theoretical basis for the principle of responsibility in the implementation and use of AI. The problem of anthropomorphism and human attachment to technologies was identified. It has been confirmed that the key risk does not stem from the use of AI itself, but rather from the environment in which it operates. It has also been established that the younger generation is the most adaptable demographic group when it comes to acculturating to AI. The education sector has a pivotal role to play in preparing society for the informed and responsible use of AI systems for the benefit of humanity.</jats:p>

title: The false hope of current approaches to explainable artificial intelligence in health care.
authors: M. Ghassemi; L. Oakden-Rayner; Andrew Beam
abstract: The black-box nature of current artificial intelligence (AI) has caused some to question whether AI must be explainable to be used in high-stakes scenarios such as medicine. It has been argued that explainable AI will engender trust with the health-care workforce, provide transparency into the AI decision making process, and potentially mitigate various kinds of bias. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this argument represents a false hope for explainable AI and that current explainability methods are unlikely to achieve these goals for patient-level decision support. We provide an overview of current explainability techniques and highlight how various failure cases can cause problems for decision making for individual patients. In the absence of suitable explainability methods, we advocate for rigorous internal and external validation of AI models as a more direct means of achieving the goals often associated with explainability, and we caution against having explainability be a requirement for clinically deployed models.

title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
authors: Hai Wang; Bretislav Hajek; Chonghe Jiang; Minwei Kong; Ao Qu; Huatian Gong; Bo Dong; Cynthia Barnhart; Jinhua Zhao
abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.

title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
authors: Md. Abdullah Al Zami; Suraiya Shanaz; Mahdi Hasan; Shoaib Ahmed Dipu; Farig Yousuf Sadeque; Md. Sabbir Ahmed
abstract: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.

title: The geometry of neural network decision boundaries
authors: Dylan M Paiton; David L Schultheiss; Matthias Kümmerer; Zac Cranko; Matthias Bethge
abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are built using well-understood mathematical operations, yet their complex nature poses significant challenges to intuitively understanding their decision-making processes. This work introduces a method for visualizing and measuring ANN decision boundary geometry directly in the high-dimensional input space, avoiding distortions found with traditional projection-based techniques. We analyze boundary curvatures and distances in diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods. Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as the size of the subspace increases, suggesting that decision boundaries are close to input samples within large, continuous subspaces. We also quantify how much boundary distances and curvatures reduce near dataset samples after adversarial training. Training methodology has a significantly stronger impact on boundary distance and curvature than architecture or test-set accuracy. These findings are contextualized within prior work, supporting or refuting several previously proposed theories of boundary behavior. Our analytically and empirically supported methodology lays the foundation for future studies to improve network interpretability and understanding.

title: The Hidden Contribution of Gig Workers in AI Customer Engagement From Virtual Connection to Physical Realization
authors: Nur Fatin Abd Hamid; Imaan Hamzah; Siti Haryani Mat Yusoff; Chok Nyen Vui; Patcharavadee Sriboonruang
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter contributes to theory by framing gig workers as value co-creators, commercial agents, and a vital component in AI-enabled engagement ecosystems. It proposes a six-step integrative model that maps the journey from AI engagement to consumer loyalty, emphasizing gig workers' strategic involvement at each stage. The investigation identifies four practical applications: engagement design, workforce management, AI integration, and performance measurement. The chapter discusses critical challenges, using real-world examples, including algorithmic control, fair compensation, data privacy, worker well-being, and the sustainability of AI ecosystems. It emphasizes the value of human complementarity to AI, addressing the structural split between AI-driven virtual contact and human-driven physical fulfillment, and illuminates the often-invisible labor that supports platform-based service delivery.</jats:p>

title: The Human Voice and Performative Being in the Synthetic Media Ecosystem
authors: Pinar Altiok Gürel
abstract: <jats:p>The rapid proliferation of synthetic media technologies has profoundly transformed digital communication, raising critical questions about authenticity and trust. Among various forms of synthetic media, the human voice holds a particularly sensitive position as a carrier of presence, identity, and emotional authenticity. As advances in voice cloning enable AI systems to replicate vocal characteristics, concerns regarding credibility, transparency, and ethical communication emerge. According to the author of this chapter, this chapter aims to provide a conceptual framework for redefining strategic communication in the age of synthetic media. Examining the role of the voice and performative being in AI-mediated communication, the chapter argues that maintaining trust requires an integrated framework combining ethical AI communication, strategic governance, and human-centered creative practices. The chapter proposes trust-oriented, transparent, and accountable policy recommendations.</jats:p>

title: The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
authors: Basavaraj R M; Harshal Chandel
abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Tools on Academic Writing Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
authors: Hind Aljuaid
abstract: With the growth of Artificial Intelligence technologies, there is interest in studying their potential impact on university academic writing courses. This study examined whether AI tools are replacing these courses by exploring how they effectively replace traditional academic writing instruction and this shift’s potential benefits and drawbacks. The researcher reviewed existing literature on integrating AI tools into academic writing instruction. The findings provide insights to educators navigating the integration of Artificial Intelligence tools into writing curricula while maintaining instructional quality and academic integrity standards. By synthesizing the latest research, this study can inform decisions about the appropriate use of Artificial Intelligence in teaching essential writing skills. Increased use of Artificial Intelligence writing tools has sparked debate about their role in academic writing instruction. Universities like Stanford have updated policies around Artificial Intelligence tool usage and academic integrity. The University of California issued guidance acknowledging the prevalence of generative Artificial Intelligence on campuses. Middlebury College banned classroom use of ChatGPT over concerns it could impede critical thinking and writing skill development. Results show that while Artificial Intelligence helps with grammar and style, questions remain about its impact on creativity and critical thinking. However, Artificial Intelligence is not replacing university writing courses. These courses teach critical thinking, research, citation, argumentation, creativity, originality, and ethics, which Artificial Intelligence lacks. Academic writing courses offer a complete learning experience. Artificial Intelligence may improve academic writing but is unlikely to replace traditional courses soon. A balanced approach integrating Artificial Intelligence support while preserving core elements of academic writing education appears most effective for preparing students for diverse writing challenges.

title: The Integration of Artificial Intelligence into Clinical Practice
authors: V. Karalis
abstract: The purpose of this literature review is to provide a fundamental synopsis of current research pertaining to artificial intelligence (AI) within the domain of clinical practice. Artificial intelligence has revolutionized the field of medicine and healthcare by providing innovative solutions to complex problems. One of the most important benefits of AI in clinical practice is its ability to investigate extensive volumes of data with efficiency and precision. This has led to the development of various applications that have improved patient outcomes and reduced the workload of healthcare professionals. AI can support doctors in making more accurate diagnoses and developing personalized treatment plans. Successful examples of AI applications are outlined for a series of medical specialties like cardiology, surgery, gastroenterology, pneumology, nephrology, urology, dermatology, orthopedics, neurology, gynecology, ophthalmology, pediatrics, hematology, and critically ill patients, as well as diagnostic methods. Special reference is made to legal and ethical considerations like accuracy, informed consent, privacy issues, data security, regulatory framework, product liability, explainability, and transparency. Finally, this review closes by critically appraising AI use in clinical practice and its future perspectives. However, it is also important to approach its development and implementation cautiously to ensure ethical considerations are met.

title: The Interplay of Privacy Authorization Frameworks and Third-party Referral Links on Purchase Intention in Generative AI Shopping
