title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
authors: Quentin Cohen-Solal
abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
authors: Bach Phan-Tat; Tung Kieu; Kris Heylen; Dirk Geeraerts; Stefano De Pascale; Dirk Speelman
abstract: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using four representations trained on WikiText-103: two count-based PPMI configurations and two Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings reveal systematic linguistic organisation at multiple geometric scales and its sensitivity to representation choices.

title: The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions
authors: Alexandra Carpentier; Nicolas Verzelen
abstract:
We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic Gaussian distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, when the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, distance-based and spectral procedures require a squared separation $Δ^2$ of order $\sqrt d$. In contrast, tensor-based procedures cluster at a polylogarithmic separation but need a sample size that is a large polynomial of $dK$, and the low-degree lower bounds known for random centers only show that $n$ must exceed $dK^2$.
  Focusing on normally distributed centers, we characterize the minimal separation for clustering with low-degree polynomials in the regime $K>d$, through a low-degree lower bound and a matching upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. In particular, for $K=d^{p/2}$ with $p> 2$ a real number, we show that a sample size of the order of $K^3 d^{(\lceil p\rceil-p)/2}$ is required to recover the clustering with subpolynomial separation, and that it suffices when $p$ is not an integer.

title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
authors: {'_id': '6afe7c1336ccf7e1781f4b1e', 'user': {'_id': '6813c4ed3ff8212e97cf1325', 'avatarUrl': '/avatars/c29cac4d858602c9226072b11c9c1aeb.svg', 'isPro': False, 'fullname': 'Jeonghwan Cho', 'user': 'jhxcho', 'type': 'user', 'name': 'jhxcho'}, 'name': 'Jeonghwan Cho', 'status': 'claimed_verified', 'statusLastChangedAt': '2026-11-19T08:45:04.868Z', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afe7c1336ccf7e1781f4b1f', 'name': 'Minsu Kim', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afe7c1336ccf7e1781f4b20', 'name': 'Junyoung Hong', 'hidden': False}; {'_id': '6afe7c1336ccf7e1781f4b21', 'name': 'Seon Joo Kim', 'hidden': False}
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

title: The potential for artificial intelligence in healthcare
authors: T. Davenport; R. Kalakota
abstract: ABSTRACT The complexity and rise of data in healthcare means that artificial intelligence (AI) will increasingly be applied within the field. Several types of AI are already being employed by payers and providers of care, and life sciences companies. The key categories of applications involve diagnosis and treatment recommendations, patient engagement and adherence, and administrative activities. Although there are many instances in which AI can perform healthcare tasks as well or better than humans, implementation factors will prevent large-scale automation of healthcare professional jobs for a considerable period. Ethical issues in the application of AI to healthcare are also discussed.

title: The Price of an Explanation: What Demanding Verifiable Artifacts Costs, and What It Buys Back
authors: Edgar A. Duéñez-Guzmán; Eduardo Dueñez; Edgar Said Hernandez Sanchez; Suzanne Sadedin
abstract: Generative models produce many candidate solutions but provide no intrinsic signal by which to rank them. One mitigation is to demand a \emph{verifiable artifact}: a program that can be executed against the available evidence. A common concern is that requiring executable verification incurs costs in both solution quality and computational budget. We measure these two costs on the $120$-task ARC-AGI-2 evaluation set. Demanding a verifiable artifact from an LLM reduced the score from $93$ to $68$ of $120$ tasks ($77\%$ to $57\%$). Of those $25$ tasks, $21$ were reached by no program-producing configuration we ran, at any budget, by sampling or by search; yet for $27$ of the $28$ tasks that only the answer-only arm solved, some program arm held a program that reproduced every demonstration and still failed the test. The bottleneck is obtaining an explanation that \emph{generalizes}, not finding one. A short evolutionary search over two already-sampled programs, at no additional model cost, beats best-of-$2$ sampled code by $9.2 \pm 1.4$ tasks, and over a single sampled program beats $1$-shot sampling by $9.9 \pm 1.3$. Moreover, because a program can be checked against the training examples, any program-producing protocol can terminate early once a task is explained: under the same stopping rule, best-of-$n$ sampling declines up to $38\%$ of its budget and the evolved arm up to $49\%$, whereas an answer-only baseline cannot terminate early. Applying the same methodology to decoder synthesis for quantum error correction yields interpretable decoders evaluated against a certified panel of published decoders on held-out exam shots.

title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
authors: I. Celik; M. Dindar; H. Muukkonen; S. Järvelä
abstract: This study provides an overview of research on teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications and machine learning methods to analyze teachers’ data. Our analysis showed that AI offers teachers several opportunities for improved planning (e.g., by defining students’ needs and familiarizing teachers with such needs), implementation (e.g., through immediate feedback and teacher intervention), and assessment (e.g., through automated essay scoring) of their teaching. We also found that teachers have various roles in the development of AI technology. These roles include acting as models for training AI algorithms and participating in AI development by checking the accuracy of AI automated assessment systems. Our findings further underlined several challenges in AI implementation in teaching practice, which provide guidelines for developing the field.

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
authors: Yuanhao Zeng; Shaocheng Lan; Ao Lu; Kuang Yan; Heng Lin; Xinang Xu; Yuan Luo; Yueting Wang; Yexin Li; Ruo Shan; Kan Ren
abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

title: Thermodynamically Consistent Neural Networks for a Universal Fluid Gibbs Free Energy Equation of State
authors: Xurui Li; Zhiguo Gan; Jiaming Zhang; Hongxi Zeng; Diannan Lu
abstract: Over the past three centuries, many thermodynamics researchers have worked to develop fluid equations of state with both high accuracy and broad applicability, proposing various theoretical frameworks and models. Building on these efforts, this study uses Gibbs free energy as the starting point and introduces thermodynamically consistent neural networks to construct a fluid equation of state based on Gibbs free energy (GEoS). This approach establishes a novel machine learning framework that provides a unified representation of fluid states. GEoS performs well on the vapor- and liquid-phase density test sets, with average absolute relative deviations (AARDs) of 5.25% and 3.96%, respectively. It outperforms conventional volume-translated cubic equations of state and existing machine learning models, demonstrating its effectiveness. Further analysis using the UMAP dimensionality reduction method shows that most molecules in the test set belong to extrapolation systems, confirming the strong generalization ability of the model. Finally, the test results show that the PC-SAFT equation fitted using GEoS maintains high predictive accuracy, providing a reliable basis for its practical application in industry.

title: The role of artificial intelligence in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals
authors: R. Vinuesa; Hossein Azizpour; Iolanda Leite; M. Balaam; Virginia Dignum; S. Domisch; Anna Felländer; S. Langhans; Max Tegmark; Francesco Nerini
abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and its progressively wider impact on many sectors requires an assessment of its effect on the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. Using a consensus-based expert elicitation process, we find that AI can enable the accomplishment of 134 targets across all the goals, but it may also inhibit 59 targets. However, current research foci overlook important aspects. The fast development of AI needs to be supported by the necessary regulatory insight and oversight for AI-based technologies to enable sustainable development. Failure to do so could result in gaps in transparency, safety, and ethical standards. Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming more and more common in people’s lives. Here, the authors use an expert elicitation method to understand how AI may affect the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.

title: The Role of Attachment Styles and Spiritual Intelligence in Predicting Women’s Emotional Divorce
authors: Zahra Shirzadi; Reza Khakpour; Anahita Khodabakhshi-Koolaee
abstract: <jats:p>Background: Emotional divorce refers to a situation in which the emotional relationship, support, passion, warmth, attention, love, and intimacy between couples (husband & wife) decline or diminish. Such conditions lead to an unaffectionate marital life to the point that the couples are only together under one roof. Accordingly, the present study aimed to explore the role of attachment styles and spiritual intelligence in predicting emotional divorce in women. Methods: This study employed a descriptive-correlational design. The research population included all women filing for divorce who were referred to marriage counseling and couple therapy centers in districts 5 and 6 in Tehran City, Iran, in 2020. In total, 400 women who met the inclusion criteria were selected as the study participants using voluntary response and convenience sampling techniques. The required data were collected by the Emotional Divorce Scale, the Adult Attachment Scale, and the Self-Report Measure of Spiritual Intelligence. The collected data were analyzed using the multiple regression analysis method in SPSS V. 22. Results: The obtained results suggested a significant positive relationship between the anxious-avoidant attachment style and emotional divorce (P<0.01). Furthermore, there was a significant negative relationship between spiritual intelligence and emotional divorce; the higher the spiritual intelligence, the lower the emotional divorce (P=0.02). Accordingly, spiritual intelligence and anxious-avoidant attachment style can predict emotional divorce (Multiple Regressions= -0.58). Conclusion: The present study data suggested that premarital education and counseling before spouse selection help in examining the personality traits of the parties. Moreover, paying attention to the role of health professionals, such as family counselors, psychologists, and psychiatric nurses in providing premarital counseling and education to couples and emphasizing the role of spiritual intelligence and attachment styles may prevent emotional separation and divorce among couples.</jats:p>

title: The Role of Personalized Metaverse Virtual Experiences in Enhancing Customer Shopping Journey Engagement
authors: Anubha
abstract: <jats:p>Shoppers, especially Gen Z, are becoming more digitally immersed, spending more time online and exploring the metaverse's potential. Although it is an emerging concept, the metaverse has captured businesses' attention as a way to interact with and target Gen Z and other young, tech-savvy consumers because of its significant potential. This chapter advances the role of personalized metaverse virtual shopping experiences in the customer purchase journey. It critically examines how integrating digital twins, blockchain, extended reality (XR), artificial intelligence (AI), and data-driven analytics is transforming traditional shopping into immersive, adaptive, and highly personalized consumer experiences that enhance engagement throughout the purchase journey. This study will bring significant insights to researchers and marketers by exploring the potential role of personalized metaverse virtual shopping experiences in the customer purchase journey, which can help them to strategize how to engage such tech-savvy young customers</jats:p>

title: The Roles of Personality Traits, AI Anxiety, and Demographic Factors in Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence
authors: Feridun Kaya; F. Aydın; A. Schepman; P. Rodway; Okan Yeti̇şensoy; Meva Demir Kaya
abstract: Abstract The present study adapted the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS) to Turkish and investigated the impact of personality traits, artificial intelligence anxiety, and demographics on attitudes toward artificial intelligence. The sample consisted of 259 female (74%) and 91 male (26%) individuals aged between 18 and 51 (Mean = 24.23). Measures taken were demographics, the Ten-Item Personality Inventory, the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, and the General Attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence Scale. The Turkish GAAIS had good validity and reliability. Hierarchical Multiple Linear Regression Analyses showed that positive attitudes toward artificial intelligence were significantly predicted by the level of computer use (β = 0.139, p = 0.013), level of knowledge about artificial intelligence (β = 0.119, p = 0.029), and AI learning anxiety (β = −0.172, p = 0.004). Negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence were significantly predicted by agreeableness (β = 0.120, p = 0.019), AI configuration anxiety (β = −0.379, p < 0.001), and AI learning anxiety (β = −0.211, p < 0.001). Personality traits, AI anxiety, and demographics play important roles in attitudes toward AI. Results are discussed in light of the previous research and theoretical explanations.

title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
authors: Afonso S. Bandeira; Yue M. Lu; Petar Nizić-Nikolac
abstract: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
authors: Sebastian Pusch; Matthia Sabatelli; Gido M. van de Ven
abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

title: The Standards Mapping Framework
authors: A. R. Deepti; Farzeen Basith
abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the challenges of cross-jurisdictional monitoring inconsistency in the implementation of blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity systems, where firms face different regulatory environments and compliance mandates that may conflict across jurisdictions. This chapter sets forth the Standards Mapping Framework (SMF), a three-dimensional architecture that studies regulatory complexity at the jurisdictional, functional, and technological levels to identify convergence across legal regimes. Building on comparative analysis of major jurisdictions, the chapter demonstrates how integrated governance architectures can satisfy multiple regulatory demands. It also examines technical integration, legal implications of smart agreements, regulatory divergences, emerging threats, and outlines future research directions.</jats:p>

title: The Translation of Humour using AI tools for subtitling and dubbing: case study of Egyptian movie “Foul El-Seen Al-Azeem”
authors: Ayah Samy ghoneimy
abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated subtitling and dubbing in translating humour from Egyptian Arabic into English using the comedy film Foul El-Seen Al-Azeem as a case study. It employed a mixed-methods design combining qualitative analysis based on Martínez-Sierra’s humour taxonomy and Anstey and Bull’s multimodality theory with a quantitative evaluation using a modified Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) rubric and audience-based surveys. The study examined two Humorous scenes containing multilingual code-switching, including Egyptian Arabic, Chinese, French, English and Lebanese Arabic, to assess how AI tools manage linguistic complexity and cultural humour. The selected AI tools included HappyScribe and CapCut for subtitling, and ElevenLabs and Perso.ai for dubbing.Keywords: AI translation, Audiovisual Translation, Humour Translation, Subtitling, Dubbingهدفت هذه الدراسة إلى استكشاف فعالية الترجمة السمعية البصرية المعتمدة على الذكاء الاصطناعي في ترجمة الفكاهة من العربية المصرية إلى الإنجليزية، وذلك من خلال اتخاذ الفيلم الكوميدي فول الصين العظيم كدراسة حالة. واعتمدت الدراسة على منهجية بحثية تجمع بين التحليل النوعي والكمي؛ حيث استند التحليل النوعي إلى تصنيف مارتينيز-سييرا للفكاهة ونظرية التعددية الوسائطية لبول وأنستي، بينما استند التقييم الكمي إلى مقياس معدل لتقييم جودة الترجمة (TQA) واستبيانات قائمة على آراء الجمهور. كما تناولت الدراسة مشهدين فكاهيين تتضمن التناوب اللغوي بين عدة لغات ولهجات، من بينها العربية المصرية، والصينية، والفرنسية، و الإنجليزية والعربية اللبنانية، بهدف تقييم قدرة أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي على التعامل مع التعقيد اللغوي والفكاهة الثقافية. وشملت الأدوات المستخدمة HappyScribe و CapCut للترجمة النصية. ElevenLabs و Perso.ai للدبلجة.

title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
authors: Jalal Mahmud; Eser Kandogan
abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

title: The Window Lever: Longer Observation Windows Outweigh the Observed Effects of Data, Capacity, and Architecture in Customer Behavior Forecasting
authors: Tara Sowrirajan; Yanqiao Wang
abstract: In our experiments on long-horizon customer-behavior forecasting, a longer observation window outweighed the observed effects of more data, more capacity and newer architectures. The window is the weeks of history a model sees before the week it forecasts from. Going from an 8- to a 16-week window adds a raw +0.070 to 0.107 log-space $R^2$ in every family at 1M. Matched test cohorts, which score the same customer-weeks at every window, show this raw comparison understates the gain in every family they cover. The direction holds on five public datasets, four spanning over a year (ridge and our transformer on all five). On our internal data, longer windows admit up to 10% more and colder training customers, which matching does not fix. Our design does not separate window length from calendar coverage, because every test anchor (the week a forecast is made from) falls in one eight-week band. On training-period anchors, the weekly ridge probe's gain persists outside the holiday season, keeping about 72% of it. We therefore report a robust positive association with longer windows and do not identify the magnitude of a calendar-independent history effect. Of four internally registered predictions, the only fully blind one failed. An activity-mixture model predicted +0.014 from 24 to 32 weeks; the weekly-aggregate probe returned -0.0004. For the sequence families, the other three levers are about an order of magnitude smaller, bounded and unresolved. Their observed effects are at most 0.006 between the nominal 1M and 10M tiers and 0.0052 among five sequence families at 16 weeks with clocks as built, both single-seed on the full test split, and 0.006 for capacity on three-seed means. These are observed intervals, not equivalence bounds. Our claim is the order-of-magnitude contrast between the window and those bounds. A team building on this class of data should start by lengthening the window.

title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
authors: Rui Li; Liyang He; Zheng Zhang; Zhenya Huang; Qi Liu
abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
authors: Junyoung Hong; Minsu Kim; Jaehyun Kim; Jeonghwan Cho; Jiwoo Lee; Seon Joo Kim
abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.

title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
authors: Zipeng Qiu; Shusheng Xu; Jiale Li; Yukun Zhou; Chenyue Li; Wenshuang Li; Tongkai Yang; Binhang Yuan
abstract: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
authors: Jinbin Luo; Xiaozhe Yao; Shang Yang; Zhijian Liu; Song Han; Qinghao Hu
abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
authors: Jacqueline Maasch; Shu Wan; Hank Zhu; Huan Liu; Zhiguang Wang
abstract: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning When to Refine Actions with Touch for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Xudi Ge; Yepeng Liu; Haifeng Liu; Enze Shi; Liangqi Zhang; Yongchao Xu
abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
authors: Zeman Li; Ali Behrouz; Yuan Deng; Praneeth Kacham; Rami Al-Rfou; Meisam Razaviyayn; Vahab Mirrokni
abstract: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
authors: Chanhwi Jeong; Dongmin You; Seungwook Kim
abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

title: TOMAS: Topology-Aware Operation Modeling and Adaptive Staging for Egocentric Hand Forecasting
authors: Guanzhong Sun; Junyi Ma; Yuxuan Wu; Erhang Zhang; Chenyang Xu; Yanzi Miao; Hesheng Wang
abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

title: Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies
authors: Geon Lee; Fanchen Bu; Soo Yong Lee; Sunwoo Kim; Kijung Shin
abstract: AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.

title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
authors: Ojas Sanghi; Anvita Bhagavathula; Alvaro Carbonero; Priya L. Donti
abstract: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.

title: Towards Autoregressive Neural Network Parameter Generation
authors: Bedionita Soro; Bruno Andreis; Song Chong; Sung Ju Hwang
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently established a new paradigm in machine learning, demonstrating exceptional zero-shot generalization and complex reasoning capabilities. Concurrently, neural network parameter generation has emerged as a promising avenue for rapid task adaptation and model synthesis. Existing weight generation techniques, however, struggle to jointly learn the distribution of diverse models, to encode heterogeneous architectures within a single generator, and to generalize out of distribution. We therefore ask whether pretrained parameters can be encoded into a discrete domain so that the zero-shot generalization LLMs exhibit in text generation can be transferred to weight generation. Following this view, we propose an LLM-inspired approach, Instruction-Guided Parameter Generation (IGPG), that formulates network parameter generation as an autoregressive modeling problem. We first quantize pretrained weights with a VQ-VAE, then train a prefix-conditioned autoregressive generator over the resulting tokens. At inference, the generated weight tokens are mapped back to parameter space by the VQ-VAE decoder. We evaluate the framework across in-distribution generation, cross-dataset transfer, and cross-architecture settings. The proposed method achieves competitive performance in in-distribution generation and provides useful parameter initializations for held-out datasets and architectural configurations, improving downstream performance over random initialization after adaptation. These results suggest that discrete autoregressive modeling provides a promising framework for learning and transferring structure across collections of pretrained neural network parameters.

title: Towards conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence
authors: Tao Tu; Mike Schaekermann; Anil Palepu; Khaled Saab; J. Freyberg; Ryutaro Tanno; Amy Wang; Brenna Li; Mohamed Amin; Yong Cheng; Elahe Vedadi; N. Tomašev; Shekoofeh Azizi; Karan Singhal; Le Hou; Albert Webson; Kavita Kulkarni; S. Mahdavi; Christopher Semturs; Juraj Gottweis; Joelle K. Barral; Katherine Chou; G. Corrado; Y. Matias; A. Karthikesalingam; Vivek Natarajan
abstract: At the heart of medicine lies physician–patient dialogue, where skillful history-taking enables effective diagnosis, management and enduring trust1,2. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems capable of diagnostic dialogue could increase accessibility and quality of care. However, approximating clinicians’ expertise is an outstanding challenge. Here we introduce AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer), a large language model (LLM)-based AI system optimized for diagnostic dialogue. AMIE uses a self-play-based3 simulated environment with automated feedback for scaling learning across disease conditions, specialties and contexts. We designed a framework for evaluating clinically meaningful axes of performance, including history-taking, diagnostic accuracy, management, communication skills and empathy. We compared AMIE’s performance to that of primary care physicians in a randomized, double-blind crossover study of text-based consultations with validated patient-actors similar to objective structured clinical examination4,5. The study included 159 case scenarios from providers in Canada, the United Kingdom and India, 20 primary care physicians compared to AMIE, and evaluations by specialist physicians and patient-actors. AMIE demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy and superior performance on 30 out of 32 axes according to the specialist physicians and 25 out of 26 axes according to the patient-actors. Our research has several limitations and should be interpreted with caution. Clinicians used synchronous text chat, which permits large-scale LLM–patient interactions, but this is unfamiliar in clinical practice. While further research is required before AMIE could be translated to real-world settings, the results represent a milestone towards conversational diagnostic AI. The conversational diagnostic artificial intelligence system AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer) has potential as a real-world tool for clinical history-taking and diagnostic dialogue, based on its performance in simulated consultations.

title: Towards High-Fidelity Learned Video Compression
authors: Bumyoon Kim; Yongseong Kim; Inhyuk Jeong; Byeungwoo Jeon
abstract: Professional video workflows operate at qualities that learned video codecs do not reach. We measure how much of a professional quality range a codec covers, from the lowest quality of the standard test conditions, VVC at QP 37, to the highest 4:2:2 grade of the production codec ProRes. To compare inter-frame coding alone, every codec receives original frames as references at the intra positions. On 10-bit YCbCr 4:2:2 test sequences, four recent learned codecs cover 24 to 38% of this range. Their encoders are feed-forward networks with a fixed latent capacity, the number of latent values per sample, of at most 0.25, and removing their quantization raises the quality by at most 1 dB. We propose a learned inter-frame codec whose encoder searches, as the encoders of conventional codecs do. It searches block motion, which a learned network refines, and it searches among learned block transforms whose latent capacity ranges up to 1, selecting the partition, the skip decisions, and the quantized coefficients by a rate-distortion cost. Our codec reaches the upper end of the range on all six sequences. With all residual blocks fixed to 16x16, whose latent capacity is 0.25, the same codec covers 55% of the range, with or without quantization.

title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Wenhao Li; Zhongyi Han; Yuhao Wei; Liang Han; Yilong Yin; Liqiang Nie
abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.

title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Johannes Hog; Neeratyoy Mallik; Steven Adriaensen; Jan Hendrik Metzen; Tom Viering; Danny Stoll; Frank Hutter
abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

title: Toward Strategic Artificial Intelligence Capabilities for Intelligent Strategic Management: A Capability Framework Developed Through a Modified Delphi Study
authors: Hasan  Fadhil AL-Thabhawee; Nasrin Razi; Mohammad Faryabi; Sajjad Naghdi
abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to develop and validate a comprehensive Strategic Artificial Intelligence Capability Framework (SAICF) for intelligent strategic management in public universities. The study employed a qualitative, two-stage design integrating a structured literature review with a three-round modified Delphi procedure. Literature published between 1985 and 2026 was searched in Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar, and eligible studies were subjected to directed qualitative content analysis to identify preliminary strategic AI capability indicators. The resulting indicators were subsequently evaluated by a purposively selected panel of 20 experts with expertise in strategic management, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, public administration, or higher-education management. Across the Delphi rounds, experts assessed the relevance, clarity, importance, and conceptual placement of the indicators. Consensus was examined using Kendall’s coefficient of concordance and the chi-square test. The second Delphi round demonstrated statistically significant and strong expert concordance regarding the retained indicators (Kendall’s W = 0.821, χ² = 741.213, df = 27, p < .001). In the final round, concordance remained consistently strong across the validated capability domains, with Kendall’s W values ranging from 0.79 to 0.87 and an overall framework coefficient of 0.82. The resulting framework comprised Strategic Data Intelligence, Advanced AI for Strategic Foresight and Analytics, AI-Driven Strategic Decision-Making, Strategic Intelligent Automation, Strategic Human–AI Integration, Responsible AI Governance, and AI-Enabled Strategic Innovation. Strategic Data Intelligence demonstrated the strongest expert concordance, followed by Advanced AI for Strategic Foresight and Analytics. The validated SAICF indicates that effective AI-enabled strategic management requires an integrated organizational capability architecture combining data intelligence, advanced analytics, strategic decision support, intelligent automation, human–AI collaboration, responsible governance, and innovation rather than reliance on isolated technological applications.</jats:p>

title: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates
authors: Xinying Hu; You Wu; Haoyi Wu; Jianchao Tan; Kefeng Zhang; Yuchen Xie; Kewei Tu
abstract: Hyper-Connections (HC) expand the residual stream of a Transformer into $N$ parallel streams, and manifold-constrained HC (mHC) stabilizes them at scale. However, mHC benefits little from more than four streams, partly because each sublayer writes a single output to all streams, limiting how differently they can be updated. In this work, we propose TPHC, which integrates tensor-parallel (TP) shards with HC streams to promote greater independence across streams. Specifically, we route a separate mixture of the residual streams to each TP shard and keep the individual shard outputs separate during write-back, so each stream can receive a different mixture of those outputs. This design makes the residual-stream updates more expressive without adding parameters or FLOPs to the attention or FFN sublayers. With native support for stream sharding under TP, TPHC requires only 9% more training time than mHC on an 8B model when both use four streams. Increasing the number of streams from four to sixteen raises its training time by only 19%. On a 1.1B model trained on 100B tokens, TPHC reduces validation loss by 0.7-1.0% and raises average zero-shot accuracy across six commonsense reasoning benchmarks by 0.3-0.7 percentage points relative to mHC at matched stream counts $N\in\{4,8,16\}$. Our code is available at https://github.com/wuyou2002/TPHC.

title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
authors: Hsi Chang; Irfan Khan
abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely ($R^2 > 0.99$) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.

title: TRACE: Attribute Execution for Sequential Image Editing
authors: Xiyang Zhang; Yuanhe Tian; Hongzhi Wang; Yan Song
abstract: Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. This lets users develop a result without repeatedly restating or repairing their decisions. The difficulty is that a retrieved image can contain a valid color on an obsolete surface, while the current image may lack the newly requested material. Neither reference selection nor a precise object mask alone specifies how to reconcile attributes occupying the same region. We present TRACE, which separates the continuing attribute from its visual carrier and prioritizes local appearance operations under complete-request checks. Active-goal binding identifies what should persist, carrier selection supplies suitable current or newly generated pixels, and tonal calibration reduces tinting near highlights and shadows. Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and complete sequential benchmarks support joint color-material recovery and show how local execution preserves the surrounding scene.

title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding
authors: Tianyuan Li; Xihan Yang; Chenglong Wang; Yuzhang Wu; Jingbo Zhu; Tong Xiao
abstract: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Zekai Chen; Yihan Sun; Xunkai Li; Xun Wu; Xinmo Jin; Yinlin Zhu; Haodong Lu; Xuaner Chen; Rong-Hua Li
abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

title: Tracking Ethological Behaviors of Broiler Chickens Through Computer Vision (YoloV11) Using an Android Mobile Device
authors: Ryan Davi Oliveira de Meneses; Glauber da Rocha Balthazar
abstract: This study developed and evaluated a computer vision model for automated ethological behavior classification of broiler chickens in climate-controlled poultry houses. Using publicly available videos preprocessed and manually annotated into three classes (sitting, standing, and feeding), the YOLOv11 model was trained and deployed on an Android application via TFLite conversion. Exploratory analysis ensured dataset consistency and visual quality, while evaluation showed class-dependent performance: higher robustness for static postures (sitting, AP=0.531; precision=100%) and lower accuracy for dynamic behaviors (feeding, AP=0.292; recall=0.20). Tests with unseen images demonstrated significant improvements, achieving accuracies of 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding. The model showed effective generalization in real farm environments, supporting its potential for continuous behavioral monitoring, early welfare assessments, and decision-making in precision poultry farming. These findings establish a technical foundation for future mobile-based applications at commercial scale, reinforcing the role of computer vision in automated animal welfare evaluation.

title: Tracking Objects Through Assembly and Decomposition
authors: Cheryl Lam; Yihong Sun; Bharath Hariharan
abstract: Tracking objects through transformations is essential for understanding real-world dynamics. Recent work has extended traditional object tracking to detect state changes. However, existing methods require an initial object prompt and detect only its decompositions, missing assembly events, which begin with multiple objects rather than one. We therefore introduce a prompt-free formulation of this task, where the goal is to recover all object tracks and detect both decomposition and assembly events given only a video. Our key insight is that assembly is decomposition in reverse. Building on this insight, we present Atlas, a zero-shot system that constructs and jointly reasons over forward and reverse spatiotemporal partitions to recover object tracks and their transformations. We further introduce OmniST, a benchmark with dense annotations of objects and both transformation types. On OmniST, Atlas recovers more than twice as many state changes as prior methods while remaining competitive on existing benchmarks that only evaluate decomposition.

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
authors: Chaipat Tirapongprasert; Rajarshi Das; Parijat Dube
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

title: Training Denoising Models of Any Architecture Without Stored Images
authors: Christos Koutlis; Ioannis Kompatsiaris; Symeon Papadopoulos
abstract: Can a pretrained denoising model replace the dataset used to train it? We investigate this question through teacher-supervised training, showing for the first time that continuous-time diffusion and flow models of any architecture and size can be trained from random initialization without stored images. Our students regress the teacher's velocity on a rolling pool of noisy samples, advanced along trajectories of random step counts to obtain independent, dense and approximately continuous noise levels. This saves considerable storage for large datasets and applies even when the data are unreleased or private. Our experiments include 12 teachers of 6 families and 6 datasets. Our method outperforms standard training of the same network on CIFAR-10 for students 4x smaller than the teacher, comes within 0.75 to 1.92 FID of it at the teacher's size and surpasses training on teacher-generated images and step reduction methods without teacher-based initialization. Our code is available at https://github.com/mever-team/ddm.

title: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
authors: Yixuan Tong; Yuanguo Bi; Mingjian Zhi; Wenchao Xu; Yuan Wu
abstract: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images and outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy. Meanwhile, FedDoG reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/YXTong17/FedDoG.

title: Training-free motion statistics match self-supervised behavior encoders
authors: Ziwen Chen
abstract: Self-supervised encoders for animal behavior are often trained on, or fed, hand-built movement features. We ask whether they beat those ingredients when compared fairly. A training-free representation, made of generic per-frame measurements summarized over fixed time windows and reduced with PCA, is compared with retrained and released encoders (BAMS, hBehaveMAE) under a preregistered protocol: frozen representations of equal size and one shared classifier. On CalMS21 it reaches 85.8 macro F1 against 82.4 for the best encoder, ties with four labelled videos, and leads when the annotator changes or new behaviors must be learned from a few videos; the reading holds for encoders retrained with three seeds. On the MABe22 mouse triplets it scores 83.7 against 80.3 for the released hBehaveMAE (gap +3.4, 95% interval +2.1 to +4.7). On a second species, the MABe22 fly groups, the same recipe scores 51.6 mean F1 over 50 tasks against 48.2 for BAMS, the best published method. On Shot7M2, the synthetic basketball benchmark built by hBehaveMAE's authors, it scores 68.8 against 64.7 for hBehaveMAE, the best method in that paper, though hBehaveMAE remains better on the shortest movements. Short time windows carry most of the result. Raw keypoints in each body's own frame, summarized over the same windows, already match or beat the encoders on both mouse datasets and on Shot7M2; on the fly groups they fall short, and the measurements add 5.3 points. On these benchmarks, current behavior encoders have yet to beat the hand-built features they learn from, and such baselines should be reported alongside them.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
authors: Alex Lin Wang; Linus Yifeng Tang; Dami Choi; Neil Chowdhury
abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

title: Training LLMs to Follow Reasoning Instructions with Minimal Edits
authors: Alexandra Yakovleva; Luat Gia Khoi Nguyen; Juho Kannala; Harri Valpola; Alexander Ilin
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on extended reasoning traces, yet the training signals used to shape this behavior remain coarse. Supervised fine-tuning on full trajectories forces the model to imitate an entire demonstration, overconstraining its output distribution, while trajectory-level reinforcement learning provides only weak credit assignment, rewarding or penalizing whole completions without identifying where they succeed or fail. We propose edit-based training, a general framework for learning from a model's own trajectories via localized textual corrections. Given a sampled completion, an editor identifies the first point of failure under a specified criterion and proposes a minimal replacement span. The model is then supervised only on these edited spans. By design, this concentrates supervision where the model's reasoning first breaks down and aims to preserve its existing reasoning patterns elsewhere. The method applies both offline and online, with the latter continually adapting supervision to the model's evolving failure modes. We instantiate this approach on reasoning instruction following with Qwen3-32B on the ReasonIF benchmark. Compared to full-trajectory imitation and trajectory-level reinforcement learning baselines, edit-based training substantially improves compliance with the reasoning instruction while largely preserving the model's skills on untargeted tasks. These results suggest that localized correction is an effective complement to these approaches for shaping how LLMs reason.

title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
authors: Timo Ropinski; Sebastian Kranz
abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
